2. Given natural numbers $m$ and $n$. On the table, there are two piles: the first pile has $n$ stones, and the second pile has $m$ stones. Petya and Vasya play the following game. Petya starts. In one move, one can split one of the existing piles on the table into several smaller piles. The player who cannot make a move loses. For which $m$ and $n$ can Petya ensure his victory regardless of Vasya's play?

(A. Khryabrov)
solution:
Answer: $m \neq n$.

Solution. If $m=n$, Vasya can repeat Petya's moves and, therefore, will always be able to make a move. Let $m>n$. Then Petya will break the pile with $m$ stones into a pile with $n$ stones and $m-n$ piles of one stone each. Nothing more can be done with the piles of one stone, so the game will continue with two piles of $n$ stones. Here, Petya will repeat Vasya's moves and, therefore, will always be able to make a move.

problem:
4. Let

$$
a_{1}=\frac{2}{3} \text { and } a_{n+1}=\frac{a_{n}}{4}+\sqrt{\frac{24 a_{n}+9}{253}}-\frac{9}{48}
$$

for every natural number $n$. Calculate the sum $a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+\ldots$.
solution:
Solution. Let $b_{n}=\sqrt{24 a_{n}+9}$. Then we have $a_{n}=\frac{b_{n}^{2}-9}{24}$, so the initial recurrence relation takes the form

$$
\frac{b_{n+1}^{2}-9}{24}=\frac{b_{n}^{2}-9}{24}+\frac{b_{n}}{16}-\frac{9}{48} \text {, i.e. }\left(2 b_{n+1}\right)^{2}=\left(b_{n}+3\right)^{2}
$$

Since $b_{n} \geq 0$, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, it follows that $2 b_{n+1}=b_{n}+3$. The last equality can be written as

$$
2\left(b_{n+1}-3\right)=b_{n}-3
$$

We set $c_{n}=b_{n}-3$ and get

$$
c_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2} c_{n} \text { and } c_{1}=b_{1}-3=\sqrt{24 a_{1}+9}-3=2
$$

Thus,

$$
c_{n}=\frac{1}{2^{n-2}}, \text { so } b_{n}=\frac{1}{2^{n-2}}+3 \text { and } a_{n}=\frac{1}{24} \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2 n-4}}+\frac{1}{2^{n}}
$$

Finally,

$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+\ldots=\frac{1}{24}\left(4+1+\frac{1}{4}+\ldots\right)+\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\ldots\right)=\frac{1}{24} \cdot \frac{4}{1-\frac{1}{4}}+\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{11}{9}
$$

problem: 7.1. In a hotel, rooms are arranged in a row in order from 1 to 10000. Masha and Alina checked into the hotel in two different rooms. The sum of the room numbers they are staying in is 2022, and the sum of the room numbers of all the rooms between them is 3033. In which room is Masha staying, if her room has a lower number than Alina's room?
solution:
Answer: 1009

Solution. If there is exactly one room between Masha's and Alina's rooms, then it is room number 3033, but then Masha's and Alina's rooms are 3032 and 3034, and their sum is not 2022.

Consider room B, whose number is 1 more than Masha's room. Also consider room V, whose number is 1 less than Alina's room. Note that the sum of the numbers of rooms B and V is also 2022, so there are at least three rooms between Alina and Masha.

If there are at least four rooms, then take rooms Γ and D adjacent to rooms B and V: M, B, Γ, .., D, V, A. The sum of the numbers of Γ and D is also 2022, but then the sum of the numbers between them is at least 4044, which is too many.

Therefore, there are exactly three rooms between Alina and Masha, the sum of the two outermost rooms is 2022, and the middle number is 1011. Then our numbers are: 1009, 1010, 1011, 1012, 1013. Masha's room number is 1009.

Then, when A and B are opened simultaneously, the total rate is $\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{15}=\frac{1}{6}$. Suppose A is opened for $a$ hours at the beginning, then B is opened for $b$ hours, and finally, both A and B are opened simultaneously for $7-a-b$ hours.
Thus: $\frac{1}{10} a+\frac{1}{15} b+\frac{1}{6}(7-a-b)=1$, simplifying to: $2 a+3 b=5$,
Since $a \geqslant 1, b \geqslant 1, \therefore a=1, b=1$,

3. Let $n$ be a given even number, and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$ be $n$ non-negative real numbers whose sum is 1. Find the maximum possible value of
$$
S=\sum_{1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n} \min \left\{(j-i)^{2},(n-j+i)^{2}\right\} a_{i} a_{j}
$$

(Fu Yunhao)
solution:
3. Solution 1 Let $n=2 k$.

When $a_{1}=a_{k+1}=\frac{1}{2}$, and the rest of $a_{i}$ are 0, $S=\frac{n^{2}}{16}$.
Let $\varepsilon=\cos \frac{2 \pi}{n}+\mathrm{i} \sin \frac{2 \pi}{n}$,
$$
z=a_{1} \varepsilon+a_{2} \varepsilon^{2}+\cdots+a_{n} \varepsilon^{n}.
$$

Then $0 \leqslant|z|^{2}=z \bar{z}$
$$
\begin{array}{l}
=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{j} \varepsilon^{j}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{j} \varepsilon^{-j}\right) \\
=\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{2}+\sum_{1 \leqslant i\sin \frac{2 \pi}{k}-\sin \frac{\pi}{k}>\cdots
$$
>\sin \frac{k \pi}{k}-\sin \frac{(k-1) \pi}{k},
$$

It is easy to see that equation (1) holds.
In summary, the maximum possible value is $\frac{n^{2}}{16}$.
Solution 2 Let $n=2 k$.
On one hand, when $a_{1}=a_{k+1}=\frac{1}{2}$, and the rest of $a_{i}$ are 0, $S=\frac{n^{2}}{16}$.
On the other hand, for any $1 \leqslant m \leqslant k$, we have
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left(\sum_{i=m}^{m+k-1} a_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{j=m+k}^{m+2 k-1} a_{j}\right) \\
\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{2 k} a_{i}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{4},
\end{array}
$$

where the indices are taken modulo $2 k$.
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Hence } \frac{n^{2}}{16}=\frac{k^{2}}{4} \\
\geqslant & k \sum_{m=1}^{k}\left(\left(\sum_{i=m}^{m+k-1} a_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{j=m+k}^{m+2 k-1} a_{j}\right)\right) \\
= & k \sum_{1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n} \min \{j-i, n-j+i\} a_{i} a_{j} \\
\geqslant & \sum_{1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n} \min \left\{(j-i)^{2},(n-j+i)^{2}\right\} a_{i} a_{j} .
\end{aligned}
$$

In summary, the maximum possible value is $\frac{n^{2}}{16}$.

problem: Which is the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $3^{2 n}-1$ is divisible by $2^{2010}$?
solution:
Solution. We will show that if $m$ is odd and $k$ is a positive integer, then $3^{2^{k} m}-1$ is divisible by exactly the $(k+2)$-th power of 2. If $k=1$, then

$$
\begin{gathered}
3^{2 m}-1=9^{m}-1=(8+1)^{m}-1= \\
=\left(8^{m}+\binom{m}{1} 8^{m-1}+\ldots+\binom{m}{m-2} 8^{2}+\binom{m}{m-1} 8+1\right)-1=8^{2} v+8 m
\end{gathered}
$$

which is indeed divisible by exactly the third power of 2. We can then prove by induction on $k$: if $k \geq 1$ and $3^{2^{k} m}-1=2^{k+2} \cdot(2 w+1)$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
3^{2^{k+1} m}-1 & =\left(3^{2^{k} m}-1\right) \cdot\left(3^{2^{k} m}+1\right)=2^{k+2}(2 w+1) \cdot\left(2^{k+2}(2 w+1)+2\right)= \\
& =2^{k+2}(2 w+1) \cdot 2\left(2^{k+1}(2 w+1)+1\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

which is divisible by exactly the $(k+3)$-th power of 2.

According to the proven results, $3^{2 n}-1$ is divisible by $2^{2010}$ if and only if $2 n$ is divisible by $2^{2008}$, i.e., $n$ is divisible by $2^{2007}$. The smallest such positive integer is therefore $n=2^{2007}$.

problem:
A right-angled triangle has one leg of $465 \mathrm{~m}$, and the acute angle adjacent to it is $51.6^{\circ}$. Provide approximate values rounded to meters for the other two sides without using a function table, by applying the approximate formula learned in problem 1151. - Calculate the sides precisely as well.[^0]


[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ K. M. L. $25(1962 / 12) 214$. p.
solution:
In the right-angled triangle $ABC$, let $AC = b = 465 \, \text{m}$, $\angle BAC = \alpha = 51.6^\circ$, $BC = a$, $AB = c$, and $\angle ABC = \beta = 38.4^\circ$. We denote the radian measure of the angles by $\alpha$ and $\beta$, which does not cause any confusion.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_d9615feaebf26de00626g-1.jpg?height=328&width=376&top_left_y=264&top_left_x=861)

I. Using the mentioned approximate formula for both acute angles:

$$
\frac{3a}{2c + b} = \alpha, \quad \frac{3b}{2c + a} = \beta
$$

we obtain a system of linear equations for $a$ and $c$:

$$
3a - 2\alpha c = \alpha b, \quad \beta a + 2\beta c = 3b
$$

From this, we get:

$$
a = \frac{\alpha}{\beta} \cdot \frac{\beta + 3}{\alpha + 3} \cdot b, \quad c = \frac{9 - \alpha \beta}{2\beta(\alpha + 3)} b,
$$

The values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ can be obtained with an error of $0.04\%$ using the approximation $\pi \approx 22/7$. On the other hand, the first significant digit of $a$ and $c$ is expected to be in the hundreds place, so we need to calculate to three significant figures. Therefore, in the initial steps of the preparatory calculations, we calculate to five, then only four significant figures:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\alpha \approx \frac{11 \cdot 51.6}{630}, \quad \beta \approx \frac{11 \cdot 38.4}{630} \\
a = \frac{51.6}{38.4} \cdot \frac{11 \cdot 38.4 + 1890}{11 \cdot 51.6 + 1890} \cdot 465 \approx \frac{119320}{94372} \cdot 465 \approx 1.264 \cdot 465 \approx 588 \, \text{m}, \\
c = \frac{9 \cdot 630^2 - 11^2 \cdot 51.6 \cdot 38.4}{2 \cdot 11 \cdot 38.4 (11 \cdot 51.6 + 1890)} \cdot 465 \approx \\
\approx \frac{3332300}{2076200} \cdot 465 \approx 1.605 \cdot 465 \approx 746 \, \text{m}
\end{gathered}
$$

II. Alternatively, using the function table, $a = b \tan \alpha \approx 465 \cdot 1.262 \approx 586.8 \, \text{m}$,

$$
c = \frac{b}{\cos \alpha} \approx \frac{465}{0.6211} \approx 1.610 \cdot 465 \approx 748.6 \, \text{m}
$$

According to these calculations, the error in neither of our calculations exceeds $0.5\%$.

Imre Bárány (Budapest-Mátyásföld, Corvin Mátyás g. I. o. t.)

Remarks. 1. It is sufficient to apply the approximate formula to the smaller angle - because this results in a smaller error - and we can replace the other equation with the Pythagorean theorem. This, however, leads to a quadratic equation, making the calculation more complex:

$$
\begin{array}{cl}
\beta a + 2 \beta c = 3b, & c^2 - a^2 = b^2 \\
a = \frac{b}{3\beta} \left(-3 \pm 2 \sqrt{9 - 3\beta^2}\right), & c = \frac{b}{3\beta} \left(6 \mp \sqrt{9 - 3\beta^2}\right)
\end{array}
$$

and we need to select the correct solution from the two. From this, we get $a \approx 586$ and $c \approx 747$, which indeed deviate even less from the exact values.

problem: A 10-member society has to pay $30 \mathrm{Ft}$ each for a common goal. Everyone only has paper money (in denominations of 20, 50, 100, and 500 Ft). What is the minimum amount of money the society has in total, if everyone can pay the 30 Ft and no one ends up owing anyone else?
solution: Since there is no 30 Ft note, everyone has money left, at least 20 Ft. Thus, everyone originally had at least 50 Ft, which totals 500 Ft. Those who have a 50 Ft note can only pay if there are also people in the group who pay with 20 Ft notes. Such a person must have at least 80 Ft, as they will receive at least 50 Ft back. A single such person is only sufficient if they have at least 180 Ft, in which case the group has at least 630 Ft. Two such people are also sufficient if they each have 80 Ft, since their 8 20 Ft notes are just enough for the other eight people who pay with 50 Ft notes. In this case, the group originally had a total of 560 Ft. In any other case, there is at least this much money together, since everyone has at least 50 Ft, but at least two people have at least 80 Ft.

problem:
15. (2001 China National Team Selection Test for IMO) Given an integer $n$ greater than 3, let real numbers $x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}, x_{n+1}, x_{n+2}$ satisfy the condition
$0<x_{1}<x_{2}<\cdots<x_{n}<x_{n+1}<x_{n+2}$.
Find the minimum value of $\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{x_{i+1}}{x_{i}}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{x_{j+2}}{x_{j+1}}\right)}{\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{x_{k+1} x_{k+2}}{x_{k+1}^{2}+x_{k} x_{k+2}}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{x_{l+1}^{2}+x_{l} x_{l+2}}{x_{l} x_{l+1}}\right)}$
and determine all real number sequences $x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}, x_{n+1}, x_{n+2}$ that achieve this minimum value.
solution:
15. (I) Let \( t_{i} = \frac{x_{i+1}}{x_{i}} (>1), 1 \leqslant i \leqslant n+1 \). The expression in the problem can be written as
\[
\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i+1}\right)}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{t_{i} t_{i+1}}{t_{i}+t_{i+1}}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}+t_{i+1}\right)\right)}.
\]

We observe that
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{t_{i} t_{i+1}}{t_{i}+t_{i+1}}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}+t_{i+1}\right)\right) = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i} - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{t_{i}^{2} + t_{i+1}}{}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}+t_{i+1}\right)\right) \\
= \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}+t_{i+1}\right)\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{t_{i}^{2}}{t_{i}+t_{i+1}}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}+t_{i+1}\right)\right) \\
\leqslant \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}+t_{i+1}\right)\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{t_{i}}{\sqrt{t_{i}+t_{i+1}}} \sqrt{t_{i}+t_{i+1}}\right)^{2} \\
= \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}\right)^{2} + \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i+1}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}\right)^{2} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i+1}\right).
\end{array}
\]

Therefore, for the real number sequence \( 00 \), we have
\[ x_{k} = t_{k \cdots 1} t_{k-2} \cdots t_{1}, a = a b^{k-1} c^{\frac{(k-1)(k-2)}{2}}, 2 \leqslant k \leqslant n+2. \]
Since \( x_{2} > x_{1} \), then \( b = \frac{x_{2}}{x_{1}} > 1 \).
Also, since \( t_{j} = b c^{j \cdot 1} > 1, 1 \leqslant j \leqslant n+1 \),
then \( c > \sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{b}} \left(\geqslant \sqrt[j]{\frac{1}{b}}, 1 \leqslant j \leqslant n+1\right) \).
(III) Conclusion:
(i) For the real number sequence \( x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}, x_{n+1}, x_{n+2} \) that meets the conditions, the minimum value of the expression in the problem is 1.
(ii) The conditions for the expression to achieve its minimum value are \( 00, b > 1, c > \sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{b}} \).

problem: 9.6. Twenty-five coins are arranged into piles as follows. First, they are arbitrarily divided into two groups. Then any of the existing groups is again divided into two groups, and so on until each group consists of one coin. Each time a group is divided into two, the product of the number of coins in the two resulting groups is recorded. What can the sum of all recorded numbers be?
solution:
Answer: 300.

Solution. First method. Let's represent the coins as points and connect each pair of points with a segment. We will get $\frac{25(25-1)}{2}$ $=300$ segments. With each division of one group of coins into two, we will erase all segments connecting points corresponding to coins that end up in different groups. Suppose at some step we divide the coins of one of the already existing groups into two groups of $x$ and $y$ coins. Then we erase $x y$ segments. This is the number we record. Thus, the sum of the recorded numbers is the total number of erased segments. Since there were initially 300 segments, and in the end, all segments are erased, the total number of erased segments is 300.

Second method. Consider the variable quantity $S$, equal at each moment to half the sum of the squares of the number of coins in the piles. Initially, $S=\frac{25^{2}}{2}=312.5$, and at the very end, $S=\frac{1^{2}+1^{2}+\ldots .+1^{2}}{2}=\frac{25}{2}=12.5$. If a pile with $x+y$ coins is divided into two piles of $x$ and $y$ coins, then $S$ decreases by $\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2}-$ $-\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2}=x y$. Thus, with each division, the quantity $S$ decreases by the next recorded number. Therefore, the sum of all recorded numbers is equal to the total decrease in the quantity $S$, which is 312.5 $-12.5=300$.

Third method. We will prove by induction that if there are initially $n$ coins, then the desired sum is $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

Base of induction. For $n=2$, after the first step, we get two piles with one coin each and record the number $1 \cdot 1=1$. Since the equality $\frac{2(2-1)}{2}=1$ is true, the statement is true for $n=2$.

Induction step. Assume the statement is true for all $n<k$ and prove that it is also true for $n=k$. Suppose on the first step $k$ coins are divided into two groups of $x$ and $y$ coins ( $k=x+y$ ). For $x$ and $y$ coins, the statement is true by the induction hypothesis.

If in such a division $x \geqslant 2$ and $y \geqslant 2$, then the recorded sum is

$$
x y+\frac{x(x-1)}{2}+\frac{y(y-1)}{2}=\frac{x^{2}-x+y^{2}-y+2 x y}{2}=\frac{(x+y)^{2}-(x+y)}{2}=\frac{k^{2}-k}{2}=\frac{k(k-1)}{2}
$$

If, however, $x=1$ and $y \geqslant 2$, then $k=y+1$ and the recorded sum in this case is $1 \cdot y+\frac{y(y-1)}{2}=\frac{(y+1)^{2}-(y+1)}{2}=$ $=\frac{k(k-1)}{2}$. According to the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is proven for any natural $n \geqslant 2$. In particular, for 25 coins, we get: $\frac{25(25-1)}{2}=300$.

problem:
6. Variant 1.

An artistic film with a duration of 192 minutes consists of four parts. It is known that the duration of any two parts differs by at least 6 minutes. What is the maximum duration that the shortest part can have? Express your answer in minutes.
solution:
Answer: 39.

Solution. Let the shortest part be $x$ minutes, then the second (in terms of duration) is no less than $x+6$, the third is no less than $x+12$, and the fourth is no less than $x+18$. Therefore, the entire film lasts no less than $4 x+36$ minutes. Solving the inequality $192 \geq 4 x+36$, we get $x \leq 39$. The durations of the parts being 39, 45, 51, and 57 minutes fit.

problem: Aerith picks five numbers and for every three of them, takes their product, producing ten products. She tells Bob that the nine smallest positive divisors of sixty are among her products. Can Bob figure out the last product?
solution:
Yes Bob can. Let the numbers be $v, w, x, y, z$ and let the missing product be $x y z$. The nine given products are $1,2,3,4,5,6,10,12,15$.

Partition these products into the three sequences

$$
s_{1}=(v y z, v z x, v x y), s_{2}=(w y z, w z x, w x y), s_{3}=(v w x, v w y, v w z)
$$

and call these sequences special. Note that $s^{\prime}=(y z, z x, x y)$ is directly proportional to the first two and inversely proportional to the last one. The multiples of 5 thus have to be in the same special sequence, WLOG $(5,10,15)$. This sequence is inversely proportional to at least one of other two special sequences, which would thus have to be a multiple of $(6,3,2)$. However, it cannot be $(6,3,2)$ itself as that would leave 1,4 , and 12 , which cannot form a special sequence. Thus, the multiple of $(6,3,2)$ has to be $(12,6,4)$, leaving $(1,2,3)$ as the final sequence. WLOG, we thus can get the equations

$((v y z, v z x, v x y),(w y z, w z x, w x y),(v w x, v w y, v w z))=((5,10,15),(1,2,3),(12,6,4))$.

We can then deduce $x y z=v y z \cdot w x z / v w z=5 \cdot 2 / 4=5 / 2$.

Indeed, $5 / 2$ is achieved by

$$
(v, w, x, y, z)=\left(2 \sqrt[3]{15}, \frac{2}{5} \sqrt[3]{15}, \sqrt[3]{15}, \frac{1}{2} \sqrt[3]{15}, \frac{1}{3} \sqrt[3]{15}\right)
$$

problem: Problem 11.3. There are 2001 towns in a country every one of which is connected with at least 1600 towns by direct bus line. Find the largest $n$ for which there exist $n$ towns any two of which are connected by direct bus line.
solution:
Solution: Let $S_{1}$ snd $S_{1}$ be two towns connected by direct bus line. If $k$ is the number of towns connected to both $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ by bus line then $(1599-k)+(1599-k)+k \leq 1999$ which implies that $k \geq 1198$. Therefore there exists town $S_{3}$ connected to both $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$. Further, let $k$ be the number of towns connected to all $S_{1}, S_{2}$ and $S_{3}$. Therefore $(1197-k)+(1598-k)+k \leq 1998$, so giving $k \geq 797$. Therefore there exists town $S_{4}$ connected to all $S_{1}, S_{2}$ and $S_{3}$. By analogy let $k$ be the number of towns connected to all $S_{1}, S_{2}, S_{3}$ and $S_{4}$. We have $(796-k)+(1597-k)+k \leq 1997$, which implies $k \geq 396$. Therefore there exists $S_{5}$ connected to all $S_{1}, S_{2}, S_{3}$ and $S_{4}$. For the number $n$ from the condition of the problem we obtain $n \geq 5$. We show that $n=5$. For, number the towns by $S_{1}, S_{2}, \ldots, S_{2001}$ and connect $S_{k}$ and $S_{m}$ with direct line for all $k$ and $m$ for which $k \not \equiv m(\bmod 5)$. Since $\left[\frac{2001}{5}\right]=400$, we have that each town is connested to 1600 or 1601 other towns, i.e. the condition of the problem is satisfied.

For arbitrary 6 towns the numbers of at least two are equal modulo 5 and therefore they are not connected to each other. Therefore $n<6$ and so $n=5$.

problem: 2. Consider the set $\{1,2,4,5,8,10,16,20,32,40,80,160\}$ and all its three-element subsets. Decide which are more numerous: the three-element subsets for which the product of their elements is greater than 2006, or those for which the product of their elements if less than 2006?
solution:
Solution. The given set is exactly the set of all (natural) divisors of the number $160=2^{5} \cdot 5$. We can group its elements into pairs in such a way that the product of the numbers in each pair equals 160 :

$$
1 \cdot 160=2 \cdot 80=4 \cdot 40=5 \cdot 32=8 \cdot 20=10 \cdot 16 \text {. }
$$

This means that if $A=\{a, b, c\}$ is a triple of mutually distinct divisors of 160 , then so is $A^{\prime}=\{160 / a, 160 / b, 160 / c\}$.

The product $a b c$ of the elements of the triple $A$ can be expressed in the form

$$
2^{k} 5^{l} \text {, where } k \in\{0,1,2, \ldots, 14\}, l \in\{0,1,2,3\} \text {. }
$$

(The number 160 has only two divisors which are multiples of $2^{5}$, hence in the prime factorization of the number $a b c$ there cannot appear the factor $2^{15}$.) It is not difficult to see that the largest natural number of the form (1) which is less than 2006 is the number $2000=2^{4} \cdot 5^{3}$, and the least natural number which is of the form (1) and is greater than 2006 is $2048=2^{11}$ (the number 2006 itself is not of the form (1)). At the same time, $2000 \cdot 2048=160^{3}$.

Consequently, if the product $a b c$ of the triple $A$ is less than 2006, then $a b c \leqslant 2000$ and the product $160^{3} /(a b c)$ of the corresponding triple $A^{\prime}$ is at least $160^{3} / 2000=2048$. Conversely, if the product $a b c$ of the triple $A$ is greater than 2006, then $a b c \geqslant 2048$ and the product of the triple $A^{\prime}$ is at most $160^{3} / 2048=2000$. In other words, the threeelement subsets whose product of elements is less than 2006 are exactly as numerous as the three-element subsets whose product of elements is greater than 2006 .

problem:
[ Convex Polygons ]

Can a convex irregular pentagon have exactly four sides of the same length and exactly four diagonals of the same length?

Can the fifth side of such a pentagon share a point with the fifth diagonal?

#
solution:
An example of a pentagon satisfying the condition of the problem is shown in the figure. Let us explain how it is constructed. Take an isosceles right triangle $EAB$, draw the perpendicular bisectors of the sides $EA$ and $AB$, and construct points $C$ and $D$ on them such that $ED = BC = AB$ (i.e., the lines $BC$ and $ED$ form angles of $30^{\circ}$ with the corresponding perpendicular bisectors). It is clear that $DE = BC = AB = EA = EB$.

Now let us prove that the fifth side and the fifth diagonal cannot have a common point. Suppose the fifth side $AB$ has a common point $A$ with the fifth diagonal. Then the fifth diagonal is either $AC$ or $AD$. Let's consider these two cases.

In the first case, $\triangle AED = \triangle CDE$, so under symmetry with respect to the perpendicular bisector of segment $ED$, point $A$ maps to point $C$. Point $B$ remains in place under this symmetry, as $BE = BD$. Therefore, segment $AB$ maps to $CB$, i.e., $AB = CB$. This is a contradiction.

In the second case, $\triangle ACE = \triangle EBD$, so under symmetry with respect to the angle bisector of $\angle AED$, segment $AB$ maps to $DC$, i.e., $AB = CD$. This is a contradiction.

4. Let $a, b, c$ and $d$ be real numbers greater than 1. Calculate the value of the expression

$$
a^{\left(\log _{b} c\right)-1} b^{\left(\log _{c} d\right)-1} c^{\left(\log _{d} a\right)-1} d^{\left(\log _{a} b\right)-1}
$$

if you know that $\log _{b} a \cdot \log _{d} c=1$
solution:
III/4. Let $S=a^{\left(\log _{b} c\right)-1} b^{\left(\log _{c} d\right)-1} c^{\left(\log _{d} a\right)-1} d^{\left(\log _{a} b\right)-1}$. We write $1=\log _{b} a \cdot \log _{d} c=$ $\frac{\log a \cdot \log c}{\log b \cdot \log d}$. Using this, we calculate

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \log (a b c d S)=\log \left(a^{\log _{b} c} b^{\log _{c} d} c^{\log _{d} a} d^{\log _{a} b}\right)= \\
& =\log a^{\log _{b} c}+\log b^{\log _{c} d}+\log c^{\log _{d} a}+\log d^{\log _{a} b}= \\
& =\log _{b} c \cdot \log a+\log _{c} d \cdot \log b+\log _{d} a \cdot \log c+\log _{a} b \cdot \log d= \\
& =\frac{\log c \cdot \log a}{\log b}+\frac{\log d \cdot \log b}{\log c}+\frac{\log a \cdot \log c}{\log d}+\frac{\log b \cdot \log d}{\log a}= \\
& =\frac{\log a \cdot \log c \cdot(\log b+\log d)}{\log b \cdot \log d}+\frac{\log b \cdot \log d \cdot(\log a+\log c)}{\log a \cdot \log c}= \\
& =\log a+\log b+\log c+\log d=\log (a b c d)
\end{aligned}
$$

from which it follows that $a b c d S=a b c d$ or $S=1$.

problem:
29.2.3 For any two elements $a=\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{2^{n}}\right)$ and $b=\left(b_{1}, b_{2}, \cdots, b_{2}{ }^{n}\right)$ in $S_{n}$, let
$$
d(a, b)=\sum_{i=1}^{i^{*}}\left|a_{i}-b_{i}\right| .
$$

If $A \subseteq S_{n}$, and for any two different elements $a, b$ in $A$, we have $d(a, b) \geqslant 2^{n-1}$, then $A$ is called a good subset. Find the maximum number of elements in a good subset of $S_{u}$.
solution:
If $a_{i} \neq b_{i}$, then $a$ and $b$ are said to have a different component at the $i$-th position. It is easy to see that $d(a, b)$ is the number of different component pairs in $a$ and $b$. If $A \subseteq S_{n}$, and any two different elements in $A$ contain at least $2^{n-1}$ different component pairs, then $A$ is called $n$-level good.
First, prove: If $A$ is $n$-level good, then $|A| \leqslant 2^{n+1}$.
In fact, if $|A| \geqslant 2^{n+1}+1$, then $A$ has at least $2^{n}+1$ elements with the same last bit. Without loss of generality, let $B \subseteq A, |B|=2^{n}+1$, and each element in $B$ has the last bit as 0.
Consider the total number of different component pairs $N$ among all elements in $B$.
On one hand, since any two different elements in $B$ have at least $2^{n-1}$ different component pairs, we have
$$
N \geqslant 2^{n-1} \cdot \mathrm{C}_{2^{n}+1}^{2} - 2^{n-1} \cdot 2^{n-1} \cdot (2^{n}+1).
$$

On the other hand, for the $i$-th component of elements in $B$ ($1 \leqslant i \leqslant 2^{n}-1$), let there be $x_{i}$ zeros and $2^{n}+1-x_{i}$ ones, then
$$
\begin{aligned}
N & = \sum_{i=1}^{2^{n}-1} x_{i} (2^{n}+1 - x_{i}) \leqslant \sum_{i=1}^{2^{n}-1} 2^{n-1} \cdot (2^{n-1} + 1) \\
& - 2^{n-1} (2^{n-1} + 1) (2^{n} - 1),
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $2^{n-1} \cdot (2^{n-1} + 1) \cdot (2^{n} - 1) \geqslant 2^{n-1} \cdot 2^{n-1} \cdot (2^{n} + 1)$, hence $0 \leqslant -1$, which is a contradiction!
Next, recursively construct an $n$-level good subset $A_{n}$ such that $|A_{n}| = 2^{n+1}$.
When $n=1$, take $A_{1} = \{(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)\}$.
Assume $A_{n}$ is an $n$-level good subset, and $|A_{n}| = 2^{n+1}$. For $a \in S_{n}, a = (a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{2}^{n})$, define
$$
a' = (1-a_{1}, 1-a_{2}, \cdots, 1-a_{2^{n}})_{\text{+ let }} A_{n+1} = \{a, a\} \text{ or } \{a, a'\} \mid a \in A_{n} \subseteq S_{n+1},
$$

Clearly,
$$
|A_{n+1}| = 2 |A_{n}| = 2^{n+2}.
$$

For different elements $a, b$ in $A_{n}$, it is easy to see:
$$
\begin{aligned}
d((b, b), (a, a')) & = 2^{n}, d((a, a), (b, b)) \\
& = 2 d(a, b) \geqslant 2 \cdot 2^{n-1} = 2^{n}, \\
d((a, a), (b, b')) & = 2^{n}, d((a, a'), (b, b')) \\
& = 2 d(a, b) \geqslant 2 \cdot 2^{n-1} = 2^{n},
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A_{n+1}$ is $(n+1)$-level good.
Thus, the maximum value of $|A|$ is $2^{n+1}$.

problem: 8.3. Given a parallelogram $A B C D, \angle D=100^{\circ}, B C=12$. On side $A D$ there is a point $L$ such that $\angle A B L=50^{\circ}, L D=4$. Find the length of $C D$.
solution:
Answer: 8.

Solution. By the property of a parallelogram, $\angle A B C=\angle D=100^{\circ}, A D=B C=12$ and $C D=A B$. Therefore, $\angle C B L=\angle A B C-\angle A B L=100^{\circ}-50^{\circ}=50^{\circ}$ and $A L=A D-L D=12-4=8$. Since $\angle A L B=\angle C B L$ (as alternate interior angles when $A D$ and $B C$ are parallel and $B L$ is the transversal) and $\angle C B L=\angle A B L=50^{\circ}$, we get that $\angle A L B=\angle A B L$, so triangle $A B L$ is isosceles and $A B=A L=8$. Therefore, $C D=A B=8$.

solution:
【Analysis】First, find the least common multiple of the periods of 2 jumps, 6 and 9, which is 18. In this cycle, there are 2 meetings. Finding the number of groups and the remainder can solve the problem.

【Solution】According to the problem, we know:

problem:
Shapovalov A.V.

Vasya wrote a correct statement:

"In this phrase $1 / 3$ of all digits are the digit 3, and $1 / 2$ of all digits are the digit $1$."

And Kolya wrote the phrase:

"In this phrase 1/... of all digits are the digit *, the fractions of digits * and * are equal and are 1/..., while the fraction of all other digits is $1 / \ldots$."

Insert three different digits in place of the asterisks, and three different numbers in place of the ellipses so that the statement is correct.
solution:
If any of the numbers replaced by ellipsis is at least three digits, then there are no fewer than 100 digits in this phrase, which is impossible (then one of the numbers consists of at least 30 digits, but then the total number of digits is no less than $10^{30}$, and so on, it is clear that this cannot be). Therefore, all numbers are either single-digit or double-digit, and the total number of digits is from 9 to 12.

The number of "1"s is no less than 4, their proportion is no less than $4 / 12 = 1 / 3$, so the denominator of the first fraction is a single-digit number, meaning there are fewer than 12 digits.

All denominators are divisors of the number of digits, greater than one. Therefore, the number of digits cannot be 11 (the number 11 has no single-digit divisors other than one), nor 9 (four terms of the form $1 / 3$ and $1 / 9$ will not sum to 1). Thus, the total number of digits is 10, and the proportion of the digit "1" is $1 / 2$. The other fractions can be equal to $1 / 5$ and $1 / 10$. The sum of the proportions must equal $1: 1 / 2 + 1 / 5 + 1 / 5 + 1 / 10 \cdot$

In the denominators, the digits 0, 2, and 5 each appear once. Any two can be mentioned explicitly, then their proportion will be $1 / 5$, and the proportion of the remaining single digit will be $\frac{1}{1} 10$.

## Answer

"In this phrase, 1/2 of all digits are the digit 1, the proportions of the digits 2 and 5 are the same and equal to 1/5, and the proportion of all other digits is $1 / 10$

(or "...the proportions of the digits 0 and 2 are the same..." or "...the proportions of the digits 0 and 5 are the same...")."

4. Given a polynomial of degree 2022 with integer coefficients and leading coefficient 1. What is the maximum number of roots it can have on the interval $(0,1)$?

(A. Kanel-Belov)
solution:
Answer: 2021

Solution. If the interval $(0,1)$ contains all 2022 roots of the polynomial, then by Vieta's theorem, the constant term of the polynomial must be equal to their product, and thus will also lie in the interval $(0,1)$ and will not be an integer. We will prove that the polynomial $P(x)=x^{2022}+(1-$ $4042 x)(3-4042 x) \ldots(4041-4042 x)$ can serve as an example. Notice that for all $k=0,1, \ldots, 2021$, the number $P\left(\frac{2 k}{4042}\right)=\left(\frac{2 k}{4042}\right)^{n}+(-1)^{k}(2 k-1)!!(4041-2 k)!!$ is positive for even $k$ and negative for odd $k$. Thus, on the interval $(0,1)$, the polynomial $P(x)$ changes sign at least 2021 times, and therefore has at least 2021 roots.

Given $x \geqslant 0, y \geqslant 0$, and $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$, then the maximum value of $x(x+y)$ is
solution:
9. $\frac{\sqrt{2}+1}{2}$.

Let $x=\cos \alpha, y=\sin \alpha, \alpha \in\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, then
$$
\begin{aligned}
x(x+y) & =\cos \alpha(\cos \alpha+\sin \alpha) \\
& =\sqrt{2} \cos \alpha \sin \left(\alpha+\frac{\pi}{4}\right) . \\
& =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left[\sin \left(2 \alpha+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)+\sin \frac{\pi}{4}\right] \\
& \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left(1+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)-\frac{\sqrt{2}+1}{2} .
\end{aligned}
$$

When $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{8}$, the equality holds. Therefore, the maximum value of $x(x+y)$ is $\frac{\sqrt{2}+1}{2}$.

problem: 29. [23] Let $P_{1}(x), P_{2}(x), \ldots, P_{k}(x)$ be monic polynomials of degree 13 with integer coefficients. Suppose there are pairwise distinct positive integers $n_{1}, n_{2}, \ldots, n_{k}$ for which, for all positive integers $i$ and $j$ less than or equal to $k$, the statement " $n_{i}$ divides $P_{j}(m)$ for every integer $m$ " holds if and only if $i=j$. Compute the largest possible value of $k$.
solution:
Answer: 144
Solution: We first consider which integers can divide a polynomial $P_{i}(x)$ for all $x$. Assume that $c \mid P_{i}(x)$ for all $x$. Then, $c$ must also divide the finite difference $Q(x)=Q_{i}(x+1)-Q_{i}(x)$. Since $Q_{i}(x)$ is degree 13 and monic, the leading term of $Q(x)$ is the leading term of $(x+1)^{13}-x^{13}$, which is $13 x^{12}$.
Continuing this process finding finite differences, we see that $c$ must divide $R(x)=Q(x+1)-Q(x)$, which has a leading term $13 \cdot 12 x^{11}$. At the end, we will see that $c \mid 13$ !, so these are the only possible values of $c$. To show that all of these values of $c$ work, consider the polynomial $P_{i}(x)=x(x+1) \cdots(x+$ 12) $+c$. It can be easily seen that the product of thirteen consecutive integers is always divisible by 13 !, so this polynomial is always divisible by $c$ and nothing more, as $P_{i}(0)=c$.
Now, we find the maximum possible value of $k$. Note that if two polynomials have values of $n_{i}$ and $n_{j}$, we cannot have $n_{i} \mid n_{j}$ since then $n_{i} \mid P_{j}(x)$ for all $x$. Hence, we wish to find as many values of $c \mid 13$ ! as possible that do not divide each other.
We prime factorize $13!=2^{10} \cdot 3^{5} \cdot 5^{2} \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13$. We claim that the maximum number of polynomials is $k=144$. This is a maximum since there are $6 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2=144$ odd factors of 13 !; and if two values $n_{i}$ and $n_{j}$ have the same odd component by the Pigeonhole Principle, then either $\frac{n_{i}}{n_{j}}$ or $\frac{n_{j}}{n_{i}}$ is a power of 2. In addition, $k=144$ is attainable by taking $2^{a} \cdot 3^{b} \cdot 5^{c} \cdot 7^{d} \cdot 11^{e} \cdot 13^{f}$ for $a+b+c+d+e+f=10$, in which there is exactly one solution for a for each of the 144 valid quintuples $(b, c, d, e, f)$. Hence, $k=144$ is the maximum.

problem:
G3. A circle $\omega$ of radius 1 is given. A collection $T$ of triangles is called good, if the following conditions hold:
(i) each triangle from $T$ is inscribed in $\omega$;
(ii) no two triangles from $T$ have a common interior point.

Determine all positive real numbers $t$ such that, for each positive integer $n$, there exists a good collection of $n$ triangles, each of perimeter greater than $t$.
solution:
Answer: $t \in(0,4]$.
Solution. First, we show how to construct a good collection of $n$ triangles, each of perimeter greater than 4 . This will show that all $t \leqslant 4$ satisfy the required conditions.

Construct inductively an $(n+2)$-gon $B A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{n} C$ inscribed in $\omega$ such that $B C$ is a diameter, and $B A_{1} A_{2}, B A_{2} A_{3}, \ldots, B A_{n-1} A_{n}, B A_{n} C$ is a good collection of $n$ triangles. For $n=1$, take any triangle $B A_{1} C$ inscribed in $\omega$ such that $B C$ is a diameter; its perimeter is greater than $2 B C=4$. To perform the inductive step, assume that the $(n+2)$-gon $B A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{n} C$ is already constructed. Since $A_{n} B+A_{n} C+B C>4$, one can choose a point $A_{n+1}$ on the small arc $\widetilde{C A_{n}}$, close enough to $C$, so that $A_{n} B+A_{n} A_{n+1}+B A_{n+1}$ is still greater than 4 . Thus each of these new triangles $B A_{n} A_{n+1}$ and $B A_{n+1} C$ has perimeter greater than 4 , which completes the induction step.

We proceed by showing that no $t>4$ satisfies the conditions of the problem. To this end, we assume that there exists a good collection $T$ of $n$ triangles, each of perimeter greater than $t$, and then bound $n$ from above.
Take $\varepsilon>0$ such that $t=4+2 \varepsilon$.

Claim. There exists a positive constant $\sigma=\sigma(\varepsilon)$ such that any triangle $\Delta$ with perimeter $2 s \geqslant 4+2 \varepsilon$, inscribed in $\omega$, has area $S(\Delta)$ at least $\sigma$.
Proof. Let $a, b, c$ be the side lengths of $\Delta$. Since $\Delta$ is inscribed in $\omega$, each side has length at most 2. Therefore, $s-a \geqslant(2+\varepsilon)-2=\varepsilon$. Similarly, $s-b \geqslant \varepsilon$ and $s-c \geqslant \varepsilon$. By Heron's formula, $S(\Delta)=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)} \geqslant \sqrt{(2+\varepsilon) \varepsilon^{3}}$. Thus we can set $\sigma(\varepsilon)=\sqrt{(2+\varepsilon) \varepsilon^{3}}$.

Now we see that the total area $S$ of all triangles from $T$ is at least $n \sigma(\varepsilon)$. On the other hand, $S$ does not exceed the area of the disk bounded by $\omega$. Thus $n \sigma(\varepsilon) \leqslant \pi$, which means that $n$ is bounded from above.

Comment 1. One may prove the Claim using the formula $S=\frac{a b c}{4 R}$ instead of Heron's formula.
Comment 2. In the statement of the problem condition (i) could be replaced by a weaker one: each triangle from $T$ lies within $\omega$. This does not affect the solution above, but reduces the number of ways to prove the Claim.

problem: Task 10.3. Determine all natural numbers $n$ that have exactly $\sqrt{n}$ natural divisors (including 1 and the number $n$ itself).
solution:
Answer: 1 and 9.

Solution. First, note that $n=1$ works, and we will assume that $n \geqslant 2$. Second, from the condition it follows that $n=k^{2}$ for some natural number $k$. The squares of natural numbers have an odd number of divisors, since all divisors, except the base of the square, are paired as $d$ and $n / d$. Thus, $k$ is an odd number greater than 1. Let $k=2 m+1$ for some natural number $m$. The number $n$ has $m$ divisors less than $k$, and $m$ divisors greater than $k$, and all divisors are odd. This means that $n$ is divisible by all odd natural numbers less than $k$, since there are exactly $m$ of them.

In particular, $k^{2}$ is divisible by $k-2$. Since $k^{2}-4=(k-2)(k+2)$ is also divisible by $k-2$, the difference $4=k^{2}-\left(k^{2}-4\right)$ is divisible by the number $k-2$. It remains to note that $k-2$ is an odd divisor of the number 4, that is, $k-2=1$, from which $k=3$ and $n=9$.

## Criteria

Authors: Kanel-Belov A.Ya., Anniyev S.S.

Does there exist a natural number divisible by 1998, the sum of whose digits is less than 27?
solution:
If a number is divisible by 1998, then it is also divisible by 999. We will show that there does not exist a number divisible by 999 whose sum of digits is less than 27.

We will divide the decimal representation of the number into groups of three digits from right to left (the last group may consist of one or two digits). We will then sum these groups. The original number is divisible by 999 if and only if the resulting sum is divisible by 999 (see the solution to problem 78550).

Consider a number divisible by 999, divide it into groups of three digits, and compute the sum of these groups. If the new number is greater than 1000, we will again divide it into groups of three digits and compute the sum, and so on, until we get a number less than 1000. This will happen because the number decreases with each operation. Indeed, if \(a_{1}, \ldots, a_{k}\) are non-negative integers, \(a_{k} \neq 0\) and \(k \geq 1\), then \(a_{0} + 1000 a_{1} + \ldots + 1000^{k} a_{k} > a_{0} + a_{1} + \ldots + a_{k}\). Thus, after several operations, we will obtain a positive number less than 1000 that is divisible by 999, so it will be equal to 999.

The sum of the digits of the number 999 is 27. It is sufficient to prove that the sum of the digits does not increase during our operations. When we split the number into groups of three digits, the sum of the digits does not change. We will show that the sum of the digits does not increase when we add them. Indeed, let \(S(X)\) denote the sum of the digits of the number \(X\). From the addition algorithm, it is clear that \(S(X+Y) = S(X) + S(Y) - 9P(X, Y)\), where \(P(X, Y)\) is the number of carries when adding \(X\) and \(Y\) in a column. Therefore,

\(S(X+Y) \leq S(X) + S(Y)\)

problem:
Task 3. Find all triples of real numbers $(x, y, z)$ that satisfy

$$
x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+1=x y+y z+z x+|x-2 y+z| .
$$
solution:
Solution I. We rewrite the given equation as

$$
\frac{1}{2} x^{2}-x y+\frac{1}{2} y^{2}+\frac{1}{2} y^{2}-y z+\frac{1}{2} z^{2}+\frac{1}{2} z^{2}-z x+\frac{1}{2} x^{2}+1=|x-2 y+z|,
$$

or equivalently as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(x-y)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(y-z)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(z-x)^{2}+1=|(x-y)+(z-y)|.
$$

Now substitute $a=x-y$ and $b=z-y$. Then $x-z=a-b$, so we get

$$
\frac{1}{2} a^{2}+\frac{1}{2} b^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(a-b)^{2}+1=|a+b|
$$

From $(a-b)^{2} \geq 0$ it follows that $a^{2}-2 a b+b^{2} \geq 0$, so $2 a^{2}+2 b^{2} \geq a^{2}+b^{2}+2 a b$, which means that $a^{2}+b^{2} \geq \frac{(a+b)^{2}}{2}$ with equality if and only if $a=b$. Of course, $(a-b)^{2} \geq 0$ also holds. Therefore,

$$
|a+b|=\frac{1}{2} a^{2}+\frac{1}{2} b^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(a-b)^{2}+1 \geq \frac{(a+b)^{2}}{4}+1
$$

Now write $c=|a+b|$, then we have

$$
c \geq \frac{c^{2}}{4}+1
$$

This can be rewritten as $c^{2}-4 c+4 \leq 0$, or $(c-2)^{2} \leq 0$. Since the left side is a square, equality must hold, so $c=2$. Furthermore, equality must also hold in our earlier estimate, so $a=b$. Substituting this into (2) gives $a^{2}+1=2$, so $a= \pm 1$. Thus, we find the triples $(y+1, y, y+1)$ and $(y-1, y, y-1)$ for any $y \in \mathbb{R}$. Substituting these triples into equation (1) (which is equivalent to the original equation) shows that these triples are indeed solutions for all $y \in \mathbb{R}$. Therefore, all solutions are given by $(y+1, y, y+1)$ and $(y-1, y, y-1)$ with $y \in \mathbb{R}$.

problem:
Problem 6.8. There are exactly 120 ways to color five cells in a $5 \times 5$ table so that each column and each row contains exactly one colored cell.

There are exactly 96 ways to color five cells in a $5 \times 5$ table without a corner cell so that each column and each row contains exactly one colored cell.

How many ways are there to color five cells in a $5 \times 5$ table without two corner cells so that each column and each row contains exactly one colored cell?
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_4984b677816e04f7f1c9g-18.jpg?height=258&width=1008&top_left_y=530&top_left_x=220)
solution:
Answer: 78.

Solution. Consider the colorings of a $5 \times 5$ table described in the problem (i.e., such that in each column and each row exactly one cell is colored).

For convenience, let's introduce some notations. Let the top-left corner cell of the $5 \times 5$ table be called $A$, and the bottom-right corner cell be called $B$. Suppose that among the colorings of the first table, exactly $a$ have the cell $A$ colored, and exactly $b$ have the cell $B$ colored. Clearly, $a=b$ due to symmetry.

Notice that the number of colorings of the second table is equal to the number of colorings of the first table where the cell $A$ is not colored. The number of colorings of the third table is equal to the number of colorings of the first table where neither $A$ nor $B$ is colored. To find this, we subtract from 120 the number of colorings of the first table where $A$ or $B$ is colored. To count the number of such colorings, we add $a$ and $b$, and then subtract what has been counted twice - the ways where both $A$ and $B$ are colored.

All colorings of the first table can be divided into two types: those in which the cell $A$ is colored, and those in which it is not. This leads to the equation $120=a+96$, i.e., $a=24$. Then $b=24$ as well.

The number of colorings where both $A$ and $B$ are colored is the same as the number of ways to color the central $3 \times 3$ square. It is easy to see that there are exactly $3!=6$ such ways (to choose the colored cell in its top row, there are 3 ways, in the middle row - 2 ways, and in the bottom row - 1 way).

Thus, the answer to the problem is the number $120-(24+24-6)=78$.

problem:
## Exercise 5

Determine all non-constant polynomials $X^{n}+a_{1} X^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1} X+a_{n}$, with integer coefficients, whose roots are exactly the numbers $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n-1}, a_{n}$ (with multiplicity).
solution:
Solution. Let $P(X)=X^{n}+a_{1} X^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1} X+a_{n}$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Then $P(X)$ is a solution to the problem if and only if

$$
P(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(X-a_{i}\right)
$$

First, suppose that $a_{n}=0$. Let $i$ be minimal such that $a_{n-i} \neq 0$. Then we have $P(X)=X^{i}\left(X^{n-i}+a_{1} X^{n-i-1}+\cdots+a_{n-i-1}\right)$, and thus (5) is satisfied if and only if $Q(X)=X^{n-i}+a_{1} X^{n-i-1}+\cdots+a_{n-i-1}$ is constant or is itself a solution to the problem. The first case corresponds to $P(X)=X^{n}$, which is indeed a solution.

We will therefore assume in what follows that $P(X)$ is a solution with $a_{n} \neq 0$. Under these conditions, we immediately deduce that we cannot have $X+a_{1}=X-a_{1}$ and thus there is no polynomial of degree 1 that is a solution. We therefore assume that $n \geq 2$. From $P(0)=a_{n}=(-1)^{n} \prod_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}$, we then deduce that

$$
(-1)^{n} \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} a_{i}=1
$$

And, since the $a_{i}$ are integers, we have $a_{i}=1$ or $a_{i}=-1$ for all $i \leq n-1$. Let $k$ be the number of them that are -1 (and thus $0 \leq k \leq n-1$). We can note that (6) then shows that $k$ and $n$ have the same parity. The relations between coefficients and roots lead to

$$
-a_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}=a_{n}+(n-1-k)-k
$$

from which we get

$$
a_{n}=2 k-n \quad \text { or } \quad a_{n}=2 k-n+2
$$

For $n=2$, since $a_{2} \neq 0$ and $k$ must be even and not exceed 1, the only possibility is $k=0, a_{1}=1, a_{2}=-2$, and thus $P(X)=X^{2}+X-2=(X-1)(X+2)$, which is indeed a solution.

We now assume that $n \geq 3$. Then

$$
a_{2}=\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n} a_{i} a_{j}=a_{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} a_{i}+\frac{k(k-1)}{2}+\frac{(n-1-k)(n-2-k)}{2}-k(n-1-k)
$$

and thus

$$
2 a_{2}=2 a_{n}(n-1-2 k)+n^{2}+4 k^{2}-4 k n-3 n+4 k+2
$$

Given (7), two cases arise:

- If $a_{n}=2 k-n$: From (8), we get $(n-2 k)^{2}+n=2-2 a_{2}$, with $a_{2}=1$ or $a_{2}=-1$. Therefore, $a_{2}=-1$ and, since $n-2 k=-a_{n} \neq 0$, the only possibility is $n=3$ and $(n-2 k)^{2}=1$. From $k \leq n-1$ and the same parity as $n$, we deduce that $k=1$, then $a_{1}=1$ and $a_{3}=-1$, hence $P(X)=X^{3}+X^{2}-X-X=(X+1)^{2}(X-1)$, which is indeed a solution.
- If $a_{n}=2 k-n+2$: As above, we get this time

$$
(n-2 k-2)^{2}+n=2-2 a_{2}
$$

and thus $a_{2}=-1, n=3, k=1, a_{1}=1, a_{3}=1$, hence $P(X)=X^{3}+X^{2}-X+1 \neq (X-1)^{2}(X+1)$, which is not a solution.

In conclusion, the solutions to the problem are the polynomials $P(X)=X^{n}$ for $n \geq 1$, $P(X)=X^{n}\left(X^{2}+X-2\right)$ or $P(X)=X^{n}\left(X^{3}+X^{2}-X-X\right)$ for $n \geq 0$.

problem: 10. Given $A_{1}, A_{2}, \cdots, A_{n}$ are $n$ non-empty subsets of the set $A=\{1,2,3, \cdots, 10\}$, if for any $i, j \in$ $\{1,2,3, \cdots, n\}$, we have $A_{i} \cup A_{j} \neq A$, then the maximum value of $n$ is $\qquad$.
solution:
Let $m$ be the maximum value of $n$ that satisfies the condition. Since the set $A$ has $2^{10}-1=1023$ non-empty subsets, each subset $A_{i}$ and its complement $\complement_{A} A_{i}$ can be grouped together, resulting in 512 groups, with $A$ being a single group. Clearly, $A$ cannot be taken, so at most 511 non-empty subsets $A_{i}$ can be taken, hence $m \leqslant 511$.
On the other hand, all 511 non-empty subsets of the set $B=\{1,2, \cdots, 9\}$ clearly satisfy the condition, so $m \geqslant 511$. In conclusion, the maximum value of $n$ is 511.

(x + 1)(y + 1)(z + 1) = 244

Now from $244 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 61$ we get that $(x + 1, y + 1, z + 1)$ is one of the triples $(2,2,61),(2,61,2),(61,2,2)$. Therefore, the desired triples are $(1,1,60)$, $(1,60,1),(60,1,1)$.

problem: Problem 2. The lighthouse keeper of Finisterre has received communication that there will be a power outage and he must operate the lighthouse using a diesel generator. This generator consumes 6 liters of diesel per hour and an additional half liter each time it needs to be started (initially, it is off). During the 10 hours of the night, the lighthouse cannot be out of service for more than 10 minutes at a time. And when it is operating, it must do so for at least 15 minutes at a time. How many liters of diesel does he need, at a minimum, to comply with the lighthouse operating regulations?
solution:
## Solution:

The best way to save fuel is to make 10-minute stops (longer stops are not allowed). With each stop, we save 1 liter of diesel, but we spend half a liter to restart the generator. It is obvious that, in principle, the best savings strategy involves alternating 15-minute operating periods (shorter periods are not allowed) with 10-minute stops. In each "start-15 minutes operating-10 minutes stop" process, 0.5 + 0.25 * 6 = 2 liters of diesel are consumed. To complete the 10 hours of night, we need 600 / 25 = 24 of these processes, so it seems that the minimum amount of fuel required is 48 liters. However, there is a way to save an additional half liter. When the 10 hours of night begin, we can go 10 minutes without turning on the lighthouse. If we then chain 23 "start-15 minutes operating-10 minutes stop" processes, we complete 10 hours minus 15 minutes. We would have to restart the generator and run it for another 15 minutes, consuming 48 liters again. However, if, for example, we make one of the operating periods 30 minutes and "save" the 10-minute intermediate stop for the last 10 minutes of the night, the operating time is the same but we save one start, i.e., half a liter of diesel. Only 47.5 liters are needed.

problem: 11. (12 points) A store has 89 gold coins waiting to be sold, numbered from $1 \sim 89$, each priced at 30 yuan, and only one of them is a “lucky coin”. Feifei can choose some of the numbers and ask the honest clerk: “Is the lucky coin’s number among them?”. If the answer is “yes”, Feifei needs to pay 20 yuan for the consultation fee; if the answer is “no”, Feifei needs to pay 10 yuan for the consultation fee. Of course, she can also choose not to ask any questions and directly buy some of the coins. Feifei needs to pay at least $\qquad$ yuan to ensure she can definitely get the lucky coin.
solution:
【Analysis】Analysis: Consider a more general case: there are $n$ gold coins for sale, and only one of them is a lucky coin.
（1）Even when $n=2$, if Feifei does not ask any questions and directly buys the two gold coins, she will of course get the lucky coin, but she will need to pay 60 yuan in total; if Feifei asks about a certain number, to ensure she gets the gold coin, she needs to pay $20+30=50$ yuan. This means that no matter what $n$ is, Feifei needs to clearly identify which one is the lucky coin before making a purchase to be the most cost-effective. Therefore: The money Feifei needs to pay = the consulting fee for identifying the lucky coin + the purchase fee for buying the lucky coin
（2）Next, we explore the pattern to find out: the consulting fee $m$ that Feifei needs to pay to identify the lucky coin from $n$ gold coins for sale (Note: it either remains unchanged or increases by 10)
\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline \begin{tabular}{l} 
Gold \\
Coins $n$ 
\end{tabular} & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & $\cdots$ \\
\hline \begin{tabular}{l} 
Consulting \\
Fee $m$ yuan
\end{tabular} & 20 & 30 & 40 & 40 & 50 & 50 & 50 & $\cdots$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

By finding the pattern, we discover:
$2 \times 10$ yuan consulting fee, can identify the lucky coin from at most 2 gold coins, denoted as $E$ (2) $=2$; $3 \times 10$ yuan consulting fee, can identify the lucky coin from at most 3 gold coins, denoted as $E$ (3) $=3$; $4 \times 10$ yuan consulting fee, can identify the lucky coin from at most 5 gold coins, denoted as $E$ (4) $=5$; $5 \times 10$ yuan consulting fee, can identify the lucky coin from at most 8 gold coins, denoted as $E \quad(5)=8$;

Listing $2,3,5,8$ separately, we find the characteristic of this sequence: starting from the 3rd term, each term equals the sum of the two preceding terms. If we continue this sequence, it becomes:
$2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89 \cdots$ Up to this point, the answer is: consulting fee 100 yuan + purchase fee 30 yuan $=130$ yuan.
（3）Below is an explanation of the pattern discovered in (2):
We re-examine the meaning of $E(m)$: a consulting fee of $10 \mathrm{~m}$ yuan can identify the lucky coin from $E(m)$ or fewer gold coins, but cannot identify the lucky coin from more than $E(m)$ gold coins.

When $m \geqslant 3$, Feifei divides the gold coins into two piles and asks a question about the first pile.
If the answer is "yes," Feifei needs to pay 20 yuan first, and the remaining $10 \times(m-2)$ yuan consulting fee is used to identify the lucky coin from the first pile, which means the number of gold coins in the first pile cannot exceed $E(m-2)$; if the answer is "no," Feifei needs to pay 10 yuan first, and the remaining $10 \times(m-1)$ yuan consulting fee is used to identify the lucky coin from the second pile, which means the number of gold coins in the second pile cannot exceed $E(m-1)$ - so $E(m) \leqslant E(m-2) + E(m-1)$;

On the other hand, when there are $E(m-2) + E(m-1)$ gold coins for sale, Feifei divides the gold coins into the first pile of $E(m-2)$ and the second pile of $E(m-1)$, and then asks a question about the first pile, which means $10 m$ yuan can be used to identify the lucky coin from $E(m-2) + E(m-1)$.

Therefore, $E(m) = E(m-2) + E(m-1)$.
【Solution】Solution: From the analysis, we get the pattern
\begin{tabular}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline \begin{tabular}{l} 
Gold \\
Coins $n$ 
\end{tabular} & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & $\cdot$ & 89 & $\cdot$ \\
\hline \begin{tabular}{l} 
Consulting \\
Fee $m$ yuan
\end{tabular} & 20 & 30 & 40 & 40 & 50 & 50 & 50 & $\cdot$ & 100 & $\cdot$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
$100 + 30 = 130$ (yuan)
Therefore: The answer is 130.

problem: There is a circle $k$ and points $K$ and $L$ inside it. Construct a quadrilateral whose vertices are on $k$, the intersection of its diagonals is $K$, and the intersection of the lines connecting the midpoints of its opposite sides is $L$
solution:
Consider the problem solved and let the sought quadrilateral be $ABCD$, with the intersection point of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ being $K$, and the midpoints of sides $AB$ and $CD$, as well as $BC$ and $AD$, being $F_1, F_3, F_2, F_4$ respectively. The lines connecting these midpoints, $F_1F_3$ and $F_2F_4$, intersect at point $L$. Furthermore, let $k$ be a circle with center $O$ and the midpoints of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ be $M$ and $N$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_52da6f048cded97a60acg-1.jpg?height=531&width=593&top_left_y=274&top_left_x=755)

It is known that the quadrilateral $F_1F_2F_3F_4$ (for any quadrilateral $ABCD$) is a parallelogram, and $L$ bisects the segments $F_1F_3$ and $F_2F_4$. Therefore, $L$ also bisects the segment $MN$, because $M$ and $N$ form parallelograms with the pairs of points $F_1, F_3$ and $F_2, F_4$ respectively. For example, the segments $F_2M$ and $NF_4$, being the midlines parallel to the common side $AB$ in triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$, are parallel and equal, making $F_2MF_4N$ a parallelogram, and $L$ is its center through the diagonal $F_2F_4$.

Moreover, $KM$ and $KN$, being the lines of the chords $AC$ and $BD$, are perpendicular to $OM$ and $ON$ respectively, so $M$ and $N$ are points on the Thales circle $k'$ with diameter $KO$ (even if $M$ and $N$ coincide with $O$), and thus $L$ is the midpoint of the chord in $k'$.

Based on this, the construction is as follows: take the chord of the circle $k'$ with diameter $OK$ whose midpoint is $L$; the lines connecting the endpoints of this chord to $K$ are the diagonals of the sought quadrilateral.

Indeed, the vertices of $ABCD$ lie on $k$, the intersection of the diagonals is $K$, and the point $L$ bisects the segment determined by the midpoints $M$ and $N$ of the diagonals, so it lies on the diagonals $F_1M$ and $F_3N$ of the parallelograms $F_1MF_3N$ and $F_2MF_4N$.

The construction steps are generally unique. If $K \not\equiv O$ and $k'$ contains $L$, but $L$ is not the center $O'$ of $k'$, then there is one solution. If $L \equiv O'$, then there are infinitely many solutions, all of which have perpendicular diagonals. If $k'$ passes through $L$, then the quadrilateral degenerates because the diagonals coincide. A degenerate case also occurs when $K \equiv O$: the radius of $k'$ is 0, so a solution is only possible if $L \equiv K \equiv O$, in which case any rectangle inscribed in $k$ can be considered a solution.

Julia Szabó (Kecskemét, public school III. grade)

Note. According to two solutions: "The problem cannot be solved due to insufficient data, as four data points are needed to construct a cyclic quadrilateral, but here there are only three: $k, K, L$." This is incorrect; the quoted statement refers to metric (segment and angle) data, whereas here we constructed using positional data; furthermore, $k$ counts as two data points: its center and radius.

problem: 5. Determine the largest number obtained by deleting 100 digits from the number 12345678910111213...99100, whose digits are the natural numbers from 1 to 100 arranged from left to right.
solution:
Solution. There are 0 one-digit numbers. From 10 to 99, there are 90 two-digit numbers. Thus, the given number has $9 + 2 \cdot 90 + 3 = 192$ digits. After deleting 100 digits, we need to obtain a 92-digit number. For any two numbers with the same number of digits, the number with the larger first digit is greater. Clearly, the number we are looking for should start with as many 9s as possible. Therefore, we first delete the first 8 digits. Then we delete the sequence of digits $101112 \ldots 181$, which consists of $9 \cdot 2 + 1 = 19$ digits. Similarly, we delete the sequences 202122...282, 303132...383, 404142...484. Thus, $8 + 19 \cdot 4 = 84$ digits have been deleted, and the number obtained is 999950515253...99100. We need to delete 16 more digits. If we delete the sequence 505152...57, which consists of 16 digits, we get the number 9999958596061...99100. However, the largest number is obtained by deleting the sequence 505152...565, which consists of 15 digits, so that the next digit we delete is not 7 but 5 from 58. Thus, the desired number is 9999978596061...99100.

problem: 7. Given the sequence $\left\{a_{n}\right\}$, where $a_{1}=2, a_{n+1}=\frac{2 a_{n}+6}{a_{n}+1}$, then $a_{n}=$
solution:
7. $\frac{2+3 \times(-4)^{n}}{(-4)^{n}-1}$

Let $f(x)=\frac{2 x+6}{x+1}$, solving the equation $f(x)=x$ yields the fixed points of $f(x)$ as -2 and 3.
Let $b_{n}=a_{n}-3, c_{n}=a_{n}+2$, then
$b_{n+1}=\frac{2 a_{n}+6}{a_{n}+1}-3=\frac{-a_{n}+3}{a_{n}+1}=-\frac{b_{n}}{a_{n}+1}$.
$c_{n-1}=\frac{2 a_{n}+6}{a_{n}+1}+2=\frac{4 a_{n}+8}{a_{n}+1}=\frac{4 c_{n}}{a_{n}+1}$.
Thus, $\frac{b_{n+1}}{c_{n+1}}=-\frac{1}{4} \frac{b_{n}}{c_{n}},\left\{\frac{b_{n}}{c_{n}}\right\}$ is a geometric sequence with a common ratio of $-\frac{1}{4}$, and the first term is $\frac{b_{1}}{c_{1}}=\frac{a_{1}-3}{a_{1}+2}=-\frac{1}{4}$.
Therefore, $\frac{b_{n}}{c_{n}}=\frac{1}{(-4)^{n}}$, and from $\frac{a_{n}-3}{a_{n}+2}=\frac{1}{(-4)^{n}}$, we get $a_{n}=\frac{2+3 \times(-4)^{n}}{(-4)^{n}-1}$.

problem:
Determine the largest positive integer $n$ for which $7^{n}$ is a divisor of the integer $\frac{200 !}{90 ! 30 !}$.

(Note: If $n$ is a positive integer, the symbol $n$ ! (read " $n$ factorial") is used to represent the product of the integers from 1 to $n$. That is, $n !=n(n-1)(n-2) \cdots(3)(2)(1)$. For example, $5 !=5(4)(3)(2)(1)$ or $5 !=120$.)
solution:
First, we count the number of factors of 7 included in 200 !.

Every multiple of 7 includes least 1 factor of 7 .

The product 200! includes 28 multiples of 7 (since $28 \times 7=196$ ).

Counting one factor of 7 from each of the multiples of 7 (these are $7,14,21, \ldots, 182,189,196$ ), we see that 200 ! includes at least 28 factors of 7 .

However, each multiple of $7^{2}=49$ includes a second factor of 7 (since $49=7^{2}, 98=7^{2} \times 2$, etc.) which was not counted in the previous 28 factors.

The product 200 ! includes 4 multiples of 49 , since $4 \times 49=196$, and thus there are at least 4 additional factors of 7 in 200 !.

Since $7^{3}>200$, then 200! does not include any multiples of $7^{3}$ and so we have counted all possible factors of 7 .

Thus, 200! includes exactly $28+4=32$ factors of 7 , and so $200!=7^{32} \times t$ for some positive
integer $t$ that is not divisible by 7 .

Counting in a similar way, the product 90 ! includes 12 multiples of 7 and 1 multiple of 49 , and thus includes 13 factors of 7 .

Therefore, $90!=7^{13} \times r$ for some positive integer $r$ that is not divisible by 7 .

Also, 30! includes 4 factors of 7 , and thus $30!=7^{4} \times s$ for some positive integer $s$ that is not divisible by 7 .

Therefore, $\frac{200!}{90!30!}=\frac{7^{32} \times t}{\left(7^{13} \times r\right)\left(7^{4} \times s\right)}=\frac{7^{32} \times t}{\left(7^{17} \times r s\right)}=\frac{7^{15} \times t}{r s}$.

Since we are given that $\frac{200!}{90!30!}$ is equal to a positive integer, then $\frac{7^{15} \times t}{r s}$ is a positive integer. Since $r$ and $s$ contain no factors of 7 and $7^{15} \times t$ is divisible by $r s$, then it must be the case that $t$ is divisible by $r s$.

In other words, we can re-write $\frac{200!}{90!30!}=\frac{7^{15} \times t}{r s}$ as $\frac{200!}{90!30!}=7^{15} \times \frac{t}{r s}$ where $\frac{t}{r s}$ is an integer.

Since each of $r, s$ and $t$ does not include any factors of 7 , then the integer $\frac{t}{r s}$ is not divisible by 7 .

Therefore, the largest power of 7 which divides $\frac{200!}{90!30!}$ is $7^{15}$, and so $n=15$.

ANSWER: 15

problem:
. A finite set of integers is called bad if its elements add up to 2010. A finite set of integers is a Benelux-set if none of its subsets is bad. Determine the smallest integer $n$ such that the set $\{502,503,504, \ldots, 2009\}$ can be partitioned into $n$ Benelux-sets.

(A partition of a set $S$ into $n$ subsets is a collection of $n$ pairwise disjoint subsets of $S$, the union of which equals $S$.)
solution:
As $502+1508=2010$, the set $S=\{502,503, \ldots, 2009\}$ is not a Benelux-set, so $n=1$ does not work. We will prove that $n=2$ does work, i.e. that $S$ can be partitioned into 2 Benelux-sets.

Define the following subsets of $S$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
A & =\{502,503, \ldots, 670\}, \\
B & =\{671,672, \ldots, 1005\}, \\
C & =\{1006,1007, \ldots, 1339\}, \\
D & =\{1340,1341, \ldots, 1508\}, \\
E & =\{1509,1510, \ldots, 2009\} .
\end{aligned}
$$

We will show that $A \cup C \cup E$ and $B \cup D$ are both Benelux-sets.

Note that there does not exist a bad subset of $S$ of one element, since that element would have to be 2010. Also, there does not exist a bad subset of $S$ of more than three elements, since the sum of four or more elements would be at least $502+503+504+505=2014>2010$. So any possible bad subset of $S$ contains two or three elements.

Consider a bad subset of two elements $a$ and $b$. As $a, b \geq 502$ and $a+b=2010$, we have $a, b \leq 2010-502=1508$. Furthermore, exactly one of $a$ and $b$ is smaller than 1005 and one is larger than 1005. So one of them, say $a$, is an element of $A \cup B$, and the other is an element of $C \cup D$. Suppose $a \in A$, then $b \geq 2010-670=1340$, so $b \in D$. On the other hand, suppose $a \in B$, then $b \leq 2010-671=1339$, so $b \in C$. Hence $\{a, b\}$ cannot be a subset of $A \cup C \cup E$, nor of $B \cup D$.

Now consider a bad subset of three elements $a, b$ and $c$. As $a, b, c \geq 502, a+b+c=2010$, and the three elements are pairwise distinct, we have $a, b, c \leq 2010-502-503=1005$. So $a, b, c \in A \cup B$. At least one of the elements, say $a$, is smaller than $\frac{2010}{3}=670$, and at least one of the elements, say $b$, is larger than 670 . So $a \in A$ and $b \in B$. We conclude that $\{a, b, c\}$ cannot be a subset of $A \cup C \cup E$, nor of $B \cup D$.

This proves that $A \cup C \cup E$ and $B \cup D$ are Benelux-sets, and therefore the smallest $n$ for which $S$ can be partitioned into $n$ Benelux-sets is $n=2$.

Remark. Observe that $A \cup C \cup E_{1}$ and $B \cup D \cup E_{2}$ are also Benelux-sets, where $\left\{E_{1}, E_{2}\right\}$ is any partition of $E$.

problem:
1. If the function
$$
f(x)=3 \cos \left(\omega x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin \left(\omega x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)(\omega>0)
$$

has the smallest positive period of $\pi$, then the maximum value of $f(x)$ in the interval $\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ is $\qquad$
solution:
$-1.2 \sqrt{3}$.
Notice,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
f(x)=3 \cos \left(\omega x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin \left(\omega x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) \\
=3 \cos \left(\omega x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin \left(\omega x+\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \\
=3 \cos \left(\omega x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+\cos \left(\omega x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \\
=4 \cos \left(\omega x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right),
\end{array}
$$

and the smallest positive period of $f(x)$ is $\pi$.
Thus, $\omega=2, f(x)=4 \cos \left(2 x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$.
When $x \in\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, $\frac{\pi}{6} \leqslant 2 x+\frac{\pi}{6} \leqslant \frac{7 \pi}{6}$.
Therefore, when $2 x+\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{6}$, i.e., $x=0$, $f(x)$ reaches its maximum value $2 \sqrt{3}$ in the interval $\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$.

## Solution.

Domain of definition: $x>0$.

Rewrite the equation as

$5^{\log _{2} x}-5 \cdot 5^{\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} x}=5-5^{\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} x} \Leftrightarrow 5^{\log _{2} x}-4 \cdot 5^{\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} x}-5=0$.

Solving this equation as a quadratic equation in terms of $5^{\frac{1}{\log _{2} x}}$, we get
$5^{\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} x}=-1$ (no solutions), or $5^{\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} x}=5 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \log _{2} x=1, \log _{2} x=2$, $x=2^{2}=4$.

Answer: 4.

problem:
## Task 4 - 280914

Three workpieces $W_{1}, W_{2}, W_{3}$ go through an assembly line with four processing machines $M_{1}, M_{2}, M_{3}, M_{4}$. Each workpiece must pass through the machines in the order $M_{1}, M_{2}, M_{3}, M_{4}$, and the order of the three workpieces must be the same at each machine.

The processing times of the workpieces on the individual machines are (in hours) given in the following table:

|  | $M_{1}$ | $M_{2}$ | $M_{3}$ | $M_{4}$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $W_{1}$ | 4 | 1 | 2 | 1.5 |
| $W_{2}$ | 2 | 2.5 | 1 | 0.5 |
| $W_{3}$ | 2 | 3.5 | 1 | 1 |

Two workpieces can never be processed simultaneously on the same machine. The times for changing the workpieces at the machines are so small that they can be neglected.

Give an order of the three workpieces for passing through the assembly line such that the total time (the time from the entry of the first workpiece into machine $M_{1}$ to the exit of the last workpiece from machine $M_{4}$) is as small as possible! Show that the order you give with its total time is better than any other order!
solution:
(Machine designation shortened to 1,2,3,4 instead of $M_{1}, M_{2}, M_{3}, M_{4}$)

In the representations of the temporal sequence, the total time is determined for each of the six possible sequences of three workpieces, assuming that each machine receives the next workpiece (in the intended sequence) as soon as possible.

When comparing these representations, it turns out:

The sequence $W_{3}, W_{1}, W_{2}$ outperforms all other sequences with its total time.

Hints:

It is also possible to proceed in a very argumentative manner. For example, one can first determine for which sequence

- the sum of the times of the first and second workpieces in $M_{1}$ plus the sum of the times of the third workpiece in $M_{1}, M_{2}, M_{3}$, and $M_{4}$

yields the smallest possible value. Instead of the sum (1), one can more easily use

- $W_{2}$ can pass through the machines $M_{1}, M_{2}, M_{3}, M_{4}$ without waiting times.

If this is the case, it follows: This sequence outperforms the total times of all sequences that do not minimize (1) or (2).

(Note: Without statement (3), such a conclusion would not be secure!) Finally, a sequence that satisfies (3) must be compared with the other one in which $W_{2}$ is also the third workpiece. The investigation of (3) and the aforementioned comparison can, for example, be carried out using the two representations above for $W_{1}, W_{3}, W_{2}$ and $W_{3}, W_{1}, W_{2}$. The consideration of (1) and (2) thus saves four such representations.

problem:
(M) Find the functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n$ we have

$$
f(n)+f(f(n))+f(f(f(n)))=3 n
$$

problem: Example 5 Let $S=\{1,2,3, \cdots, 98,99,100\}$, if a three-element subset $A=\{a, b, c\}$ of $S$ satisfies $a+b=3 c$, then $A$ is said to have property $P$. Find the number of all three-element subsets of $S$ that have property $P$.
solution:
Let $S_{k}=\{n \mid n \equiv k(\bmod 3), n \in S\}, k=0,1,2$. Then $\left|S_{0}\right|=\left|S_{2}\right|=$ $33,\left|S_{1}\right|=34$.

If $A=\{a, b, c\}$ has property $P$, then either $a, b \in S_{0}$, or one of $a, b$ belongs to $S_{1}$ and the other to $S_{2}$. When $a, b$ both belong to $S_{0}$ and $a \neq b$, the unordered pair $\{a, b\}$ has $C_{33}^{2}$ possibilities. When one of $a, b$ belongs to $S_{1}$ and the other to $S_{2}$, the unordered pair $\{a, b\}$ has $C_{33}^{1} C_{34}^{1}$ possibilities. Therefore, the number of unordered pairs $\{a, b\}$ that satisfy $a+b \equiv 0(\bmod 3)$ is $C_{33}^{2}+C_{33}^{1} C_{34}^{1}$. However, among these, the unordered pairs $\{a, b\}$ where $a=2 b$ or $b=2 a$ do not form a three-element set $A$, as $c=b$ or $c=a$ cannot be achieved. Such unordered pairs are $\{k, 2 k\}(k=1,2, \cdots, 50)$, totaling 50. Therefore, the number of three-element subsets with property $P$ is $C_{33}^{2}+C_{33}^{1} C_{34}^{1}-50=1600$.

problem: 7. As shown in Figure 1, there is a solid metal sphere with a radius of 20. A circular hole with a radius of 12 is drilled along a certain diameter as the central axis, and the remaining part is melted and cast into a new solid sphere. What is the radius of the new sphere? $\qquad$
solution:
7. 16 .

Compare the upper half of the geometric solid obtained from the problem with a hemisphere of radius 16, placing their bases on the same horizontal plane, and examine the cross-sectional areas at a height of $h$ from the two solids. The cross-section formed by the first solid is an annulus, with an outer radius of $\sqrt{20-h^{2}}$ and an inner radius of 12, so the area is $\pi\left(20^{2}-h^{2}-12^{2}\right)=\pi\left(16^{2}-h^{2}\right)$, which is precisely the area of the circular cross-section formed by the second hemisphere. According to Zu Chongzhi's principle, the volumes of the two solids are equal.

problem: 5. Given the equation about $x$: $(2 a-1) \sin x+(2-a) \sin 2 x=\sin 3 x$, if all solutions of the equation in the range $x \in[0,2 \pi]$ form an arithmetic sequence in ascending order, then the range of the real number $a$ is $\qquad$ .
solution:
$$
\begin{array}{l}
(2 a-1) \sin x+2(2-a) \sin x \cos x=3 \sin x-4 \sin ^{3} x \\
\Rightarrow \sin x\left[2 \cos ^{2} x+(a-2) \cos x-a\right]=\sin x(\cos x-1)(2 \cos x+a)=0 .
\end{array}
$$

Notice that $\sin x(\cos x-1)=0$ has all roots $0, \pi, 2 \pi$ in $[0,2 \pi]$, forming an arithmetic sequence; when $a=0$, $\cos x=0$ has all roots $\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3 \pi}{2}$ in $[0,2 \pi]$, and at this time, these 5 numbers can form an arithmetic sequence; when $a \in(-2,0) \cup(0,2)$, the two roots of $\cos x=-\frac{a}{2}$ in $[0,2 \pi]$ cannot form an arithmetic sequence with $0, \pi, 2 \pi$. In summary, the range of real number $a$ is $(-\infty,-2] \bigcup\{0\} \bigcup[2,+\infty)$.

problem: King Arthur's bodyguards held a knightly tournament. At the end of the tournament, it turned out that the king could find a third one for any two bodyguards who participated, who had defeated both of them. What is the minimum number of bodyguards who participated in the tournament?
solution:
Let's indulge in the idea that the king has at least two bodyguards, one of whom is $A$. This bodyguard $A$ was certainly replaced by someone, let's say $B$, and there was a bodyguard $C$ who defeated both $A$ and $B$. Now, $B$ could not have defeated $A$ and $C$, since $B$ was replaced by $C$, so this must have been a different bodyguard, say $D$. Bodyguard $A$ was defeated by $B$, $C$, and $D$, and since $A$ could be any bodyguard, every bodyguard must have lost at least three times.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_e557b6445c78e790253bg-1.jpg?height=469&width=488&top_left_y=351&top_left_x=813)

Let's denote the number of knights participating in the tournament by $k$. In every match, one participant won and the other lost, and since every bodyguard lost at least three times, there were at least $3k$ matches. On the other hand, every knight fought with every other knight at most once, so

$$
3 k \leqq \frac{k(k-1)}{2}
$$

from which $k \leqq 7$, meaning at least 7 bodyguards participated in the tournament.

The table shows that the conditions described in the problem can be satisfied with 7 knights. No matter which two rows we choose, there is a column where both rows intersect with a star.

problem: 5. (3 points) In how many ways can the figure shown in the diagram be colored cell by cell in blue, red, and white so that adjacent (i.e., having common sides) cells are colored differently?
solution:
Answer: $3 \cdot 48^{4}$

Solution: The central cell can be painted in three ways. After this, we need to paint four identical figures consisting of six cells each, with the same restriction on the color of the cell adjacent to the central one (let's call it cell A).

Consider a $2 \times 2$ square. In such a square, there must be two cells of the same color, and they must be positioned diagonally. There are two ways to choose the diagonal, three ways to choose its color, and two ways to choose the color for each of the remaining cells, totaling 24 ways. However, squares painted in two colors have been counted twice, so there are 18 ways left.

Obviously, for each of the three colors, there are 6 ways such that the cell adjacent not only to the cells of the square but also to the central cell has exactly this color. Let's call this cell cell B.

Cell A can be painted in two ways. For each of these ways, there are 6 ways to paint the square such that cell B is painted in the same color. Then the cell between them can be painted in two ways, totaling $2 \cdot 6 \cdot 2 = 24$ variants.

In addition, for each way to paint cell A, there are 12 ways to paint the square such that cell B has a different color. In this case, the cell between them is painted uniquely, so we again get 24 ways. In total, there are 48 ways to paint each such figure.

Therefore, the answer to the problem is $3 \cdot 48^{4}$.

solution:
Problem 3. In each of the 16 cells of a $4 \times 4$ square, one of the numbers $1,2,3, \ldots, 16$ is written. The sum of the numbers in each column is calculated. If one of the obtained sums is strictly greater than the other three, it is denoted by $S$.

a) Give an example of a completion of the square where $S=40$.

b) What is the smallest possible value of $S$?

## Solution

a) An example of such a completion is:

| 1 | 2 | 3 | $\mathbf{1 0}$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 8 | 7 | 6 | $\mathbf{5}$ |
| 9 | 4 | 11 | $\mathbf{1 2}$ |
| 16 | 15 | 14 | $\mathbf{1 3}$ |

$\qquad$
b) The sum of the numbers written in the cells of the square is $1+2+3+\ldots+16=136$. Since $136=4 \cdot 34$, it follows that either the sum of the numbers in each column is 34, or there is a column whose sum is at least 35. In the first case, there is no $S$, and from the second case, it follows that $S$ is at least 35. To show that the minimum value of $S$ is 35, it remains to give an example of a completion of the square such that one column has a sum of 35, while the other columns have smaller sums. Here is such a completion:

| 1 | 2 | 3 | $\mathbf{4}$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 8 | 7 | 6 | $\mathbf{5}$ |
| 9 | 10 | 11 | $\mathbf{1 2}$ |
| 16 | 15 | 13 | $\mathbf{1 4}$ |

(The sum of the numbers in the last column is 35, while the sums in the first three columns are 34, 34, and 33, respectively, so the last column is the one with $S=35$.)

2 \log _{x}\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right) \leq \log _{x} a+\log _{x} b

hold for all positive numbers $a$ and $b$ ?
solution:
15.12. $0<x<1$

$$
\log _{x}\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right) \leq \log _{x} \sqrt{a b} .
$$
