B1. On a sheet of paper, there is a grid of 101 by 101 white squares. A snake is formed by coloring squares gray as shown in the accompanying figure. The snake starts at the top left and continues until it can no longer proceed. Only a part of the grid is depicted. How many squares are gray in total in the complete 101 by 101 grid? 5201

Solution We can think of the figure of $101^{2}$ squares as being built up as follows. First, one square at the top left, then two L-shaped pieces, one of three squares (with one gray square) and one of five

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_04_17_cb8708f0b7aaf218de84g-2.jpg?height=285&width=277&top_left_y=473&top_left_x=1683)
squares (all five gray) around it. Then again two L-shaped pieces, one of seven squares (one of which is gray) and one of nine squares (all nine gray), and so on. The last two L-shaped pieces consist of the first one with 199 squares (one of which is gray) and the second one with 201 squares (all gray). In total, we look at 50 pairs of L-shaped pieces. The number of gray squares we count is $1+(1+5)+(1+9)+(1+13)+\ldots+(1+201)=1+(6+10+14+\ldots+202)=1+\frac{1}{2} \cdot 50 \cdot(6+202)=5201$. Alternative solution For every two of these L-shaped pieces, there are 4 more gray squares than white squares. There are thus $50 \cdot 4=200$ more gray squares than white squares out of the $101^{2}-1=10200$ squares in the 100 L-shaped pieces in total, so that involves 5000 white and 5200 gray squares. With the top left square included, there are thus a total of 5201 gray squares.

## - Roots and factorization of polynomials

Here we see that the knowledge of the roots of a polynomial allows us to factorize it. Recall that $\mathbb{K}$ denotes $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{Q}$.

Definition 1.10. An element $x \in \mathbb{K}$ is called a root of a polynomial $P \in \mathbb{K}[X]$ if $P(x)=0$.

Example 1.11. The real polynomial $X^{2}-1$ has two real roots, which are 1 and -1. The polynomial $X^{2}+1$ has no real roots. The real polynomial $X^{2}-2$ has two real roots, but the polynomial with rational coefficients $X^{2}-2$ has no rational roots because $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

Theorem 1.12. Let $P \in \mathbb{K}[X]$ and $a \in \mathbb{K}$. The following two propositions are equivalent:

1. a is a root of $P$, that is, $P(a)=0$.
2. There exists a polynomial $Q \in \mathbb{K}[X]$ such that:

$$
P(x)=Q(x)(x-a) \text {. }
$$

Proof. It is clear that the second point implies the first. As for the converse, the key is to use Euclidean division. Indeed, suppose that $P(a)=0$. Then write the Euclidean division of $P$ by $X-a$ in the form $P(x)=Q(x)(x-a)+R(x)$ with $R$ a polynomial of degree at most $1-1=0$. Thus, $R$ is a real number, denoted by $c$. In short, $P(x)=Q(x)(x-a)+c$. Evaluate this quantity at $x=a: 0=P(a)=Q(a)(a-a)+c$. Therefore, $c=0$, which is what we wanted to prove.

Theorem 1.13. A polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ different roots.

Proof. By contradiction, let $P \in \mathbb{R}[X]$ of degree $n$ having at least $n+1$ different roots, denoted $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{n+1}$. According to the previous theorem, there exists a polynomial $Q$ such that $P(x)=$ $Q(x)\left(x-r_{1}\right)$. But then, for $2 \leq i \leq n+1,0=P\left(r_{i}\right)=Q\left(r_{i}\right)\left(r_{i}-r_{1}\right)$. Since $r_{i}-r_{1} \neq 0$, this implies $Q\left(r_{i}\right)=0$. We repeat this reasoning with $Q$ to finally obtain the existence of a polynomial $T$ such that $P(x)=T(x)\left(x-r_{1}\right) \cdots\left(x-r_{n+1}\right)$. Then, according to Proposition 1.6:

$$
n=\operatorname{deg}(P)=\operatorname{deg} T+n+1>n
$$

which is absurd.

Remark 1.14. There exist polynomials that have no real roots, for example $P(x)=$ $x^{4}+1$.

This important theorem implies some corollaries giving information about the polynomial given something about its roots.

Corollary 1.15. Let $P(x)=a_{0}+a_{1} x+\cdots+a_{n} x^{n}$ be a polynomial of degree $n$. Suppose it has $n$ different roots $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{n}$. Then:

$$
P(x)=a_{n}\left(x-r_{1}\right) \cdots\left(x-r_{n}\right)
$$

Proof. By revisiting the previous proof, we see that there exists a polynomial $T$ such that $P(x)=T(x)\left(x-r_{1}\right) \cdots\left(x-r_{n}\right)$. By comparing the degrees of the terms on the left and right, it follows that $T$ is of degree zero, hence a real number. By looking at the leading coefficient on both sides of the equality, we find that $T(x)=a_{n}$.

Corollary 1.16. A polynomial of degree $n$ having $n+1$ roots is zero. Thus, a polynomial having an infinite number of roots is necessarily the zero polynomial.

problem: A group of five friends decides to play Secret Santa, each buying a gift for their secret friend. According to the rules of the game, each person gives exactly one gift and receives exactly one gift. In how many ways can the gifts be distributed so that no one gives a gift to themselves?
solution:
First, let's observe that the number of ways to distribute the gifts without any restrictions is $5!=5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1=120$. From this, we need to subtract the "bad" cases, that is, the cases where at least one friend ends up with their own gift. These cases to be eliminated can be listed by the number of friends who end up with their own gift.

- All 5 friends end up with their own gifts. There is only one possibility for this to happen.
- Exactly 4 friends end up with their own gifts. This is not possible.
- Exactly 3 friends end up with their own gifts. In this situation, the other two friends swap the gifts. Thus, we choose 3 people out of 5, which is $\frac{5 \times 4 \times 3}{3 \times 2}=10$ possibilities.
- Exactly 2 friends end up with their own gifts. In this case, we choose 2 people out of 5, which is $\frac{5 \times 4}{2}=10$ possibilities. The other 3 friends swap the gifts among themselves, giving a total of $10 \times 2=20$ possibilities.
- Lastly, exactly one friend ends up with their own gift. In this case, we choose one person out of a total of 5, and multiply by the number of ways the other friends do not end up with their own gifts, which are 9 ways. Thus, in this situation, we have a total of $5 \times 9=45$ possibilities.

Therefore, we have $120-45-20-10-1=44$ ways to distribute the gifts without anyone ending up with their own gift.

problem:
Pedro decided to take all his children, boys and girls, for ice cream at the Ice Cream Math parlor. At the parlor, there are 12 different ice cream flavors, and each child ordered a combo with 3 scoops of ice cream. After leaving the parlor, Pedro realized that exactly two scoops of each available flavor were ordered in total.

a) Knowing that Pedro did not have ice cream, what is the total number of his children (girls and boys)?

b) Pedro looked more closely at the flavors each one ordered and noticed that no flavor was chosen by both a boy and a girl, that is, if a boy chose a flavor, no girl chose that same flavor. Knowing that at least one of his children is a boy and that he has more daughters than sons, determine the number of his daughters.
solution:
Solution

a) Let $n$ be the number of Pedro's children. In total, $3 n$ scoops of ice cream were ordered. Since each of the 12 flavors was ordered twice, we have $3 n=2 \cdot 12$, that is, $n=8$. Therefore, Pedro has 8 children.

b) Let $x$ be the number of boys and $y$ be the number of girls. From the previous item, we know that $x+y=8$. Since there is at least one child and there are more girls than boys, we know that: $0<x<y$. Given that no flavor was ordered simultaneously by boys and girls, the flavors can be separated into boys' flavors and girls' flavors. Thus, $3 x$ is equal to twice the number of boys' flavors, as exactly two scoops of each flavor were ordered and no girl could order one of the boys' flavors. Consequently, $x$ is even. Similarly, $y$ is also even. Since $0<x<y$ and $x+y=8$, we can conclude that $x=2$ and $y=6$. Therefore, Pedro has 6 daughters.

## Solution

Vectors are collinear if there exists a number $\gamma$ such that $c_{1}=\gamma \cdot c_{2}$. That is, vectors are collinear if their coordinates are proportional.

We get:

problem: A regular tetrahedron has edges of $13, \sqrt{281}$, and 20 units in length. Determine the dihedral angle between two of its faces.
solution:
Solution. The opposite edges of an equilateral tetrahedron are of equal length, so the diagonals of the faces of the enclosing parallelepiped are equal, meaning the parallelogram faces are rectangles, and the enclosing parallelepiped is a rectangular prism. The edges of the tetrahedron are the face diagonals of the enclosing rectangular prism, so the edges of the rectangular prism can be calculated using the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
a^{2}+b^{2}=281, \quad b^{2}+c^{2}=169, \quad c^{2}+a^{2}=400
$$

The solution to the system of equations is $a=16, b=5, c=12$. Place the tetrahedron conveniently in the coordinate system:

$$
A(0,0,0), \quad B(16,5,0), \quad C(16,0,12), \quad D(0,5,12)
$$

Since two-two-two edges are equal, there are three different dihedral angles. Let the dihedral angles determined by the planes $A B C, A C D$, the planes $A B C, A B D$, and the planes $A C D, A B D$ be $\varphi_{1}, \varphi_{2}, \varphi_{3}$, respectively. For the plane $A B C$, the vector $\underline{n}(U, V, 1)$ perpendicular to both $\overrightarrow{A B}$ and $\overrightarrow{A C}$ is the normal vector of the plane. This vector is perpendicular to both non-parallel vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \overrightarrow{A B} \cdot \underline{n}=16 U+5 V=0 \\
& \overrightarrow{A C} \cdot \underline{n}=16 U+12=0
\end{aligned}
$$

From this system of equations, $\underline{n}\left(-\frac{3}{4}, \frac{12}{5}, 1\right)$, or the parallel $\underline{n}_{A B C}(15,-48,-20)$. The equation of the plane $A B C$ passing through point $A$ is then

$$
15 x-48 y-20 z=0
$$

Similarly, the equation of the plane $A C D$ is

$$
-15 x-48 y+20 z=0
$$

The normal vectors of the two planes are

$$
\underline{n}_{A B C}(15,-48,-20), \quad \underline{n}_{A C D}(-15,-48,20)
$$

Since the normal vectors are perpendicular to the respective planes, and in this case point in the direction opposite to the angle domain, if we take their dot product, we get the supplementary angle of the desired $\varphi_{1}$ dihedral angle. Thus,

$$
\underline{n}_{A B C} \cdot \underline{n}_{A C D}=\left|\underline{n}_{A B C}\right| \cdot\left|\underline{n}_{A C D}\right| \cdot \cos \left(180^{\circ}-\varphi_{1}\right)
$$

From this,

$$
\cos \varphi_{1}=-\frac{-15^{2}+48^{2}-20^{2}}{15^{2}+48^{2}+20^{2}}=-\frac{1679}{2929}, \quad \varphi_{1} \approx 124.98^{\circ}
$$

To determine the other angles, the normal vector of the plane $A B D$ is

$$
\underline{n}_{A B D}(15,-48,20)
$$

By a completely similar calculation, taking into account the direction of the normal vectors when writing the dot product, we get that

$$
\varphi_{2}=\arccos \frac{2129}{2929} \approx 43.38^{\circ}, \quad \text { and } \quad \varphi_{3}=\arccos \frac{2479}{2929} \approx 32.18^{\circ}
$$

problem:
Solve the following inequality:

$$
[5 x] \geqq[x]+\frac{[2 x]}{2}+\frac{[3 x]}{3}+\frac{[4 x]}{4}+\frac{[5 x]}{5}
$$
solution:
I. Solution. By definition, $[x]$ represents the largest integer that is not greater than $x$.

The fractional part of $x$ is conventionally denoted as

$$
\{x\}=x-[x]
$$

Thus, the inequality can be transformed into the following form:

$$
[5[x]+5\{x\}] \geqq[[x]+\{x\}]+\frac{[2[x]+2\{x\}]}{2}+\ldots+\frac{[5[x]+5\{x\}]}{5}
$$

Using the fact that for an integer $n$, $[n+t]=n+[t]$, we can further transform it:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 5[x]+[5\{x\}] \geqq[x]+[\{x\}]+\frac{2[x]}{2}+\frac{2[\{x\}]}{2}+\ldots+\frac{5[x]}{5}+\frac{[5\{x\}]}{5} \\
& {[5\{x\}] \geqq[\{x\}]+\frac{[2\{x\}]}{2}+\frac{[3\{x\}]}{3}+\frac{[4\{x\}]}{4}+\frac{[5\{x\}]}{5} }
\end{aligned}
$$

Now we examine four cases:

1. If $0 \leqq\{x\}<\frac{1}{5}, \quad$ then $\quad[\{x\}]+\ldots+\frac{[5\{x\}]}{5}=0=[\{5 x\}]$;
2. If $\frac{1}{5} \leqq\{x\}<\frac{2}{5}, \quad$ then $\quad[\{x\}]+\ldots+\frac{[5\{x\}]}{5} \leqq \frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{5}=\frac{47}{60}<[5\{x\}]=1$;
3. If $\frac{2}{5} \leqq\{x\}<\frac{3}{5}, \quad$ then $\quad[\{x\}]+\ldots+\frac{[5\{x\}]}{5} \leqq$ $\leqq \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{4}+\frac{2}{5}=1 \frac{11}{15}<[5\{x\}]=2$
4. If $\frac{3}{5} \leqq\{x\}<1, \quad$ then $\quad[\{x\}]+\ldots+\frac{[5\{x\}]}{5} \leqq$ $\leqq \frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{4}+\frac{4}{5}=2 \frac{43}{60}<3 \leqq[5\{x\}]$

Thus, we find that every real $x$ is a solution to the inequality.

II. Solution. It is easily verifiable that for every pair of real numbers $(a, b)$, $[a]+[b] \leqq[a+b]$. Applying this multiple times, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
120[5 x] & =24[5 x]+30[5 x]+20[5 x]+20[5 x]+15[5 x]++10[5 x]+[5 x] \geqq \\
& \geqq 24[5 x]+30([4 x]+[x])+20([3 x]+[2 x])+20([3 x]+[x]+[x])+15([2 x]+ \\
& +[2 x]+[x])+10([2 x]+[x]+[x]+[x])+([x]+[x]+[x]+[x]+[x])= \\
& =120[x]+60[2 x]+40[3 x]+30[4 x]+24[5 x],
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, for every real $x$,

$$
120[5 x] \geq 120[x]+60[2 x]+40[3 x]+30[4 x]+24[5 x]
$$

Dividing this by 120, we get the inequality of the problem, which means that every real number is a solution to the inequality.

problem:
8. (5 points) The founder of a noble family received a plot of land. Each man in the family, upon dying, divided the land he inherited equally among his sons. If he had no sons, the land went to the state. No other members of the family gained or lost any land in any other way. In total, there were 180 people in the family. What is the smallest fraction of the original plot that any member of the family could have received?

Answer: $\frac{1}{2 \cdot 3^{59}}$
solution:
Solution: Consider the person with the smallest share. Let his father have $a_{1}$ sons, his grandfather $a_{2}$, and so on up to the founder of the lineage, who had $a_{n}$. Then the share of this person is $\frac{1}{a_{1} a_{2} \ldots a_{n}}$, and we know that $a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}$ does not exceed 179 (since the founder of the lineage is definitely not included in this sum).

Thus, we are looking for a set of numbers with a sum not exceeding 179 and the maximum product. We will prove that any set, except for the set consisting of 59 threes and one two, does not have the maximum product, as it can be increased.

Firstly, if the sum of the numbers in the set is less than 179, add another number to make it equal to 179. The product will not decrease.

Secondly, suppose there is a number $a \geqslant 4$ in our set. Replace $a$ with a pair of numbers $b$ and $c$ greater than one, such that $b+c=a$. We will prove that $b c \geqslant b+c$. Indeed, $b c-b-c=(b-1)(c-1)-1$, which is non-negative for $b$ and $c$ greater than one.

Thirdly, if there is a number 1 in the set, we can replace any number $a$ and 1 with $a+1$, thereby increasing the product of these numbers by 1.

Thus, any set can be transformed into a set of twos and threes without decreasing the product of its numbers.

Furthermore, if there are at least three twos, their product is 8. If we replace three twos with two threes, the sum of the numbers remains the same, but the product becomes 9, which is again an increase. Thus, we can ensure that the number of twos is no more than two.

Since $179=59 \cdot 3+2$, the final set will have exactly one two.

Therefore, any set of natural numbers with a sum not exceeding 179 can be transformed into a set of 59 threes and one two, and the product of the numbers in the set will not decrease. This means that the final set has the largest product, equal to $3^{59} \cdot 2$, which gives us the smallest inheritance share as the reciprocal of this number.

problem: 3. In the Slytherin faculty at Hogwarts, there are 30 students. Some are friends (friendship is mutual, i.e., if A is friends with B, then B is also friends with A), but there are no 3 people who are pairwise friends with each other. On New Year's, each student sent cards to all their friends. What is the maximum number of cards that could have been sent?
solution:
Answer: 450.

Solution: Let's find the person with the most friends. Suppose there are no fewer than 15, and denote their number as $15+a$. We will divide the students into two groups: the first group will consist of these $15+a$ students. According to the condition, they cannot be friends with each other, so each of them has no more than 15-a friends. The second group will consist of the remaining 15-a, each of whom has no more than $15+a$ friends. Thus, each group will send no more than 225- $a^{2}$ cards. Therefore, in total, no more than 450-2 $a^{2}$ cards will be sent, which does not exceed 450.

Note that this value is achievable. Divide the students into two groups of 15 people each, and let each representative of one group be friends with all representatives of the other group.

problem:
12.95 Find all positive integer solutions $(x, y, z, n)$ that satisfy the equation $x^{2 n+1}-y^{2 n+1}=x y z+2^{2 n+1}$, where $n \geqslant 2, \quad z \leqslant 5 \cdot 2^{2 n}$.
(6th China High School Mathematics Winter Camp, 1991)
solution:
[Solution] Let the positive integer tuple $(x, y, z, n)$ satisfy the equation
$$
x^{2 n+1}-y^{2 n+1}=x y z+2^{2 n+1} \text {. }
$$

Obviously, $x-y>0$, and $x$ and $y$ have the same parity.

Otherwise, if one of $x$ and $y$ is odd and the other is even, then the left side of the equation is odd, while the right side is even. This is impossible.
Thus,
$$
x-y \geqslant 2 \text {. }
$$
(1) When $y=1, x=3$, the equation (1) becomes
$$
\begin{array}{l}
3^{2 n+1}-1=3 z+2^{2 n+1} . \\
z=3^{2 n}-\frac{1}{3}\left(1+2^{2 n+1}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

Since $z \leqslant 5 \cdot 2^{2 n}$, we get the inequality
$$
\begin{array}{l} 
3^{2 n}-\frac{1}{3}\left(1+2^{2 n+1}\right) \leqslant 5 \cdot 2^{2 n}, \\
3^{2 n} \leqslant 5 \cdot 2^{2 n}+\frac{1}{3}\left(1+2^{2 n+1}\right) \\
\leqslant 2^{2 n}\left[5+\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{2^{2 n}}+2\right)\right] \\
\leqslant 6 \cdot 2^{2 n} .
\end{array}
$$

That is,
$$
\begin{array}{c}
\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{2 n} \leqslant 6, \\
n \leqslant \frac{\lg 6}{\lg 9-\lg 4}2^{2 n+1}+1,
\end{array}
$$
(2) and (3) are contradictory.

Therefore, when $y=1, x \geqslant 4$, the equation has no solution.
(3) When $y \geqslant 2$, since $x-y \geqslant 2, \quad z \leqslant 5 \cdot 2^{2 n}$ and $n \geqslant 2$, then
$$
\begin{array}{l}
x^{2 n+1}-x y z \\
=x\left(x^{2 n}-y z\right) \\
\geqslant x\left[(y+2)^{2 n}-y z\right] \\
\geqslant x\left[y^{2 n}+4 n y^{2 n-1}+4 n(2 n-1) y^{2 n-2}+\cdots+2^{2 n}-5 \cdot 2^{2 n} y\right] \\
>x y^{2 n}+x \cdot 2^{2 n}+y\left[4 n y^{2 n-2}+4 n(2 n-1) y^{2 n-3}-5 \cdot 2^{2 n}\right] \\
>y^{2 n+1}+2^{2 n+1}+2^{2 n-3} y[8 n+4 n(2 n-1)-40] \\
\geqslant y^{2 n+1}+2^{2 n+1} .
\end{array}
$$

That is,
$$
x^{2 n+1}-x y z>y^{2 n+1}+2^{2 n+1} .
$$
(4) contradicts (1).

Therefore, when $y \geqslant 2$, the equation has no solution.
In summary, the original equation has only one unique positive integer solution:
$$
(x, y, z, n)=(3,1,70,2) .
$$

problem: 4. The sum of the first ten terms of an arithmetic sequence is 160 . The sum of the next ten terms of the sequence is 340 . What is the first term of the sequence?
solution:
4. $\frac{79}{10}$ Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{20}$ be the arithmetic sequence, and let $d$ be its common difference. Then $a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{10}=160$ and $a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{10}+a_{11}+$ $a_{12}+\cdots+a_{20}=160+340=500$. Recalling the formula for the sum of an arithmetic series involving the first term $a_{1}$ and common difference $d$, the first equation yields $5\left(2 a_{1}+9 d\right)=160$ or $2 a_{1}+9 d=32$, while the second equation yields $10\left(2 a_{1}+19 d\right)=500$ or $2 a_{1}+19 d=50$. Thus, we get a system of linear equations:
$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
2 a_{1}+9 d & =32 \\
2 a_{1}+19 d & =50 .
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the system gives the value of $a_{1}$.

problem: Example 19 If $a \geqslant b \geqslant c>0$, and $a<b+c$, solve the equation $b \sqrt{x^{2}-c^{2}}+c \sqrt{x^{2}-b^{2}}=a x$.
solution:
Given $a \geqslant b \geqslant c>0$, and $a<b+c$, so $a, b, c$ can form a triangle. Construct $\triangle A B C$ such that $B C=a, A C=b, A B=c$. Draw perpendiculars from $A$ to $A C$ and $A B$, and let them intersect at point $D$. Then the quadrilateral $A B D C$ is cyclic, as shown in Figure 3-23. At this point, $A D$ is the diameter, $\sin \angle B A D=\frac{B D}{A D}=\frac{\sqrt{A D^{2}-c^{2}}}{A D}, \sin \angle C A D=\frac{C D}{A D}=\frac{\sqrt{A D^{2}-b^{2}}}{A D}, \sin \angle C A B=\frac{a}{A D}$.

Applying Ptolemy's theorem or the three-chord theorem to $A D, A C, A B$, we have $A C \cdot \sin \angle B A D + A B \cdot \sin \angle C A D = A D \cdot \sin \angle C A B$, which is $b \cdot \frac{\sqrt{A D^{2}-c^{2}}}{A D} + c \cdot \frac{\sqrt{A D^{2}-b^{2}}}{A D} = A D \cdot \frac{a}{A D}$, or $b \cdot \sqrt{A D^{2}-c^{2}} + c \cdot \sqrt{A D^{2}-b^{2}} = a \cdot A D$.

Since $S_{\triangle A B C} = \frac{1}{2} b c \cdot \sin \angle C A B = \frac{a b c}{2 A D}$, and $S_{\triangle A B C} = \sqrt{p(p-a)(p-b)(p-c)}$, where $P = \frac{1}{2}(a+b+c)$, it follows that $A D = \frac{a b c}{2 \sqrt{p(p-a)(p-b)(p-c)}}$ is the solution to the original equation.

problem: Example 2 Find the sum $S=\sum_{k=1}^{n} k^{2}$.

6.17 Suppose there are $n$ tennis players who are to play doubles matches with the rule that each player must play exactly one match against every other player as an opponent. For which natural numbers $n$ can such a tournament be organized?
solution:
[Solution] $n$ satisfies $n \equiv 1(\bmod 8)$.
Assume the tournament has been conducted as required. Thus, for tennis player $A$, his opponents must be paired. Therefore, $n$ must be an odd number. Additionally, according to the problem, $A$ participates in $\frac{1}{2}(n-1)$ matches. Therefore, $n$ people participate in $\frac{1}{2} n(n-1)$ matches (including repeated counts). Since each match involves 4 people, in the above counting process, each match is counted exactly 4 times. Thus, $\frac{1}{2} n(n-1)$ should be a multiple of 4, i.e., $n-1$ is a multiple of 8.

Next, we prove that for $k=1,2, \cdots$, the doubles tournament for $n=8k+1$ players can be conducted as required.

When $k=1$, we place 9 players at the vertices of a regular nonagon $A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{9}$.

First, select $A_{1} A_{2}$ and $A_{3} A_{5}$ to play a doubles match, and connect the opponents with line segments. Then, we rotate these line segments by multiples of $\frac{2 \pi}{9}$ to get the structure of the other eight matches. In this structure, each chord $A_{ij}$ appears exactly once.

For $k>1$, we first select one player from the $8k+1$ tennis players, then divide the rest into $k$ groups of 8 people each, and sequentially conduct the matches for each group and the selected player according to the above procedure for 9 people. The remaining matches are between opponents from different groups, which can be achieved by dividing each group into four teams (each team of two people) and then conducting matches between different groups.

problem:
Problem 1. Let $k \leq 2022$ be a positive integer. Alice and Bob play a game on a $2022 \times 2022$ board. Initially, all cells are white. Alice starts and the players alternate. In her turn, Alice can either color one white cell in red or pass her turn. In his turn, Bob can either color a $k \times k$ square of white cells in blue or pass his turn. Once both players pass, the game ends and the person who colored more cells wins (a draw can occur).

For each $1 \leq k \leq 2022$, determine which player (if any) has a winning strategy.

(David Hruška)
solution:
Solution. Answer: For $k \in\{1,3,337,1011\}$ the game ends in a draw, otherwise Alice wins.

Fix $k$. Number the rows from top to bottom and the columns from left to right using numbers $1, \ldots, 2022$. We say that a cell is critical if its row-number and column-number are both divisible by $k$. Note that Bob colors exactly one critical cell in each his turn. Let $c=\lfloor 2022 / k\rfloor^{2}$ be the number of critical cells.

We distinguish 3 cases based on the value 2022/k.

(1) $2022 / k \notin \mathbb{Z}$. Then Alice can force a win, e.g. by primarily coloring the critical cells (and then coloring the rest): If she follows this strategy then Bob will color a $k \times k$ square in at most $c / 2$ of his turns, so in total he will color $\frac{1}{2} c \cdot k^{2}<\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2022^{2}$ cells.

(2) $2022 / k$ is an odd integer. Then Alice can force a win by the same strategy: In this case $c$ is odd, so Bob will color a $k \times k$ square in at most $\lfloor c / 2\rfloor<\frac{1}{2} c$ of his turns, so in total he will color strictly less than $\frac{1}{2} c \cdot k^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2022^{2}$ cells.

(3) $2022 / k$ is an even integer. Then both players can guarantee at least a draw: Alice by the above strategy, Bob by always coloring a $k \times k$ square whose bottom right corner cell is critical. Since in this case $c$ is even and each Alice's move prevents Bob from coloring at most 1 such square, using this strategy he will color at least $\frac{1}{2} c \cdot k^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2022^{2}$ cells.

Since $2022=2 \cdot 3 \cdot 337$, case (3) occurs if and only if $k \in\{1,3,337,1011\}$.

## Solution.

Domain of definition: $a \neq 1$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{2 a^{4}+a^{3}+4 a^{2}+a+2}{2 a^{3}-a^{2}+a-2}=\frac{\left(2 a^{4}+2 a^{2}\right)+\left(a^{3}+a\right)+\left(2 a^{2}+2\right)}{\left(2 a^{3}-2 a^{2}\right)+\left(a^{2}-a\right)+(2 a-2)}= \\
& =\frac{2 a^{2}\left(a^{2}+1\right)+a\left(a^{2}+1\right)+2\left(a^{2}+1\right)}{2 a^{2}(a-1)+a(a-1)+2(a-1)}=\frac{\left(a^{2}+1\right)\left(2 a^{2}+a+2\right)}{(a-1)\left(2 a^{2}+a+2\right)}=\frac{a^{2}+1}{a-1} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: $\frac{a^{2}+1}{a-1}$.

problem: 6. The brakes of a car allow it to stand on an inclined asphalt surface with an angle at the base of no more than $30^{\circ}$. Determine the minimum braking distance of this car when moving at a speed of $30 \, \text{m/s}$ on a flat horizontal road with the same surface. The acceleration due to gravity $g=10 \, \text{m/s}^2, \cos 30^{\circ} \approx 0.866, \sin 30^{\circ}=0.5 .(15$ points)
solution:
Answer: 78 m

Solution. For the situation when the car is on an inclined plane:
$F_{mp}=m g \sin \alpha$ (2 points), $\mu m g \cos \alpha=m g \sin \alpha$ (2 points). Therefore, the coefficient of friction: $\mu=\frac{\sin 30^{\circ}}{\cos 30^{\circ}} \approx 0.577$ (3 points). For the situation when the car is moving on a horizontal surface: $F_{mp}=m a, \mu m g=m a$ (2 points), $\mu g=a=5.77$ (3 points).

problem: 3. On the table, there are 140 different cards with numbers $4, 8, 12, \ldots, 556, 560$ (each card has exactly one number, and each number appears exactly once). In how many ways can 3 cards be chosen so that the sum of the numbers on the selected cards is divisible by 3?
solution:
Answer: 149224.

Solution. The given numbers, arranged in ascending order, form an arithmetic progression with a difference of 4. Therefore, the remainders of these numbers when divided by 3 alternate. Indeed, if one of these numbers is divisible by 3, i.e., has the form $3k$, where $k \in \mathbb{N}$, then the next number is $3k+4=3(k+1)+1$ - and it gives a remainder of 1 when divided by 3, followed by $3k+8=3(k+2)+2$, which gives a remainder of 2 when divided by 3, and then $-3k+12$, which is again divisible by 3. Thus, the remainders of the given numbers when divided by 3 go in the order $\ldots 0 ; 1 ; 2 ; 0 ; 1 ; 2 ; 0 \ldots$

Among the given numbers, there are 47 that give a remainder of 1 when divided by 3 (they form the set $A=\{4 ; 16 ; 28 ; \ldots ; 556\}$), 46 numbers that are divisible by 3 ($B=\{12 ; 24 ; 36 ; \ldots ; 552\}$), and 47 numbers that give a remainder of 2 when divided by 3 ($C=\{8 ; 20 ; 32 ; \ldots ; 560\}$).

The sum of three numbers can be divisible by 3 in the following cases.

1) All three numbers give the same remainder when divided by 3. There are $C_{46}^{3}$ ways to choose 3 numbers from set $B$ and $C_{47}^{3}$ ways to choose 3 numbers from sets $A$ and $C$. In total, we get $\frac{46 \cdot 45 \cdot 44}{6}+2 \cdot \frac{47 \cdot 46 \cdot 45}{6}=15180+2 \cdot 16215=47610$ ways.
2) If not all remainders are the same, then only the case where all three remainders are different fits, i.e., we must choose one number from each of the sets $A, B, C$. We get $47 \cdot 47 \cdot 46=$ 101614 ways.

In total, we get 149224 ways.

problem: 12.269. Two vertices of an equilateral triangle with side $a$ lie on the circumference of the upper base of a cylinder, while the third vertex lies on the circumference of the lower base. The plane of the triangle forms an angle $\alpha$ with the generatrix of the cylinder. Find the lateral surface area of the cylinder.
solution:
## Solution.

Let the side $BC$ of the equilateral triangle $ABC$ (Fig. 12.133) lie on the upper base of the cylinder, and the vertex $A$ on the circumference of the lower base, $BC=a, AM$ is the generator of the cylinder, $K$ is the midpoint of $BC$. Then $BM=CM, MK \perp BC, AK \perp BC$. Therefore, the line $BC$ is perpendicular to the plane $AMK$, which means the planes $AMK$ and $ABC$ are perpendicular.

In the plane $AMK$, a perpendicular $ML$ is drawn to $AK$. Then $AK$ is the projection of the line $AM$ on the plane $ABC$ and $\angle MAK=\alpha$.

$$
AK=\frac{a \sqrt{3}}{2}
$$

In $\triangle AMK\left(\angle AMK=90^{\circ}\right):$

$AM=AK \cos \angle MAK=\frac{a \sqrt{3}}{2} \cos \alpha ; MK=AK \sin \angle MAK=\frac{a \sqrt{3}}{2} \sin \alpha$.

In $\triangle AMB\left(\angle AMB=90^{\circ}\right):$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& BM^{2}=AB^{2}-AM^{2}=a^{2}-\frac{3 a^{2}}{4} \cos ^{2} \alpha=\frac{a^{2}}{4}\left(4-3 \cos ^{2} \alpha\right)= \\
& =\frac{a^{2}}{4}\left(1+3 \sin ^{2} \alpha\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The radius of the circle circumscribed around $\triangle BMC$:

$R=\frac{BM \cdot CM \cdot BC}{4 S_{\triangle BMC}}=\frac{BM^{2} \cdot BC}{4 \cdot \frac{1}{2} BC \cdot MK}=\frac{BM^{2}}{2 MK}=\frac{\frac{a^{2}}{4}\left(1+3 \sin ^{2} \alpha\right)}{a \sqrt{3} \sin \alpha}=$ $=\frac{a\left(3 \sin ^{2} \alpha+1\right)}{4 \sqrt{3} \sin \alpha}$.

The lateral surface area of the cylinder

$$
S=2 \pi R \cdot AM=2 \pi \cdot \frac{a\left(3 \sin ^{2} \alpha+1\right)}{4 \sqrt{3} \sin \alpha} \cdot \frac{a \sqrt{3}}{2} \cos \alpha=\frac{1}{4} \pi a^{2} \operatorname{ctg} \alpha\left(3 \sin ^{2} \alpha+1\right)
$$

Answer: $\frac{1}{4} \pi a^{2} \operatorname{ctg} \alpha\left(3 \sin ^{2} \alpha+1\right)$.

Example 4. Integrate the equation

$$
x(x+2 y) d x+\left(x^{2}-y^{2}\right) d y=0
$$
solution:
Solution. In this case

$$
P(x, y)=x(x+2 y), Q(x, y)=x^{2}-y^{2}
$$

from which

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=2 x, \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=2 x
$$

Condition (9.34) is satisfied, so the given equation is an equation in total differentials. Therefore,

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=x^{2}+2 y x, \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=x^{2}-y^{2}
$$

From the first equality, we obtain

$$
u(x, y)=\int\left(x^{2}+2 x y\right) d x
$$

or

$$
u(x, y)=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2} y+\varphi(y)
$$

Differentiating the function $u(x, y)$ with respect to $y$, we find

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=x^{2}+\varphi^{\prime}(y)
$$

Since

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=x^{2}-y^{2}
$$

then

$$
x^{2}+\varphi^{\prime}(y)=x^{2}-y^{2}
$$

from which

$$
\varphi^{\prime}(y)=-y^{2}
$$

and

$$
\varphi(y)=-\int y^{2} d y=-\frac{y^{3}}{3}+C_{1}
$$

Substituting the found expression for $\varphi(y)$ into the formula for $u(x, y)$, we get

$$
u(x, y)=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2} y-\frac{y^{3}}{3}+C_{1}=C_{2}
$$

or

$$
\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2} y-\frac{y^{3}}{3}=C_{3}
$$

Thus, the general integral can be written in the form

$$
x^{3}+3 x^{2} y-y^{3}=C, \text { where } C=3 C_{3}
$$

6.1. In an isosceles triangle \(ABC\), one of the angles is equal to the difference of the other two, and one of the angles is twice another. The angle bisectors of angles \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) intersect the circumcircle of the triangle at points \(L\), \(O\), and \(M\) respectively. Find the area of triangle \(LOM\), if the area of triangle \(ABC\) is 8. If the answer is not an integer, round it to the nearest integer.
solution:
Answer: 11. Solution. Let in triangle $ABC$ the angle $\alpha$ be equal to the difference of angles $\beta-\gamma$. Since $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^{\circ}$, then $\beta-\gamma+\beta+\gamma=180^{\circ}$ and therefore $\beta=90^{\circ}$. If $\beta=90^{\circ}$ is twice one of the angles $\alpha$ or $\gamma$, then the triangle will be isosceles, which contradicts the condition. Let for definiteness $\alpha>\gamma$. Then $\beta=90^{\circ}, \alpha=60^{\circ}, \gamma=30^{\circ}$.

By the inscribed angle theorem:

$\angle MLC = \angle MBC = 45^{\circ}, \angle CLO = \angle CAO = 30^{\circ}$. Therefore, $\angle MLO = 75^{\circ}$. Similarly,

$\angle LOM = \angle LOA + \angle AOM = \angle LCA + \angle ABM = 15^{\circ} + 45^{\circ} = 60^{\circ}$,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_1415bcd4b27ed98bd836g-05.jpg?height=569&width=596&top_left_y=2177&top_left_x=1324)
$\angle OML = \angle OMB + \angle BML = \angle OAB + \angle BCL = 30^{\circ} + 15^{\circ} = 45^{\circ}$.

Thus, the angles of triangle $LOM$ are $\alpha_{1}=75^{\circ}, \beta_{1}=60^{\circ}, \gamma_{1}=45^{\circ}$.

Using the sine rule, we get the formula for the area of a triangle inscribed in a circle of radius $R: S=\frac{1}{2} a b \sin \gamma=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 R \sin \alpha \cdot 2 R \sin \beta \cdot \sin \gamma=2 R^{2} \sin \alpha \sin \beta \sin \gamma$.

Therefore, $\frac{S_{LOM}}{S_{ABC}}=\frac{2 R \cdot \sin \alpha_{1} \sin \beta_{1} \sin \gamma_{1}}{2 R \cdot \sin \alpha \sin \beta \sin \gamma}=\frac{\sin 75^{\circ} \sin 60^{\circ} \sin 45^{\circ}}{\sin 90^{\circ} \sin 60^{\circ} \sin 30^{\circ}}=\sqrt{2} \cdot \sin 75^{\circ}$. Since $\sin 75^{\circ}=\sin \left(45^{\circ}+30^{\circ}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2}}{4}$, we get: $\frac{S_{LOM}}{S_{ABC}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2}$.

Therefore, $S_{LOM}=4 \sqrt{3}+4 \approx 11$.

$$
300 m+200 d=170 S \text { i.e. } 3 d+2 m=17
$$

Then we get $2 d=17-3 m$. $m$ can take values from 1 to 5, and since $2 d$ is even, $m$ can be 1, 3, and 5. If $m=1, d=7, m+d=8$; if $m=3, d=4, m+d=7$; if $m=5, d=1, m+d=6$. Since $m+d$ is odd, we get that the number of boys is 3 and the number of girls is 4.

problem: 13.291. If the execution of an order for a set of several books is entrusted to one of three typesetters, then the first will complete the work 10 hours faster, and the third will complete it 6 hours faster than the second. If one of the ordered books is set by the first typesetter, and another book is set simultaneously by the second, then in 9 hours they will set as many pages as the second and third, working together, will set in 10 hours under the same conditions. How much time will each typesetter need to set all the ordered books when working separately?
solution:
## Solution.

Let's assume the entire volume of work is 1. Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be the work rates (number of pages typed per hour) of the first, second, and third typists, respectively.

According to the problem, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{1}{\beta}-\frac{1}{\alpha}=10, \\
\frac{1}{\beta}-\frac{1}{\gamma}=6, \\
9(\alpha+\beta)=10(\beta+\gamma)
\end{array} \quad \text { from which } \alpha=\frac{1}{20}, \beta=\frac{1}{30}, \gamma=\frac{1}{24}\right.
$$

Then the first typist will complete the entire work in $\frac{1}{\alpha}=20$ (hours), the second $-3a \frac{1}{R}=30$ (hours), and the third $-3a \frac{1}{\gamma}=24$ (hours).

Answer: 20, 30, and 24 hours.

problem:
[ Homothetic Circles]

Given a triangle $ABC$. Four circles of equal radius $\rho$ are constructed such that one of them is tangent to the other three, and each of these three is tangent to two sides of the triangle. Find $\rho$, if the radii of the inscribed and circumscribed circles of the triangle are $r$ and $R$ respectively.
solution:
Let $A_{1}, B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ be the centers of the circles touching the sides of the triangle, $O$ be the center of the circle touching these circles, $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$ be the centers of the inscribed and circumscribed circles of triangle $A B C$. The lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$ and $C C_{1}$ are the angle bisectors of triangle $A B C$, so they intersect at point $O_{1}$. Therefore, triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ is transformed into triangle $A B C$ by a homothety with center $O_{1}$, and the coefficient of homothety is the ratio of the distances from point $O_{1}$ to the sides of triangles $A B C$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$, i.e., it is equal to $(r-\rho) / r$. Under this homothety, the circumscribed circle of triangle $A B C$ is transformed into the circumscribed circle of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$. Since $O A_{1}=O B_{1}=O C_{1}=2 \rho$, the radius of the circumscribed circle of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ is $2 \rho$. Therefore, $R(r-\rho) / r=2 \rho$, i.e., $\rho=r R /(2 r+R)$.

problem:
$2 \cdot 65$ When integers $x$ and $y$ are not both zero, find the minimum value of $f=|5 x^{2}+11 x y-5 y^{2}|$.
(Soviet Union University Mathematics Competition, 1977)
solution:
【Sol】When $x=1, y=0$
$$
f=\left|5 \cdot 1^{2}+11 \cdot 1 \cdot 0-5 \cdot 0^{2}\right|=5 \text {. }
$$

When $x, y$ are not both even, $f$ is odd.
When $x, y$ are both even, $\frac{x}{2}, \frac{y}{2}$ are integers, at this time we have
$$
f(x, y)>f\left(\frac{x}{2}, \frac{y}{2}\right) .
$$

If $\frac{x}{2}, \frac{y}{2}$ are still both even, the above process can continue. Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is obtained when $x$, $y$ are not both even, at this time $f$ is odd, and the minimum value of $f$ can only be 1, 3, or 5.
If the minimum value of $f$ is 1, then there exist $x_{0}, y_{0}$ such that
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left|5 x_{0}^{2}+11 x_{0} y_{0}-5 y_{0}^{2}\right|=1, \\
5 x_{0}^{2}+11 x_{0} y_{0}-5 y_{0}^{2}= \pm 1, \\
100 x_{0}^{2}+220 x_{0} y_{0}-100 y_{0}^{2}= \pm 20, \\
\left(10 x_{0}+11 y_{0}\right)^{2}-221 y_{0}^{2}= \pm 20 .
\end{array}
$$

Since $221=13 \cdot 17,20=13+7$, there exists an integer $t=10 x_{0}+11 y_{0}$, such that
$$
13 \mid t^{2} \pm 7
$$

Given
$$
\begin{array}{l}
t^{2}=(13 k)^{2} \equiv 0 \\
t^{2}=(13 k \pm 1)^{2} \equiv 1 \\
t^{2}=(13 k \pm 2)^{2} \equiv 4 \\
t^{2}=(13 k \pm 3)^{2} \equiv 9 \\
t^{2} \equiv(13 k \pm 4)^{2} \equiv 3 \\
t^{2} \equiv(13 k \pm 5)^{2} \equiv 12 \\
t^{2} \equiv(13 k \pm 6)^{2} \equiv 10
\end{array}
$$

At this time
$$
t^{2} \pm 7 \not \equiv 0
$$
$(\bmod 13)$, $(\bmod 13)$, $(\bmod 13)$, $(\bmod 13)$, $(\bmod 13)$, $(\bmod 13)$, $(\bmod 13)$, $(\bmod 13)$.
Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ cannot be 1.
If the minimum value of $f$ is 3, then there exist $x_{1}, y_{1}$ such that
$$
5 x_{1}^{2}+11 x_{1} y_{1}-5 y_{1}^{2}= \pm 3 \text {, }
$$

which means
$$
\left(10 x_{1}+11 y_{1}\right)^{2}-221 y_{1}^{2}= \pm 60 \text {. }
$$

Thus, there exists an integer $r$, such that $r=10 x_{1}+11 y_{1}$, and
$$
13 \mid t^{2} \pm 8 \text {. }
$$

From the above, this is also impossible. Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is 5.

problem: Example 3 As shown in Figure 1.4.4, in quadrilateral $A B C D$, $\angle B=\angle C=60^{\circ}, B C=1$, a circle is drawn with $C D$ as its diameter intersecting $A B$ at point $M$ and tangent to $A B$ at point $M$, and intersects $B C$ at point $E$. Find the length of segment $B E$.
solution:
Solution 1 (Cutting out an isosceles triangle) Connect $O M$, then $O M \perp A B$, so by the given conditions, it is easy to know $\angle C O M=150^{\circ}$. Connect $O E$, it is easy to know $\triangle C O E$ is an equilateral triangle, thus $\triangle E O M$ is an isosceles right triangle, i.e., $O M=O E=C E, \angle B M E=\angle E M O=45^{\circ}$, hence
$$
M E=\sqrt{2} O E=\sqrt{2} C E=\sqrt{2}(1-B E)
$$

From $E M: \sin 60^{\circ}=B E: \sin 45^{\circ}$ we know $M E=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} B E$.
From $\sqrt{2}(1-B E)=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} B E$ we find $B E=4-2 \sqrt{3}$.
Solution 2 (Cutting out a parallelogram) Connect $O E$, it is easy to know $O E=C E$ and $O E \parallel A B$. Connect $O M$, then $O M \perp A B$, draw $O F \parallel B C$ intersecting $A B$ at $F$, we get $\square B E O F$. Thus
$$
M F=\frac{1}{2} O F=\frac{1}{2} B E, F B=O E=C E=1-B E
$$

And
$$
B M^{2}=B E \cdot 1=B E
$$

So
$$
\left(\frac{1}{2} B E+1-B E\right)^{2}=B E
$$

That is $B E^{2}-8 B E+4=0$. Hence $B E=4-\sqrt{3}$.
Solution 3 (Cutting out a square) Connect $O M, O E$, draw $E N \perp B M$ at $N$, then $E O M N$ is a square. Thus
$$
B N=\frac{1}{2} B E, M N=O E=C E=1-B E
$$

So
$$
B M=\frac{1}{2} B E+1-B E
$$

Thus
$$
\left(\frac{1}{2} B E+1-B E\right)^{2}=B M^{2}=B E \cdot 1=B E
$$

That is $B E=4-2 \sqrt{3}$.
Solution 4 (Completing a regular triangle) Extend $B A$ and $C D$ to intersect at $P$, then $\triangle B C P$ is a regular triangle, thus $C P=B P=B C=1$, by the secant-tangent theorem we know
$$
B M^{2}=B E \cdot B C=B E,(1-B M)^{2}=P M^{2}=P D \cdot P C=1-C D
$$

Connect $O E$, it is easy to know $O C=E C$, so
$$
(1-B M)^{2}=1-2 C E=1-2(1-B E)=2 B E-1
$$

Thus
$$
(1-\sqrt{B E})^{2}=2 B E-1
$$

That is $B E=4-2 \sqrt{3}$.
Solution 5 (Completing a right triangle) Connect $M O$ and extend it to intersect the extension of $B C$ at $Q$, then $M Q \perp A B$, and $\angle Q=30^{\circ}$, thus $B M=\frac{1}{2}(1+C P)$. Connect $O E$, it is easy to know $O C$ is the median of the hypotenuse of $\mathrm{Rt} \triangle E Q O$, i.e., $C P=C E=1-B E$, substituting into the above equation gives $B M=1-\frac{1}{2} B E$, and $B M^{2}=B E$, so $\sqrt{B E}=1-\frac{1}{2} B E$, thus $B E=4-2 \sqrt{3}$.

problem: Let $A$ and $G$ be two opposite vertices of a unit cube. What is the distance between the plane $S_{A}$ determined by the vertices adjacent to $A$, and the plane $S_{G}$ determined by the vertices adjacent to $G$?
solution:
I. Solution. We will show that the planes $S_{A}$ and $S_{G}$ trisect the body diagonal $A G$ of the cube, and thus their distance is $\frac{A G}{3}=\sqrt{3} / 3$.

The $120^{\circ}$ rotations around the $A G$ diagonal map the cube onto itself. Therefore, during these rotations, the planes $S_{A}$ and $S_{G}$ map onto themselves, meaning both planes are perpendicular to the body diagonal $A G$. Due to symmetry, the distance from point $G$ to the plane $S_{G}$ is equal to the distance from point $A$ to the plane $S_{A}$. Therefore, it is sufficient to show that, for example, the latter distance is equal to the distance between the planes $S_{A}$ and $S_{G}$.

1987-03-113-1.eps

Figure 1

Reflect the cube over the midpoint of the face diagonal $B D$. Thus, we obtain a cube $A B C D G^{\prime} H^{\prime} E^{\prime} F^{\prime}$ that shares a face with the original one (Figure 1). The reflection of the plane $S_{A}=E B D$ is itself, and thus the distance from point $A$ to the plane $S_{A}$ is equal to the distance from the reflected point and the reflected plane, i.e., the distance from point $C$ to the plane $S_{A}$. The latter is precisely the distance between the planes $S_{A}$ and $S_{G}$, since point $C$ lies in the plane $S_{G}$. This completes the proof.

II. Solution. Label the vertices of the cube as shown in Figure 1, and consider the vectors $\overrightarrow{A B}, \overrightarrow{A D}$, and $\overrightarrow{A E}$ from point $A$ to the adjacent vertices (Figure 2).

1987-03-114-1.eps

Figure 2

It is known that the vector from point $A$ to the centroid $T_{A}$ of triangle $E B D$ is the arithmetic mean of the vectors to the vertices of the triangle, $\overrightarrow{A T_{A}}=\frac{1}{3}(\overrightarrow{A B}+\overrightarrow{A D}+\overrightarrow{A E})$. On the other hand, clearly $\overrightarrow{A B}+\overrightarrow{A D}+\overrightarrow{A E}=\overrightarrow{A B}+\overrightarrow{B C}+\overrightarrow{C G}=\overrightarrow{A G}$, so $\overrightarrow{A G}=3 \overrightarrow{A T_{A}}$.

The obtained equality means that points $A, T_{A}$, and $G$ lie on the same line, and the point $T_{A}$, and thus the plane $S_{G}$, trisects the segment $A G$. This is of course also true for the plane $S_{G}$. Since the body diagonal $A G$ is perpendicular to the planes $S_{A}$ and $S_{G}$, the distance between the two planes is one-third of the body diagonal, $\sqrt{3} / 3$.

Remark. In both solutions, only the perpendicularity of the planes in question and the body diagonal to the cube's special properties (3rd order rotational symmetry) was needed for the proof, so the solutions generally show that in any parallelepiped, the planes through the vertices adjacent to the endpoints of a body diagonal trisect the body diagonal.

2. Find all pairs of natural numbers $a$ and $b$ such that

$$
\operatorname{HCF}(a+1, b+1)=a^{2}-b^{2}
$$
solution: 2. Let $a+1=d x$ and $b+1=d y$, where $d, x, y$ are natural numbers, $x>y$ and GCD $(x, y)=1$. Then LCM $(a+1, b+1)=d x y=(d x-1)^{2}-(d y-1)^{2}=$ $d(x-y)(d x+d y-2)$ and hence $d x+d y-2=\frac{x y}{x-y}$. Since $x-y$ is coprime with both $x$ and $y$, it must be $x-y=1$. The previous equation becomes $d(2 x-1)-2=x(x-1)$, so $2 x-1\left|x^{2}-x+2\right|(2 x-1)^{2}+7$, thus $2 x-1 \mid 7$, i.e., $x=1$ or $x=4$. The first possibility obviously fails, and the second gives $d=2$ and $(a, b)=(7,5)$.

solution:
Answer: $A=376,625$.

Solution. By the condition, $A^{2}-A=A(A-1)$ is divisible by $1000=2^{3} \cdot 5^{3}$. Due to the mutual simplicity of $A$ and $A-1$, one of them is divisible by $2^{3}=8$, and the other by $5^{3}=125$.

If $A$ is divisible by 125, then $A \in\{125,250,375,500,625,750,875\}$ and $A-1 \in\{124,249,374,499,624,749,874\}$ - is divisible by 8, which is only possible when $A=625$.

problem:
## Task 6 - 070836

A two-digit natural number is sought with the following properties:

1) The difference between its digits is three.
2) If its digits are swapped, the new number is nine less than twice the original number.
solution:
(I) Since the number is supposed to be two-digit, it must be greater than 9. This implies that its double, reduced by 9, must be greater than the number itself.

Due to the second condition, this means that by reversing the digits of the number, a larger number should result. Therefore, its first digit must be smaller than its second.

(II) Furthermore, the double reduced by 9 should again be two-digit, i.e., at most 99.

This implies that the number can be at most 54. Given the first condition, the following possibilities remain: 14, 25, 36, and 47.

Of these, only the number 36 satisfies all the conditions of the problem.

Thus, the cosine of the angle is:

$\cos (\overrightarrow{A B}, \overrightarrow{A C})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

and consequently, the angle

problem: 8.5. Given a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$ with side $A D$ equal to 3. Diagonals $A C$ and $B D$ intersect at point $E$, and it is known that the areas of triangles $A B E$ and $D C E$ are both 1. Find the side $B C$, given that the area of $A B C D$ does not exceed 4.
solution:
# Answer: 3.

Solution: Triangles $A B D$ and $A C D$ have the same area, as they are composed of the common $A E D$ and equal-area $A B E$ and $D C E$. Since $A B D$ and $A C D$ have the same base $A D$, their heights to this base are equal. Therefore, $B C$ is parallel to $A D$, meaning our quadrilateral is a trapezoid.

Let $B C$ be $x$. Triangles $B E C$ and $A E D$ are similar, so $B E / E D = B C / A D = x / 3$. Additionally, the area of $B E C$ is $B E / E D$ of the area of $B C D$, since these triangles have the same base, and their heights are in the ratio of $B E$ to $E D$. Therefore, the area of $B E C$ is $x / 3$. Similarly, the area of $A E D$ is $3 / x$.

Since the area of the entire quadrilateral does not exceed 4, $x / 3 + 3 / x \leq 2$.

However, the sum of the reciprocals of positive quantities is always at least 2, and equality is achieved only when the terms are equal, i.e., in our case, $x / 3 = 3 / x$, from which $x$ equals 3.

Criteria: Only the answer - 0 points. Proved that $A B C D$ is a trapezoid - plus 2 points. Obtained the equation - plus 1 point. Not explained why the inequality is possible only when the terms are equal - deduct 1 point.

problem: 4.3. Find the number of non-empty subsets of the set $\{1,2, \ldots, 20\}$ in which the number of elements does not exceed the smallest of them.
solution:
4.3. Answer: $17711=F_{21}$ (21st Fibonacci number).

It is clear that the number of subsets of the required type, containing exactly $m$ elements, is $C_{21-m}^{m}$. Then the desired number is $-S_{21}$, where $S_{n}=\sum_{k+m=n} C_{k}^{m}$. Note that from the equality $C_{k}^{m}=C_{k-1}^{m}+C_{k-1}^{m-1}$ it follows that $S_{n}=S_{n-1}+S_{n-2}$. Since $S_{0}=S_{1}=1$, then $S_{n}$ is the $n$-th Fibonacci number.

problem: 3B. Determine the smallest natural number, the product of whose digits is equal to 75600.
solution:
Solution. We factorize the number 75600 into prime factors and get $75600=2^{4} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{2} \cdot 7$. Since all prime divisors of 75600 are single-digit numbers, this means there exists a number such that the product of its digits is equal to 75600.

The desired number contains the digits 5, 5, and 7, because multiplying any of the numbers 2, 3, 5, 7 by 5 or 7 results in a number greater than 9. The product $2^{4} 3^{3}$ can be written with at most 7 digits ($2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3$), and with at least 3 digits (6$\cdot$8.9). Since we are looking for the smallest natural number, we conclude that it is written with the digits $6,8,9,5,5,7$, which is the number 556789.

problem:
Exercise 6. Do there exist non-negative rational numbers $x, y$ and $z$ such that:

$$
x^{5}+2 y^{5}+5 z^{5}=11
$$
solution:
## Solution.

We will show that there are no such rationals $x, y, z$. We proceed by contradiction, assuming that such rationals do exist. Let $d$ be the smallest common denominator of $x, y$, and $z$. We can then write $x=\frac{a}{d}$, $y=\frac{b}{d}$, and $z=\frac{c}{d}$ for some integers $a, b$, and $c$. The equation we want to solve becomes:

$$
a^{5}+2 b^{5}+5 c^{5}=11 d^{5}
$$

Let's study this equation modulo 11. An exhaustive search (or the use of Fermat's Little Theorem) shows that a fifth power is congruent to 0, 1, or -1 modulo 11. We deduce that the congruence $a^{5}+2 b^{5}+5 c^{5} \equiv 0(\bmod 11)$ implies that $a, b$, and $c$ are all multiples of 11. Thus, $a^{5}+2 b^{5}+5 c^{5}$ is divisible by $11^{5}$, from which we deduce that $d$ is also divisible by 11. The fractions $\frac{a}{d}, \frac{b}{d}$, and $\frac{c}{d}$ can therefore all be simplified by 11. This contradicts the minimality of $d$ and completes the proof.

problem: 14*. What are the necessary and sufficient conditions for a given convex dihedral angle to be inscribed in a surface of a cone of revolution so that the edges of the angle are generators of the conical surface?
solution:
14. Let a convex quadrilateral angle be inscribed in a surface of a cone of revolution. Since the axis of rotation $l$ lies in the plane of symmetry of each pair of generators, the dihedral angles formed by the plane of the face and two planes passing through the axis and adjacent edges are congruent to each other. Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ be the magnitudes of the dihedral angles at the edges of the quadrilateral angle, and let $\alpha^{\prime}, \alpha^{\prime \prime}, \beta^{\prime}, \beta^{\prime \prime}, \gamma^{\prime}, \gamma^{\prime \prime}, \delta^{\prime}, \delta^{\prime \prime}$ be the magnitudes of the parts of these angles, obtained by dividing them by planes passing through the edges and the axis of the conical surface. To make the picture more vivid, intersect the surface with a plane perpendicular to the axis. Then we get the figure shown in Figure 109. Here $O$ is a point on the axis, and $A, B, C, D$ are points on the edges. First, consider case (a), where the axis lies inside the angle. Then we get: $\alpha+\gamma=\alpha^{\prime}+\alpha^{\prime \prime}+\gamma^{\prime}+\gamma^{\prime \prime}$, $\beta+\delta=\beta^{\prime}+\beta^{\prime \prime}+\delta^{\prime}+\delta^{\prime \prime}$. But $\alpha^{\prime}=\delta^{\prime \prime}, \alpha^{\prime \prime}=\beta^{\prime}, \gamma^{\prime}=\beta^{\prime \prime}$ and $\gamma^{\prime \prime}=\delta^{\prime}$. Therefore, $\alpha+\gamma=\beta+\delta$. Cases (b) and (c) are considered similarly: in all cases, the condition $\alpha+\gamma=\beta+\delta$ will be satisfied (prove this). Therefore, this condition is necessary.

Now suppose we are given that in a convex quadrilateral angle with vertex $S$, the sums are equal: $\alpha+\gamma=\beta+\delta$.

First, assume that not all angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ are equal to each other, and let $\alpha>\beta$; then $\gamma<\delta$. Consider a similar section (Figure 110), where $A, B, C, D$ are points on the edges of the quadrilateral angle. Construct inside angle $\alpha$ an angle equal in magnitude to $\beta$, and inside $\delta$ an angle equal in magnitude to $\gamma$. Let $(S M)$ be the intersection of the new planes, $(S P)$ be the intersection of the planes $S D M$ and $S B C$, and $S N$ be the intersection of the planes $S A M$ and $S B C$. The trihedral angles $S A B N$ and $S C D P$ are symmetric due to the congruence of the angles at the faces $S A B$ and $S C D$. The trihedral angle $S A D M$ is also symmetric because the angles at the edges $[S A)$ and $[S D)$ are congruent: $\alpha-\beta=\gamma-\delta$ (from the main condition). Therefore, the plane of symmetry of the edges $[S A)$ and $[S B)$ will pass through the edge $[S N)$, the plane of symmetry of the edges $[S C)$ and $[S D)$ will pass through the edge $[S P)$, and the plane of symmetry of the edges $[S A)$ and $[S D)$ will pass through the edge $[S M)$. At the same time, these three planes are the planes of symmetry of the trihedral angle $S N M P$ and therefore intersect along one line $S O$, the points of which are equidistant from all four edges: $[S A)$, $[S B)$, $[S C)$, $[S D)$. In the case of equal dihedral angles, the sufficiency of the condition is proved more simply by considering the planes of symmetry of this quadrilateral angle.

problem: Example 5 (2005 National High School Mathematics League Test Question) Define the function $f(k)=\left\{\begin{array}{l}0, k \text { is a perfect square } \\ {\left[\frac{1}{\{\sqrt{k}\}}\right], k \text { is not a perfect square, }}\end{array}\right.$ Find $\sum_{k=1}^{240} f(k)$.
solution:
Solve $15^{2}<240<16^{2}$.
Since $k$ is a perfect square when $f(k)=0$, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=1}^{240} f(k) & =\sum_{k=1+1}^{2^{2}-1} f(k)+\sum_{k=2^{2}+1}^{3^{2}-1} f(k)+\cdots+\sum_{k=14^{2}+1}^{15^{2}-1} f(k)+\sum_{k=226}^{240} f(k) \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{14} \sum_{k=n^{2}+1}^{(n+1)^{2}-1} f(k)+\sum_{k=226}^{240} f(k) .
\end{aligned}
$$

When $n^{2}+1 \leqslant k \leqslant(n+1)^{2}-1$, $[\sqrt{k}]=n,\{k\}=\sqrt{k}-[k]=\sqrt{k}-n$.
Thus, $\left[\frac{1}{\{\sqrt{k}\}}\right]=\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}-n}\right]=\left[\frac{\sqrt{k}+n}{k-n^{2}}\right]=\left[\frac{[\sqrt{k}+n]}{k-n^{2}}\right]=\left[\frac{2 n}{k-n^{2}}\right]$.
Therefore, $\sum_{k=n^{2}+1}^{(n+1)^{2}-1} f(k)=\sum_{k=n^{2}+1}^{(n+1)^{2}-1}\left[\frac{2 n}{k-n^{2}}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{2 n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=226}^{240} f(k) & =\sum_{k=226}^{240}\left[\frac{2 \cdot 15}{k-15^{2}}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{15}\left[\frac{30}{i}\right] . \\
\text { Hence } \sum_{k=1}^{240} f(k) & =\sum_{n=1}^{14} \sum_{i=1}^{2 n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]+\sum_{i=1}^{15}\left[\frac{30}{i}\right] \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{14}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]+\sum_{i=n+1}^{2 n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{15}\left[\frac{30}{i}\right] \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{14}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]+n\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{15}\left[\frac{30}{i}\right] \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{14} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]+\sum_{i=1}^{15}\left[\frac{30}{i}\right]+\sum_{n=1}^{14} n \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{15} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right]+105 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $T_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{2 n}{i}\right], 1 \leqslant n \leqslant 15$.
Then $T_{1}=\left[\frac{2}{1}\right]=2, T_{2}=\left[\frac{4}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{4}{2}\right]=4+2=6$,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
T_{3}=\left[\frac{6}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{6}{2}\right]+\left[\frac{6}{3}\right]=6+3+2=11, \\
T_{4}=\left[\frac{8}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{8}{2}\right]+\left[\frac{8}{3}\right]+\left[\frac{8}{4}\right]=8+4+2 \times 2=16, \\
T_{5}=\left[\frac{10}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{10}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{10}{5}\right]=10+5+3+2 \times 2=22, \\
T_{6}=\left[\frac{12}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{12}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{12}{6}\right]=12+6+4+3+2 \times 2=29, \\
T_{7}=\left[\frac{14}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{14}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{14}{7}\right]=14+7+4+3+2 \times 3=34, \\
T_{8}=\left[\frac{16}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{16}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{16}{8}\right]=16+8+5+4+3+2 \times 3=42, \\
T_{9}=\left[\frac{18}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{18}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{18}{9}\right]=18+9+6+4+3 \times 2+2 \times 3=49, \\
T_{10}=\left[\frac{20}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{20}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{20}{10}\right]=20+10+6+5+4+3+2 \times 4=56, \\
T_{11}=\left[\frac{22}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{22}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{22}{11}\right]=22+11+7+5+4+3 \times 2+2 \times 4=63, \\
T_{12}=\left[\frac{24}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{24}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{24}{12}\right]=24+12+8+6+4 \times 2+3 \times 2+2 \times 4=72, \\
T_{13}=\left[\frac{26}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{26}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{26}{13}\right]=26+13+8+6+5+4+3 \times 2+2 \times 5=78, \\
T_{14}=\left[\frac{28}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{28}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{28}{14}\right]=28+14+9+7+5+4 \times 2+3 \times 2+2 \times 5=87, \\
T_{15}=\left[\frac{30}{1}\right]+\left[\frac{30}{2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac{30}{15}\right]=30+15+10+7+6+5+4+3 \times 3+2 \times 5=96, \\
\text { Hence } \sum_{k=1}^{240} f(k)=\sum_{n=1}^{15} T_{n}+105 \\
=2+6+11+16+22+29+34+42+49+56+63+72+78+87+96+105 \\
=768.
\end{array}
$$

problem:
## Task 22/61

The trough of a ship lift weighs $a$ t in its empty state, and the water filling weighs $b$ t. To balance, counterweights with a total weight of $(a+b)$ t are attached.

How great is the excess weight of the trough with its contents if a ship with a weight (including cargo) of $c \mathrm{t}$ is in the trough?
solution:
The excess weight is zero!

According to Archimedes' principle, a floating body displaces a volume of liquid with the same weight as its own. When the ship enters the trough, therefore, $c$ tons of water have flowed out and the weight of the trough with its contents has thus remained unchanged.

problem:
7.142. $\left\{\begin{array}{l}\log _{2} x+\log _{4} y=4, \\ \log _{4} x+\log _{2} y=5\end{array}\right.$

The system of equations is:
\[
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\log _{2} x+\log _{4} y=4, \\ 
\log _{4} x+\log _{2} y=5
\end{array}\right.
\]
solution:
Solution.

Domain of definition: $\left\{\begin{array}{l}x>0, \\ y>0 .\end{array}\right.$

Let's switch to base 2. We have

$\left\{\begin{array}{l}\log _{2} x+\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} y=4, \\ \frac{1}{2} \log _{2} x+\log _{2} y=5\end{array} \Leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}2 \log _{2} x+\log _{2} y=8, \\ \log _{2} x+2 \log _{2} y=10\end{array} \Rightarrow\right.\right.$

$\Rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}\log _{2} x^{2} y=8, \\ \log _{2} x y^{2}=10\end{array} \Leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}x^{2} y=2^{8}, \\ x y^{2}=2^{10} .\end{array}\right.\right.$

From the first equation of the system $y=\frac{2^{8}}{x^{2}}$. From the second equation $x \cdot\left(\frac{2^{8}}{x^{2}}\right)^{2}=2^{10}, x^{3}=2^{6}$, hence $x=4, y=16$.

Answer: $(4 ; 16)$

problem:
The radius of the Earth is approximately $6670 \mathrm{~km}$. Suppose a wire is adjusted to fit exactly over the Equator, which is a circle with a radius approximately equal to $6670 \mathrm{~km}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_01_a444074f1f8ae50444d5g-06.jpg?height=236&width=228&top_left_y=1633&top_left_x=1466)

Next, suppose the length of the wire is increased by $1 \mathrm{~m}$, so that the wire and the Equator form concentric circles around the Earth. Can a man standing, an ant, or an elephant pass under this wire?

## List 6
solution:
Given that the radius of the Earth is very large, and only an additional $1 \mathrm{~m}$ was added to the length of the wire, it seems that the clearance between the wire and the Equator is very small. Moreover, if we replace the Earth with Jupiter or a marble and perform the same experiment, it seems that the height of the clearance between the extended wire and the equator of the sphere also changes, such that the larger the sphere considered, the smaller the clearance between the wire and the equator of the sphere.

Let's see that this intuitive idea is false and that the height of the clearance between the wire and the Equator is approximately $16 \mathrm{~cm}$, regardless of the radius of the sphere on which the experiment is performed.

Consider a circle of radius $R$. Its circumference is equal to $2 \pi R$. Let's also consider a circle with the same center, but with a circumference equal to $2 \pi R + 1$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_01_a444074f1f8ae50444d5g-25.jpg?height=329&width=331&top_left_y=2153&top_left_x=1407)

This circle has a radius equal to $R + h$, where $h$ is the height of the clearance between the two circles. Since a circle with radius $R + h$ has a circumference of $2 \pi (R + h)$, we obtain the equation $2 \pi (R + h) = 2 \pi R + 1$. Simplifying this expression, we get $h = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \approx \frac{1}{6.28} \approx 0.16$. Therefore, for any value of $R$, the height of the clearance is approximately $16 \mathrm{~cm}$.

Thus, only the ant is able to pass under the wire.

Since $|m|>1$ and $|n|>1$, we have $x \neq 0$ and $y \neq 0$.

we have $9 x^{2}+16 y^{2}=144\left(\frac{x^{2}}{16}+\frac{y^{2}}{9}\right)=144(x+y-1)^{2}$.

problem: We * Does there exist an injective function $f: \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$, such that for any $x \in \mathbf{R}$, we have $f\left(x^{2}\right)-f^{2}(x) \geqslant \frac{1}{4}$?
solution:
If there exists an injective function satisfying the conditions, then let $x=0$ and 1, we get 
\[
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
f(0)-f^{2}(0) \geqslant \frac{1}{4}, \\
f(1)-f^{2}(1) \geqslant \frac{1}{4},
\end{array}\right.
\]
thus $\left(f(0)-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} \leqslant 0,\left(f(1)-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} \leqslant 0$. Therefore, $f(0)=f(1)=\frac{1}{2}$, which contradicts the fact that $f$ is injective. Hence, there does not exist an injective function that meets the requirements.

problem: Question 233: Let the difference between any two adjacent interior angles of a convex $\mathrm{n}$-sided polygon be $20^{\circ}$, find the maximum possible value of $\mathrm{n}$.
solution:
Question 233, Solution: Let the convex $n$-sided polygon satisfying the conditions be $A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{n}$.
Let the exterior angle of $A_{i}(1 \leq i \leq n)$ be $\alpha_{i}$, then $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_{i}=360$, and $\alpha_{i+1}-\alpha_{i} \in\{20,-20\}$, where $1 \leq i \leq n$, and $\alpha_{n+1}=\alpha_{1}$.
Let $\alpha_{i+1}-\alpha_{i}=k_{i} \cdot 20^{\circ}$, where $k_{i} \in\{-1,1\}$, then
$$
\begin{array}{l}
0=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\alpha_{i+1}-\alpha_{i}\right)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} k_{i}\right) \cdot 20^{\circ} \\
\Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{n} k_{i}=0
\end{array}
$$

Thus, the number of 1s and -1s in $k_{1}, k_{2}, \ldots, k_{n}$ is the same, so $n$ is even. Let $n=2 t$.
According to the conditions, $\alpha_{2i-1}+\alpha_{2i}>20^{\circ}(1 \leq i \leq t)$. Therefore,
$$
360^{\circ}=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(\alpha_{2 i-1}+\alpha_{2 i}\right)>20 t^{\circ}
$$

Thus, $t<18$, which means $t \leq 17$. Therefore, $n=2 t \leq 34$.
On the other hand, when $n=34$, take $\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{3}=\ldots=\alpha_{33}=\frac{10}{17}^{\circ}, \alpha_{2}=\alpha_{4}=\ldots=\alpha_{34}=\frac{350}{17}^{\circ}$, which satisfies the conditions.
In summary, the maximum value of $n$ that satisfies the conditions is 34.

problem:
Using the numbers from 1 to 22 exactly once each, Antoine writes 11 fractions: for example, he can write the fractions $\frac{10}{2}, \frac{4}{3}, \frac{15}{5}, \frac{7}{6}, \frac{8}{9}, \frac{11}{19}, \frac{12}{14}, \frac{13}{17}, \frac{22}{21}, \frac{18}{16}$, and $\frac{20}{1}$.

Antoine wishes to have as many fractions as possible with integer values among the fractions written: in the previous example, he wrote three fractions with integer values: $\frac{10}{2}=5, \frac{15}{5}=3$, and $\frac{20}{1}=20$. What is the maximum number of fractions that can have integer values?
solution:
First, it is possible to make 10 integers with the fractions

$$
\left\{\frac{22}{11}, \frac{20}{10}, \frac{18}{9}, \frac{16}{8}, \frac{14}{7}, \frac{12}{6}, \frac{21}{3}, \frac{19}{1}, \frac{15}{5}, \frac{4}{2}, \frac{17}{13}\right\}
$$

Furthermore, it is impossible to have 11 integer fractions. Indeed, there are 3 prime numbers that have no multiple smaller than 22: 19, 17, and 13. Thus, the only way for one of these three numbers to form an integer fraction is with the number 1, which can only be used with one of these three numbers.

Comment from the graders: The exercise was generally very well done. However, some students, although they noticed the importance of 13, 17, and 19, did not think to associate two of them in the same fraction, and therefore only obtain 9 integer fractions, which is a pity. Other students were content with a configuration of 10 fractions without justifying that it is optimal. Finally, we remind you that $\frac{19}{8}$ is definitely not an integer.

problem: 23.4. Is it possible to color 25 cells on a grid paper so that each of them has an odd number of colored neighbors? (Neighboring cells are those that share a common side.)
solution:
23.4. Let several cells be colored on a grid paper, and let $n_{k}$ be the number of colored cells that have exactly $k$ colored neighbors. Let $N$ be the number of common sides of colored cells. Since each of them belongs to exactly two colored cells, $N=\left(n_{1}+2 n_{2}+3 n_{3}+4 n_{4}\right) / 2=\left(n_{1}+n_{3}\right) / 2+n_{2}+$ $+n_{3}+2 n_{4}$. Since $N$ is an integer, the number $n_{1}+n_{3}$ is even.

We have proved that the number of colored cells having an odd number of colored neighbors is always even. Therefore, it is impossible to color 25 cells so that each of them has an odd number of colored neighbors.

problem:
9,10
In the tournament, each chess player scored half of all their points in matches against the participants who took the last three places.
How many people in total participated in the tournament

#
solution:
For brevity, let's call the players who took the last three places "bad," and all others "good." The bad players played three games among themselves, and in these games, a total of three points were scored. According to the condition, this is half of all the points scored by the bad players; therefore, in games with the good players, the bad players scored another 3 points. However, a total of \(3(n-3)\) games were played between the bad and good players, and the same number of points were distributed (\(n\) is the total number of players). Of these, 3 points were taken by the bad players, and the rest by the good players. Therefore, in games with the bad players, the good players won \(3(n-3) - 3 = 3(n-4)\) points, and thus, the good players scored (in total) \(3(n-4)\) points in games with each other. Between the good players, there were \(\frac{1}{2}(n-3)(n-4)\) games and the same number of points were distributed. Therefore, \((n-3)(n-4) = 6(n-4)\), from which \(n=4\) or \(n=9\). The first option should be excluded, as in this case, the only good player would have scored 0 points, meaning he would not have been the first. The only solution left is \(n=9\). For nine players, this could have happened: an example of the corresponding tournament table is given below.

## Answer

9 people.

problem: Problem 1. (4 points) On the plane, a line is given. Using a compass, find two points on a line perpendicular to the given one. It is allowed to draw the compass so that the resulting circle passes through a given point or through two given points (the distance between which is less than the diameter of the compass). It is assumed that it is not possible to draw the compass so that the circle touches the given line.
solution: Solution. Let's mark three points $A, B$, and $C$ on the given line $l$ such that $AB$ and $BC$ are smaller than the diameter of the circle. Let's draw the circle so that it passes through points $A$ and $B$. This gives us two circles $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$, symmetric with respect to the line $l$. In the same way, we obtain circles $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$, which pass through $B$ and $C$. Then the intersection points $D=k_{1} \cap n_{1}$ and $E=k_{2} \cap n_{2}$ are symmetric with respect to $l$, i.e., they determine a line perpendicular to $l$.

problem:
## Task 2 - 310512

Maik meets with six classmates. One of them is named Heino, one is named Torsten, and four are named Steffen. Furthermore, four of these seven students have the last name Lehmann, one has the last name Krull, and two have the last name Pfitzner, but with different first names.

a) Show that for two of the seven students, the first and last name can be uniquely determined from these details! Provide the first and last names of these two students!

b) Investigate whether the first and last names of any additional students can be uniquely determined from the given information or if for each additional student, there are multiple possibilities to combine first and last names to satisfy the above details!
solution:
a) If no student were named Steffen Lehmann, then the four students named Steffen and the four students named Lehmann would be eight different students, which is not possible. Therefore, at least one student must be named Steffen Lehmann.

If none of the other six students were named Steffen Lehmann, then three students named Steffen and three students named Lehmann would already be these six different students. Thus, the last name Pfitzner would only apply to students with the first name Steffen, which contradicts the given information. Therefore, at least one more student must be named Steffen Lehmann.

b) For the remaining five students, it is consistent with the given first names Steffen, Steffen, Maik, Heino, Torsten to combine the last names Lehmann, Lehmann, Pfitzner, Pfitzner, Krull as well as the last names Pfitzner, Krull, Lehmann, Lehmann, Pfitzner.

Therefore, the first and last names of none of the remaining five students can be uniquely determined from the given information.

problem: Squares $A B K L, B C M N, C A O P$ are drawn externally on the sides of a triangle $A B C$. The line segments $K L, M N, O P$, when extended, form a triangle $A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime}$. Find the area of $A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime}$ if $A B C$ is an equilateral triangle of side length 2 .
solution:
Solution: Triangle $A B C$ has area $\sqrt{3}$, and each of the three squares has area 4 . The three remaining regions are congruent, so just consider the one that includes vertex $B$. Triangle $K B N$ has two sides of length 2 and an angle of $120^{\circ}$ between them, to bisecting that angle we get two halves of an equilateral triangle of side length 2 , so the area is again $\sqrt{3}$. The remaining region is an equilateral triangle of side length $2 \sqrt{3}$, so its area is $(2 \sqrt{3})^{2} \sqrt{3} / 4=3 \sqrt{3}$. Therefore the area of $A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime}$ is $\sqrt{3}+3 \cdot 4+3 \cdot \sqrt{3}+3 \cdot 3 \sqrt{3}=\mathbf{1 2}+\mathbf{1 3} \sqrt{\mathbf{3}}$

Note that this problem is still solvable, but much harder, if the first triangle is not equilateral.

problem:
. Determine all infinite sequences $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots\right)$ of positive integers satisfying

$$
a_{n+1}^{2}=1+(n+2021) a_{n}
$$

for all $n \geq 1$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_04_17_e27e300a283338a2e031g-03.jpg?height=183&width=365&top_left_y=134&top_left_x=180)

BALTIC WAY

REYKJAVÍK$\cdot$ 2021

## Baltic Way

Reykjavík, November 11th - 15th
Solutions
solution:
Clearly $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n=1}^{\infty}=(n+2019)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is a solution. We claim that it is the only one. Assume $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is a solution. Let $\left(b_{n}\right)_{n=1}^{\infty}=\left(a_{n}-n\right)_{n=1}^{\infty}$. We claim:

1) If $b_{n}b_{n+1}>b_{n}$.
2) If $b_{n}>2019$, then $2019<b_{n+1}<b_{n}$.

It is clear that these claims imply that $b_{n}=2019$ for all $n$.

Let us prove the claims:

1) Clearly $a_{n}<n+2019$ implies that $a_{n+1}<(n+1)+2019$ which already proves one part of the inequality. Suppose that $b_{n+1} \leq b_{n}$. Then

$$
\left(n+1+b_{n}\right)^{2} \geq a_{n+1}^{2}=1+(n+2021)\left(n+b_{n}\right) .
$$

Expanding gives

$$
\left(n+b_{n}\right)\left(b_{n}-2019\right) \geq 0
$$

which shows that $b_{n} \geq 2019$ contradicting our assumption.

2) It follows in exactly the same way, by just reversing all the inequality signs.

problem: Given $f(x)$ is a function defined on the set of real numbers with a period of 2, and it is an even function. It is known that when $x \in [2,3]$, $f(x) = x$. Find the analytical expression of $f(x)$ when $x \in [-2,0]$.
solution:
Analysis From $T=2$, we can derive the analytical expressions of $f(x)$ when $x \in[-2,-1]$ and $x \in[0,1]$. Then, by the odd-even properties, we can obtain the analytical expressions of $f(x)$ when $x \in[-2,0]$.

Solution Since the function $f(x)$ is a periodic function with a period of $T=2$, we have $f(x+2)=f(x)$. When $x \in[-2,-1]$, $x+4 \in[2,3]$, so $f(x+4)=x+4$, then $f(x)=f(x+4)=x+4$. When $x \in[0,1]$, $x+2 \in[2,3]$, so $f(x+2)=x+2$, then $f(x)=f(x+2)=x+2$. Since $f(x)$ is an even function, we have $f(-x)=f(x)$. When $x \in[-1,0)$, $-x \in(0,1]$, then $f(x)=f(-x)=-x+2$. Therefore, $f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{l}3-(-x-1)=x+4(x \in[-2,-1]) \\ 3-(x+1)=-x+2(x \in(-1,0))\end{array}=3-|x+1|(x \in[-2\right.$, $0])$.

problem:
8. Find the smallest positive integer $k$ such that the equation $2 x y-3 x-5 y=k$ has an odd number of positive integral solutions.
(1 mark)
求最小的正整數 $k$, 使方程 $2 x y-3 x-5 y=k$ 的正整數解數目為奇數。
solution:
8. 5
8. We have
$$
\begin{aligned}
2 x y-3 x-5 y & =k \\
x y-\frac{3}{2} x-\frac{5}{2} y & =\frac{k}{2} \\
\left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)\left(y-\frac{3}{2}\right) & =\frac{k}{2}+\frac{15}{4} \\
(2 x-5)(2 y-3) & =2 k+15
\end{aligned}
$$

When $k$ is a positive integer, the number of positive integral solutions to the above equation is precisely the number of positive divisors of $2 k+15$. For this number to be odd, $2 k+15$ has to be a perfect square. The smallest such $k$ is 5 . Indeed, we can check that when $k=5$, the original equation has 3 solutions, namely, $(3,14) ;(5,4)$ and $(15,2)$.

problem: 9.2. During breaks, schoolchildren played table tennis. Any two schoolchildren played no more than one game with each other. By the end of the week, it turned out that Petya played half, Kolya - a third, and Vasya - a fifth of the total number of games played during the week. How many games could have been played during the week, given that at least in two games neither Vasya, Petya, nor Kolya participated?
solution:
Answer: 30.

Solution: From the condition, it follows that half, a third, and a fifth of the total number of games played are integers. Since the least common multiple of the denominators - the numbers 2, 3, 5 - is 30, the total number of games played is also a multiple of 30. Let this number be $30p$. Then, Pete played $15p$, Kolya $10p$, and Vasya $6p$ games. Let $y$ be the number of games played among Pete, Kolya, and Vasya (this number is 0, 1, 2, or 3), and $z$ be the number of games played without the participation of Pete, Kolya, and Vasya $(z \geqslant 2)$. Then $15p + 10p + 6p - y + z = 30p$, which means $p = y - z$. The only possible positive value of $p$ is 1, and it is achieved when $y = 3, z = 2$.

Remark: The condition is consistent: such a situation could indeed have occurred (i.e., 30 games could have been played according to the condition).

Comment: It is proven that the total number of games is divisible by $30 - 2$ points.

problem: 3. In a right triangle $ABC (\angle B=90^{\circ})$, a circle $\Gamma$ with center $I$ is inscribed, touching sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $K$ and $L$ respectively. A line passing through point $I$ intersects sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $M$ and $N$ respectively. Find the radius of the circle $\Gamma$ if $MK=144$, $NL=25$. Find $AC$ if it is additionally known that line $MN$ is parallel to $AC$.
solution:
Answer: $r=60, AC=390$.

Solution. Angles $KIM$ and $LNI$ are equal as corresponding angles when lines $BC$ and $KI$ are parallel, so right triangles $KIM$ and $LNI$ are similar. Therefore, $\frac{MK}{KI}=\frac{IL}{LN}$, or (if we denote the radius of the circle by $r$) $\frac{144}{r}=\frac{r}{25}$, from which $r=60$.

Then $BM=BK+KM=r+KM=204, BN=BL+LN=r+LN=85$, hence $MN^2=$ $204^2+85^2=17^2\left(12^2+5^2\right)=17^2 \cdot 13^2, MN=17 \cdot 13$. Let $h$ be the height of triangle $BMN$ drawn from the right angle vertex $B$. Then the area of triangle $BMN$ can be expressed in two ways: $2S_{\triangle BMN}=BN \cdot BM=MN \cdot h$, so $85 \cdot 204=17 \cdot 13 \cdot h, h=\frac{1020}{13}$.

If $MN \parallel AC$, then triangles $BAC$ and $BMN$ are similar, and the similarity coefficient $k$ is the ratio of the heights of these triangles drawn from vertex $B$. It remains to note that the height of triangle $ABC$ drawn from $B$ is equal to $r+h=60+\frac{1020}{13}=\frac{1800}{13}$. Therefore, $k=\frac{h+r}{h}=\frac{1800}{13} : \frac{1020}{13}=\frac{30}{17}$ and $AC=k \cdot MN=\frac{30}{17} \cdot 13 \cdot 17=390$.
