problem: 16. Let $\lfloor x\rfloor$ be the greatest integer smaller than or equal to $x$. How many solutions are there to the equation $x^{3}-\left\lfloor x^{3}\right\rfloor=(x-\lfloor x\rfloor)^{3}$ on the interval $[1,20]$ ?
solution:
16. Answer: 9241.

Let $n=\lfloor x\rfloor,\{x\}=x-n$. The equation becomes $(n+\{x\})^{3}-\{x\}^{3}=\left\lfloor(n+\{x\})^{3}\right\rfloor$. Then
$$
3 n\{x\}(n+\{x\})=\left\lfloor 3 n\{x\}(n+\{x\})+\{x\}^{3}\right\rfloor .
$$

The right-hand side is an integer. The above holds if and only if $3 n\{x\}(n+\{x\})$ is an integer.
Note that $0 \leq 3 n\{x\}(n+\{x\})<3 n(n+1)$. There are exactly $3 n(n+1)$ solutions in $[n, n+1)$, $n=1,2, \ldots$. So on $[1,20]$, the total number of solutions is
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 3(1 \times 2+2 \times 3+\cdots 20 \times 21)+1 \\
= & \left(2^{3}-1^{3}\right)+\left(3^{3}-2^{3}\right)+\cdots+\left(21^{3}-20^{3}\right)-20+1 \\
= & 21^{3}-20=9241 .
\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Example 1 Let $S$ be a subset of the set $\{1,2,3, \cdots, 50\}$, and the sum of any two elements in $S$ cannot be divisible by 7. What is the maximum number of elements in $S$?
solution:
Analysis We pay attention to "7", and construct drawers.
Solution We divide these 50 numbers into 7 sets according to their remainders when divided by 7:
$$
\begin{array}{l}
A_{0}=\{7,14,21,28,35,42,49\} \\
A_{1}=\{1,8,15,22,29,36,43,50\} \\
A_{2}=\{2,9,16,23,30,37,44\} \\
A_{3}=\{3,10,17,24,31,38,45\} \\
A_{4}=\{4,11,18,25,32,39,46\} \\
A_{5}=\{5,12,19,26,33,40,47\} \\
A_{6}=\{6,13,20,27,34,41,48\}
\end{array}
$$

Apart from the 7 elements in $A_{0}$, the elements in the other six sets cannot be divided by 7, and the sum of any two elements in each of these six sets cannot be divided by 7. However, if we take one element from each of the pairs $A_{1}$ and $A_{6}$, $A_{2}$ and $A_{5}$, $A_{3}$ and $A_{4}$, the sum of these two elements can be divided by 7. Therefore, the elements of the required set can be constructed as follows: take one element from $A_{0}$, and then take all elements from one of the two sets in each of the pairs $A_{1}$ and $A_{6}$, $A_{2}$ and $A_{5}$, $A_{3}$ and $A_{4}$. To maximize the number of elements, we must take 8 elements from $A_{1}$, and then 7 elements from $A_{2}$ and $A_{3}$. Therefore, the set $S$ can have at most $1+8+7+7=23$ elements.
Comment Note the application of the drawer principle in sets.

Let $A=1 \cdot 4 \cdot 7 \cdot \ldots \cdot 2014$ be the product of the numbers less or equal to 2014 that give remainder 1 when divided by 3 . Find the last non-zero digit of $A$.
solution:
Solution. Grouping the elements of the product by ten we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (30 k+1)(30 k+4)(30 k+7)(30 k+10)(30 k+13)(30 k+16) \\
& (30 k+19)(30 k+22)(30 k+25)(30 k+28)= \\

& (30 k+19)(15 k+11)(120 k+100)(15 k+14)
\end{aligned}
$$

(We divide all even numbers not divisible by five, by two and multiply all numbers divisible by five with four.)

We denote $P_{k}=(30 k+1)(15 k+2)(30 k+7)(30 k+13)(15 k+8)(30 k+19)(15 k+11)(15 k+14)$. For all the numbers not divisible by five, only the last digit affects the solution, since the power of two in the numbers divisible by five is greater than the power of five. Considering this, for even $k, P_{k}$ ends with the same digit as $1 \cdot 2 \cdot 7 \cdot 3 \cdot 8 \cdot 9 \cdot 1 \cdot 4$, i.e. six and for odd $k, P_{k}$ ends with the same digit as $1 \cdot 7 \cdot 7 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 9 \cdot 6 \cdot 9$, i.e. six. Thus $P_{0} P_{1} \ldots P_{66}$ ends with six. If we remove one zero from the end of all numbers divisible with five, we get that the last nonzero digit of the given product is the same as the one from $6 \cdot 2011 \cdot 2014 \cdot 4 \cdot 10 \cdot 16 \cdot \ldots .796 \cdot 802$. Considering that $4 \cdot 6 \cdot 2 \cdot 8$ ends with four and removing one zero from every fifth number we get that the last nonzero digit is the same as in $4 \cdot 4^{26} \cdot 784 \cdot 796 \cdot 802 \cdot 1 \cdot 4 \cdot \ldots \cdot 76 \cdot 79$. Repeating the process we did for the starting sequence we conclude that the last nonzero number will be the same as in $2 \cdot 6 \cdot 6 \cdot 40 \cdot 100 \cdot 160 \cdot 220 \cdot 280 \cdot 61 \cdot 32 \cdot 67 \cdot 73 \cdot 38 \cdot 79$, which is two.

problem: 1. Find the sum of all even natural numbers $n$ for which the number of divisors (including 1 and $n$ itself) is equal to $\frac{n}{2}$. (For example, the number 12 has 6 divisors: $1,2,3,4,6,12$.)
solution:
Solution. Let the canonical decomposition of the number $n$ be: $n=2^{t_{1}} \cdot 3^{t_{2}} \cdot 5^{t_{3}} \cdots \cdots \cdot p^{t_{k}}$. Then the number of divisors of the number $n$ is $\left(t_{1}+1\right)\left(t_{2}+1\right)\left(t_{3}+1\right) \cdots\left(t_{k}+1\right)$. From the condition of the problem, we have the equality

$$
\left(t_{1}+1\right)\left(t_{2}+1\right)\left(t_{3}+1\right) \cdots\left(t_{k}+1\right)=2^{t_{1}-1} \cdot 3^{t_{2}} \cdot 5^{t_{3}} \cdots \cdots \cdot p^{t_{k}} \cdot\left({ }^{*}\right)
$$

Note that $2^{t_{1}-1}>t_{1}+1$ for $t_{1} \geq 4, 3^{t_{2}}>t_{2}+1$ for $t_{2} \geq 1, \ldots, p^{t_{k}}>t_{k}+1$ for $t_{k} \geq 1$. Therefore, $t_{1}$ can take the values 1, 2, or 3. Substituting the specified values into the equality $(*)$, we find that $n=8$ or $n=12$.

Transform the cube in such a way that we get a 9-faced (planar) body, where each face is a hexagon and the faces can be grouped into 2 categories based on congruence.

See the article by Lajos Szilassi in this issue!
solution:
Since the solid to be produced from the cube $A B C D, A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ needs to have three more faces than the cube itself, we perform the drilling with a triangular prism. To meet the requirements of congruence of the faces, we choose a regular triangle as the cross-section of the prism, and we align the axis of the prism with one of the cube's body diagonals. This ensures that the drilling will create the same change on 3 of the cube's faces.

Let's project the cube (perpendicularly) onto a plane perpendicular to the body diagonal $A C_{1}$. Since the edges of the cube are of equal length and form equal angles with the body diagonal, the resulting projection is a regular hexagon. The projection of the prism that drills through the cube along the selected body diagonal is a regular triangle, whose centroid is the projection of the body diagonal (Figure 1).

# $1984-04-160-1 . \mathrm{eps}$ 

Figure 1

If we rotate either the cube or the prism $120^{\circ}$ around the body diagonal $A C_{1}$, they map onto themselves. This rotational symmetry already ensures that the solid (toroid) obtained by drilling has 9 faces that can be grouped into at most three categories of congruence. Faces derived from the 3 faces of the cube meeting at $C_{1}$ are congruent to each other, as are the faces derived from the 3 faces meeting at $A$, and the inner faces bounding the hole are also congruent.

To ensure that the lower faces are congruent to the upper ones, establishing additional symmetry helps. The cube is also symmetric about other axes: a $180^{\circ}$ rotation about the axis connecting the midpoints of two opposite edges, $B C$ and $A_{1} D_{1}$, swaps the 6 faces in pairs. The dashed line in Figure 1 is the projection of one such symmetry axis, which reflects the cube's three "lower" faces into the three "upper" ones. This axis is perpendicular to the body diagonal $A C_{1}$ of the cube, as it swaps the endpoints of the diagonal, and thus it is also perpendicular to the edges of the triangular prism. If we place the prism such that its projection is symmetric about the dashed line, then a $180^{\circ}$ rotation about the new axis will map the prism onto itself, and the outer faces of the resulting toroid will be congruent due to the two rotational symmetries. Note that in this position, the sides of the prism are parallel to the cube's diagonal planes.

## Task A-2.2.

A 2021-digit number is written. Each two-digit number formed by two consecutive digits of this number (without changing the order) is divisible by 17 or 23. The unit digit of this number is 7. What is its first digit?
solution:
## Solution.

Two-digit multiples of 17 are 17, 34, 51, 68, and 85. Two-digit multiples of 23 are 23, 46, 69, and 92.

If the digit 7 is the last one, the digit before it must be 1. Before the 1 is 5, before the 5 is 8, and before the 8 is necessarily 6. Then, these digits must be preceded by 4, then 3, then 2, then 9, and then 6 again.

The last four digits are $\overline{8517}$, and among the remaining 2017 digits, the block $\overline{92346}$ of five digits repeats 403 times (since $2017=403 \cdot 5+2$).

Before all of this, only two more digits from the block $\overline{92346}$ appear, and these are the digits 4 and 6. Therefore, 4 is the first digit of the written number.

problem: Divide the first 1414 positive integers into groups so that the sum of the numbers in each group is exactly 1981.
solution:
The sum of the first 1414 positive integers

$$
1+2+\ldots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}
$$

According to the formula, $\frac{1414 \cdot 1415}{2}=1000405=505 \cdot 1981$, so we need to form 505 groups.

$1981=1414+567=1413+568=\ldots=991+990$, which means the 848 numbers from 567 to 1414 can be divided into 424 pairs such that the sum of the numbers in each pair is 1981.

Now, it is sufficient to group the first 566 positive integers in the desired manner.

$$
\begin{gathered}
1+2+\ldots+566=(1+282)+(2+281)+\ldots+ \\
+(141+142)+(283+566)+(284+565)+\ldots+(424+425)
\end{gathered}
$$

Thus, the first 566 positive integers can be divided into 141 pairs with a sum of 283 and 142 pairs with a sum of $3 \cdot 283$. Since $1981=7 \cdot 283$, we are now ready, because

$$
\begin{gathered}
141 \cdot 283+142 \cdot 3 \cdot 283=70 \cdot 283+71 \cdot 283+71 \cdot 6 \cdot 283= \\
=10 \cdot(7 \cdot 283)+71 \cdot(7 \cdot 283)=81 \cdot 1981
\end{gathered}
$$

To form the additional 81 groups, we need to arrange the 141 and 142 pairs into groups with a sum of $7 \cdot 283$, which can be done based on the above equations. It is clear that each of the first 1414 positive integers appears in exactly one group. This solves the problem.

Both brothers entered the house. Almost immediately, one of them came out and silently stood next to Alice. Soon, the second brother emerged from the house with a "sign" that read:

Is a square drawn on the back of this sign?

The brother standing next to Alice, in response, drew a circle in the air.

Who is Trololala?

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_5afa4e43618f5800e92dg-085.jpg?height=559&width=714&top_left_y=1945&top_left_x=705)
solution: 76. Who is who? On the reverse side of the sign, either a square or a circle is drawn. Suppose a square is drawn. Then the square means "yes," and the circle means "no." Consequently, the second brother answers the question with "no," which means he is lying! Now suppose a circle is drawn on the reverse side of the sign. Then the circle means "yes," and the second brother answers the question with "yes," which again means he is lying, since a square is not drawn on the reverse side of the sign! Therefore, the second brother lied, so his name is Turlalala.

problem:
3.3. (Canada, 83). Solve the equation

$$
x!+y!+z!=u!
$$

in natural numbers.
solution:
3.3. Let the numbers $x, y, z, u \in \mathbf{N}$ satisfy the original equation, and let $v$ denote the largest of the numbers $x, y, z$. Then $1 \leq v < u$ and

$$
u v! \leq u(u-1)! = u! = x! + y! + z! \leq 3 v!
$$

from which $u v! \leq 3 v!$, hence $u \leq 3$. For $u=3$, we have the equalities

$$
3! = 3 v! = x! + y! + z!
$$

which are valid only in the case $x = y = z = v = 2$. For $u=2$, the equation has no solutions, since in this case

$$
u! = 2 < 3 < x! + y! + z!
$$

Thus, the original equation has the unique solution $x = y = z = 2, u = 3$.

problem:
10.1. Propose a word problem that reduces to solving the inequality

$$
\frac{11}{x+1.5}+\frac{8}{x} \geqslant \frac{12}{x+2}+2
$$

Write the problem statement, its solution, and the answer.

Example of the required problem. Points A and B are connected by two roads: one is 19 km long, and the other is 12 km long. At 12:00, a pedestrian left point A on the longer road and walked the first 11 km at a constant speed, and then, getting tired, walked the remaining distance to point B at an average speed 1.5 km/h slower. At 14:00, a second pedestrian left point A on the shorter road and walked the entire distance at an average speed 0.5 km/h faster than the first pedestrian initially. What was the average speed of the first pedestrian for the last 8 km of the journey, if it is known that he arrived at point B no earlier than the second pedestrian?

Brief solution. If \( x \) is the required average speed of the first pedestrian (in km/h) on the second part of the journey, then \( x+1.5 \) is his speed on the first part, and \( (x+1.5)+0.5 = x+2 \) is the average speed of the second pedestrian. Then, by calculating the time each pedestrian spent on the journey, we obtain the required inequality. Since by the problem's condition \( x > 0 \), both sides of the inequality can be multiplied by the quantity \( x(x+1.5)(x+2) > 0 \), then we get \( 11x(x+2) + 8(x+1.5)(x+2) \geqslant 12x(x+1.5) + 2x(x+1.5)(x+2) \), or, after transformations, \( (x-4)(x+1)(x+3) \leqslant 0 \). Therefore, \( 0 < x \leqslant 4 \), and all found values of \( x \) satisfy the problem's condition.
solution: Answer: no more than 4 km/h.

problem: There are $2 n$ different numbers in a row. By one move we can interchange any two numbers or interchange any three numbers cyclically (choose $a, b, c$ and place a instead of $b, b$ instead of $c$ and $c$ instead of $a$ ). What is the minimal number of moves that is always sufficient to arrange the numbers in increasing order?
solution:
If a number $y$ occupies the place where $x$ should be at the end, we draw an arrow $x \rightarrow y$. Clearly at the beginning all numbers are arranged in several cycles: Loops

$\bullet \bullet$, binary cycles $\bullet \rightleftarrows \bullet$ and "long" cycles $\bullet_{\nwarrow}^{\nearrow} \succeq \bullet$ (at least three numbers). Our aim is to obtain $2 n$ loops.

Clearly each binary cycle can be rearranged into two loops by one move. If there is a long cycle with a fragment $\cdots \rightarrow a \rightarrow b \rightarrow c \rightarrow \cdots$, interchange $a, b, c$ cyclically so that at least two loops, $a \oslash, b \oslash$, appear. By each of these moves, the number of loops increase by 2 , so at most $n$ moves are needed.

On the other hand, by checking all possible ways the two or three numbers can be distributed among disjoint cycles, it is easy to see that each of the allowed moves increases the number of disjoint cycles by at most two. Hence if the initial situation is one single loop, at least $n$ moves are needed.

problem:
10. find all pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ of positive real numbers with the following properties:

(a) For all positive real numbers $x, y, z, w$ applies

$$
x+y^{2}+z^{3}+w^{6} \geq \alpha(x y z w)^{\beta}
$$

(b) There is a quadruple $(x, y, z, w)$ of positive real numbers such that equality holds in (a).

## Solution
solution:
Let $(\alpha, \beta)$ be a pair as in the problem. We first note that for fixed $\beta$ there exists at most one $\alpha$ as in (b), because $\alpha$ is then the largest positive real number for which (a) applies. Now set $x=t^{6}, y=t^{3}, z=t^{2}$ and $w=t$ for $t>0$, then in particular $4 t^{6} \geq \alpha t^{12 \beta}$, i.e.

$$
t^{6-12 \beta} \geq \frac{\alpha}{4}
$$

for all $t>0$. For very small $t$, this estimate can only apply if the exponent on the left-hand side is not negative. For large $t$, on the other hand, only if the exponent is not positive. Consequently, $\beta=\frac{1}{2}$ must be.

On the other hand, AM-GM

$$
\begin{aligned}
x+y^{2}+z^{3}+w^{6} & =(\underbrace{\frac{x}{6}+\ldots+\frac{x}{6}}_{6})+\left(\frac{y^{2}}{3}+\frac{y^{2}}{3}+\frac{y^{2}}{3}\right)+\left(\frac{z^{3}}{2}+\frac{z^{3}}{2}\right)+w^{6} \\
& \geq 12 \sqrt[12]{\left(\frac{x}{6}\right)^{6} \cdot\left(\frac{y^{2}}{3}\right)^{3} \cdot\left(\frac{z^{3}}{2}\right)^{2} \cdot w^{6}}=\left(2^{\frac{4}{3}} 3^{\frac{1}{4}}\right) \sqrt{x y z w} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Equality applies to $(x, y, z, w)=(6, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt[3]{2}, 1)$, so (a) and (b) are fulfilled for the only pair $(\alpha, \beta)=\left(2^{\frac{4}{3}} 3^{\frac{1}{4}}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$.

problem: 4.1. Vasya loves to collect mushrooms. He calculated that over the autumn he collected a number of mushrooms that is expressed by a three-digit number, the sum of the digits of which is 14. Then Vasya calculated that 8% of the collected mushrooms were white, and 14% were boletus. How many mushrooms did Vasya collect?
solution:
Answer: 950.

Solution. For $14 \%$ of the number of mushrooms to be an integer, it is necessary for the total number of mushrooms to be a multiple of 50. Then the last two digits are 00 or 50. But if a three-digit number ends with two zeros, the sum of the digits cannot be greater than 9, therefore, the last two digits are 50, i.e., the first digit is $14-5-0=9$.

problem: 7. Due to traffic congestion at the city exit, the intercity bus traveled the first third of the journey one and a half times slower than the calculated time. Will the bus be able to arrive at the destination on time if it increases its speed by a third for the remaining part of the journey?
solution:
Answer: Yes.

Solution. The bus spent $\frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{2}$ of the calculated time on the first third of the journey. If it increases its speed by a third, it will cover the remaining two-thirds of the journey in $\frac{2 / 3}{4 / 3}=\frac{1}{2}$ of the calculated time, meaning it will be able to arrive at the destination without being late.

problem:
[ GMT - line or segment ] Complex [ The ratio of the areas of triangles with a common base or common height] Classes

On the sides $P Q, Q R, R P$ of triangle $P Q R$, segments $A B, C D, E F$ are laid out. Inside the triangle, a point $S_{0}$ is given. Find the geometric locus of points $S$ lying inside triangle $P Q R$ for which the sum of the areas of triangles $S A B, S C D, S E F$ is equal to the sum of the areas of triangles $S_{0} A B, S_{0} C D, S_{0} E F$. Consider the special case when
$$
\frac{A B}{P Q}=\frac{C D}{Q R}=\frac{E F}{R P}
$$
solution:
Let's assume that $\frac{A B}{P Q} \geq \frac{C D}{Q R} \geq \frac{E F}{R P}$. On the sides $Q R$ and $P R$, we mark segments $Q D^{\prime}=C D \cdot \frac{P Q}{A B}$ and $P E^{\prime}=F E \cdot \frac{P Q}{A B}$. Then,

$S_{\triangle S A B} + S_{\triangle S C D} + S_{\triangle S E F} = \frac{A B}{P Q} \left(S_{\triangle S P Q} + S_{\triangle S Q D^{\prime}} + S_{\triangle S E^{\prime} P}\right) = $

$= \frac{A B}{P Q} \left(S_{P Q D^{\prime} E^{\prime}} \pm S_{\triangle S D^{\prime} E^{\prime}}\right)$.

In the last expression, the plus sign is taken if point $S$ lies outside the quadrilateral $P Q D^{\prime} E^{\prime}$, and the minus sign if inside. From the obtained formula, it follows that for points $S$ of the desired geometric locus, the area of triangle $S D^{\prime} E^{\prime}$ must be constant. Therefore, the desired geometric locus (GML) is a segment of a line parallel to $D^{\prime} E^{\prime}$ and passing through point $S_{0}$. In a special case, the desired GML is the entire triangle $P Q R$.

problem:
* Find the positive integer solutions of the equation: $n!+1=(-1)^{2}$.

The equation simplifies to $n!+1=1$, since $(-1)^2=1$. Therefore, $n! = 0$. The only value of $n$ that satisfies this equation is $n=0$, but since we are looking for positive integer solutions, there are no solutions.
solution:
Parse: It is easy to verify, $m \geqslant 3$. Rewrite the equation as $n!=m!(m!-2) \cdots$ (1). Clearly, $n>m$. From (1), we get $n(n \cdots 1) \cdots(m+1)=m!\cdots 2 \cdots$ (2). Since $3 \mid m!$, it follows that $3 \nmid m!-2$, hence the left side of (2) cannot have more than two factors (otherwise, the product of three consecutive natural numbers is divisible by 3). Therefore, $n-m=1$ or $n-m=2$. In the first case, we have $m+1=m!-2$, which means $m!=m+3 \leqslant 2 m$, so $m=3, n=4$. In the second case, we have
$$
m!=(m+1)(m+2)+2 \leqslant 4 m(m-1) .
$$

Thus, $m=3$ or $m=4$, with no other solutions. Upon verification, only $m=3, n=4$ is a solution to the equation.

problem:
## 1. Centipede

Centipede Milica has exactly a hundred legs, 50 left and 50 right. Every morning she puts on 50 pairs of shoes, first all the left ones, and then all the right ones. It takes her one second to put on each left shoe. But then she gets tired, and it takes her more time for the right shoes. It takes one second for the first right shoe, three seconds for the second, five seconds for the third, and so on, with each subsequent right shoe taking two seconds longer than the previous one. In the evening, when she takes off her shoes, it takes her three times less time in total than it does to put them on. How many seconds does it take centipede Milica to take off all her shoes?

Result: $\quad \mathbf{8 5 0}$
solution:
## Solution.

Putting on all the left shoes takes $(50 \cdot 1) \mathrm{s}=50 \mathrm{~s}$.

Putting on all the right shoes takes $(1+3+\cdots+99) \mathrm{s}=(25 \cdot 100) \mathrm{s}=2500 \mathrm{~s}$.

Therefore, for putting on all the left and all the right shoes, it takes, in total, $(50+2500) \mathrm{s}=2550 \mathrm{~s}$.

Taking off the shoes takes her (2550 : 3) s $=850 \mathrm{~s}$.

problem: 29th USAMO 2000 Problem B1 How many squares of a 1000 x 1000 chessboard can be chosen, so that we cannot find three chosen squares with two in the same row and two in the same column? Solution
solution: : 1998. Choose every square in the first row or column but not both. We prove the slightly more general result that the maximum number for an m x n rectangle is n if m = 1, or m + n - 2 for m, n > 1. We may assume m ≤ n. We use induction on m. The result for m = 1 is obvious. For m = 2, if we choose two in the same row, then we cannot choose any more, so it is better (or no worse for n = 2) to choose all the squares in a column giving n = m + n - 2 in total. That establishes the result for m = 1 and 2. Now suppose n ≥ m > 2 and that the result is true for smaller m. We can certainly do at least m + n - 2 by choosing all the squares in the first row or column but not both. Assume we have m columns. If no two are in the same row, then there are at most n which we know is not optimal. So assume there are two in the same row. Now there cannot be any more in the two corresponding columns. So consider the remaining m-2 columns. If m > 3, then by induction we cannot choose more than m-2 + n - 2 in those columns and with the two already chosen that gives m + n - 2. If m = 3, then we cannot choose more than n in the remaining column. But we can combine at most n-1 of those with the existing two, since if we pick the square in the same row as the two squares already chosen, then we cannot choose any others. So for this case also we can do at most n+1 = m + n - 2. Hence the result is true for all m. 29th USAMO 2000 © John Scholes jscholes@kalva.demon.co.uk 11 May 2002

problem: Let's find all the quadruples of real numbers $x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}$, such that when we add any one of them to the product of the other three, the sum is always 2.
solution:
I. solution. None of the $x_{i}$ can be 0, because it is easily seen that then the others could only be 2, but then $0+2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \neq 2$. Let us denote the product $x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} x_{4}$ by $y$, then we have to solve the system of equations

$$
x_{i}+\frac{y}{x_{i}}=2 \quad(i=1,2,3,4)
$$

From this,

$$
x_{i}^{2}-2 x_{i}+y=0, x_{i}=1 \pm \sqrt{1-y}, \text { or }\left|x_{i}-1\right|=\sqrt{1-y}
$$

According to this, by reducing the unknowns by 1, we can get at most two different numbers. This can happen in three ways:

$\alpha$) all four $x_{i}-1$ differences are equal,

$\beta$) three are equal, the fourth is -1 times as large,

$\gamma$) two are equal, the other two are -1 times as large.

In the $\alpha$ case, $x_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}=x_{4}$, so from (1)

$$
x_{1}+x_{1}^{3}=2, \quad x_{1}^{3}+x_{1}-2=\left(x_{1}-1\right)\left(x_{1}^{2}+x_{1}+2\right)=0
$$

and since the second factor is positive for all real $x_{1}$ values:

$$
x_{1}^{2}+x_{1}+2=\left(x_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+\frac{9}{4} \geqq \frac{9}{4}>0
$$

only $x_{1}=1$ is possible. The number quadruple $1,1,1,1$ indeed satisfies the requirements.

In the $\beta$ case, for example, $x_{1}-1=x_{2}-1=x_{3}-1$, and thus $x_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}$, and $x_{4}-1=1-x_{1}$. So $x_{4}=2-x_{1}$, and from (1) for $i=4$

$$
2-x_{1}+x_{1}^{3}=2, \quad x_{1}\left(x_{1}^{2}-1\right)=0
$$

and since $x_{1} \neq 0, x_{1}$ can be 1 or -1. The first leads to the previous solution, the latter to the number quadruple $-1,-1,-1,3$, which is also indeed a solution.

In the $\gamma$ case, for example, $x_{1}-1=x_{2}-1=1-x_{3}=1-x_{4}=x_{4}$, so $x_{1}=x_{2}$, and $x_{3}=x_{4}=2-x_{1}$, and from (1) for $i=3$

$$
2-x_{1}+x_{1}^{2}\left(2-x_{1}\right)=2, \quad x_{1}\left(x_{1}-1\right)^{2}=0
$$

we only get the solution $1,1,1,1$.

According to all this, two real number quadruples satisfy the requirement: $1,1,1,1$ and $-1,-1,-1,3$.

János Lórincz (Sárospatak, Rákóczi F. g. IV. o. t.)

II. solution. There is one solution where $x_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}=x_{4}$, as we saw in the previous solution: $x_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}=x_{4}=1$. If there are different numbers among the numbers, then there is one that differs from at least two others. Choose the numbering so that $x_{1} \neq x_{2}, x_{1} \neq x_{3}$ holds. Write the requirement starting from $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$, then form the difference of the two equalities:

$$
\begin{gathered}
x_{1}+x_{2} x_{3} x_{4}=2, \quad x_{2}+x_{1} x_{3} x_{4}=2 \\
x_{1}-x_{2}+x_{3} x_{4}\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)=\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)\left(1-x_{3} x_{4}\right)=0
\end{gathered}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\left(x_{1}-x_{3}\right)\left(1-x_{2} x_{4}\right)=0
$$

Then from (3) and (4) $x_{3} x_{4}=1$, and $x_{2} x_{4}=1$, so from (2) $x_{1}+x_{2}=2$, and $x_{1}+x_{3}=2$, so $x_{2}=x_{3}$.

From the equation $x_{4}+x_{1} x_{2} x_{3}=2$ starting from $x_{4}$, $x_{1}$, $x_{3}$, $x_{4}$ can be easily eliminated if we multiply by $x_{2}$:

$$
\begin{gathered}
x_{2} x_{4}+x_{1} x_{2}^{2} x_{3}=1+\left(2-x_{2}\right) x_{2}^{3}=2 x_{2}, \quad x_{2}^{4}-2 x_{2}^{3}+2 x_{2}-1=0 \\
x_{2}^{4}-1-2 x_{2}\left(x_{2}^{2}-1\right)=\left(x_{2}^{2}-1\right)\left(x_{2}^{2}+1-2 x_{2}\right)=\left(x_{2}-1\right)^{3}\left(x_{2}+1\right)=0
\end{gathered}
$$

From this, either $x_{2}=x_{3}=1, x_{1}=2-x_{2}=1, x_{4}=1 / x_{2}=1$, which does not contain different values, or $x_{2}=x_{3}=-1$, $x_{4}=1 / x_{2}=-1, x_{1}=2-x_{2}=3$, and this indeed satisfies the requirements.

problem: 5. A $3 \times 3$ table is initially filled with zeros. In one move, any $2 \times 2$ square in the table is selected, and all zeros in it are replaced with crosses, and all crosses with zeros. We will call any arrangement of crosses and zeros in the table a "pattern." How many different patterns can be obtained as a result of such moves? Patterns that can be obtained from each other by rotating $90^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$ are considered different.
solution:
Solution. First method. Different drawings differ by at least one cell in the table, either plus or minus. The symbol in a given specific cell is determined by the parity (even or odd) of the number of swaps performed in each $2 \times 2$ square containing that cell. Each $2 \times 2$ square contains exactly one corner cell of the table, and each such square has its own unique corner cell. The parity of the number of swaps in each square corresponds to the symbol in its unique corner cell (if there is a cross in the corner cell, the number of swaps was odd; if there is a circle, the number of swaps was even). Therefore, each combination of symbols in the table uniquely corresponds to a combination of circles and crosses in the corner cells of the table. Since the number of different combinations in four cells is $2^{4}=16$, there are 16 drawings in total.

Second method. One can create a transition table and show that when swaps are performed multiple times, cycles arise, and some drawings transition into others. The images below show all possible ways to place crosses and circles, and the number of corresponding drawings in one group. Drawings in the same group differ from each other by rotations of $90^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$. The presence of cycles proves that the number of drawings is limited, and fewer than $2^{9}$.

problem: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a circle, and $A, B, C, D$ four points on it. Suppose that $(AB)$ and $(CD)$ intersect at a point $M$. Find two similar triangles.
solution:
We can assume that $A, B, M$ and $C, D, M$ are collinear in this order. In this case, $M A B$ and $M D C$ are similar.

Note: We thus have $M A \times M B = M C \times M D$. If the point $M$ is fixed, for any line passing through $M$ and intersecting the circle at $E$ and $F$, the product $M E \times M F$ is therefore constant. This quantity is called the power of $M$ with respect to the circle $\mathcal{C}$. A course on this subject can be found in the old geometry polycopied.

Solution to exercise $3$: $B, C^{\prime}, B^{\prime}, C$ are on the circle with diameter $[B C]$, so $\widehat{A C B} = \widehat{B^{\prime} C B} = 180^{\circ} - \widehat{B^{\prime} C^{\prime} B} = \widehat{A C^{\prime} B^{\prime}}$. Since $\widehat{C^{\prime} A B^{\prime}} = \widehat{A B C}$, we deduce that $A B C$ and $A C^{\prime} B^{\prime}$ are similar. Similarly, $B A^{\prime} C^{\prime}$ and $B C A$ are similar, and $C A^{\prime} B^{\prime}$ and $C B A$ are also similar.

Moreover, $\widehat{H C A^{\prime}} = 90^{\circ} - \widehat{C^{\prime} B A^{\prime}} = \overline{C^{\prime} A H}$, so the right triangles $B A A^{\prime}$ and $H C A^{\prime}$ are similar.

Solution to exercise $4$: $\frac{M E}{M F} = \frac{D A}{D C}$ if and only if $M E F$ and $D A C$ are similar. We note that $A, E, F, M$ are on the circle with diameter $[A M]$, so $\widehat{M E F} = \widehat{M A F} = \widehat{D A C}$ by the inscribed angle theorem. Similarly, $\widehat{E F M} = \widehat{E A M} = \widehat{B A C}$. But $\widehat{B A C} = \widehat{A C D}$ because they are alternate interior angles. Thus $M E F$ and $D A C$ are similar, which concludes.

Solution to exercise $5$: $A, D, F, M$ are concyclic, because $\widehat{A F M} = \widehat{A D M} = 90^{\circ}$. Thus $\widehat{M D F} = \widehat{M A F}$. Similarly, $\widehat{M E D} = \widehat{M B D} = \widehat{M B A}$ because $B, D, E, M$ are concyclic. Finally, $\widehat{M A F} = \widehat{M B A}$ because $(A F)$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $M B A$. Thus $\widehat{M D F} = \widehat{M E D}$.

Similarly, we prove that $\widehat{M D E} = \widehat{M F D}$. Therefore, $M D F$ and $M E D$ are similar, which implies that $M D / M F = M E / M D$, or $M D^2 = M E \times M F$.

problem:
Exercise 18. Find all integers $n \geqslant 1$ for which the function:

$$
x \longmapsto x^{x}
$$

takes all possible values modulo $n$ as $x$ runs through $\llbracket 0, n-1 \rrbracket$.

We say that it is a surjection in $\mathbb{Z} / \mathrm{n} \mathbb{Z}$.
solution:
Solution to Exercise 18 Let's note that if $\mathrm{n}$ satisfies the property, then any divisor $\mathrm{d}$ of $\mathrm{n}$ also satisfies it. Let $\mathrm{f}$ be the function that maps $x$ in $\mathbb{N}^{*}$ to $\mathbb{Z} / \mathrm{n} \mathbb{Z}$.

For $n=p^{2}$ with $p$ prime, note that $p$ is not in the image of $f$. Indeed, if $f(x) \equiv p\left(\bmod p^{2}\right)$, $p$ divides $x^{x}$, so $p$ divides $x$. In particular, since $x \geqslant p \geqslant 2, p^{2}$ divides $x^{x}=f(x)$, a contradiction. In particular, if $n$ satisfies the property, in its prime factorization, all the $p$-adic valuations are at most 1.

For $n=p$ prime, let us take $y \in \mathbb{N}$. We seek $x$ a positive integer such that $x^{x} \equiv y(\bmod p)$. For this, we use Fermat's little theorem: if $p-1$ divides $x-1, x^{x} \equiv x^{x-1} \times x \equiv x(\bmod p)$. In particular, it suffices to take $x$ strictly positive such that $x \equiv 1(\bmod p-1)$ and $x \equiv y(\bmod p)$. This is possible by the Chinese remainder theorem, since $p$ and $p-1$ are coprime, so $f$ is surjective.

It remains to treat the case where $n$ is a product of distinct prime factors: suppose $\mathrm{n}=\mathrm{p}_{1} \ldots \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{k}}$ with the $\left(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}}\right)$ primes and pairwise distinct. We can try to use the previous argument again: let $y \in \mathbb{N}$, we seek $x$ a strictly positive integer such that $x^{x}=y(\bmod n)$, this is equivalent by the Chinese remainder theorem to $x^{x}=y\left(\bmod p_{i}\right)$ for all $i$ between 1 and $k$. It suffices to take $x$ such that $x \equiv 1\left(\bmod p_{i}-1\right)$ and $x \equiv y\left(\bmod p_{i}\right)$ for all $i$, that is, $x \equiv 1\left(\bmod \prod_{i=1}^{k}\left(p_{i}-1\right)\right)$ and $x \equiv y$ $\left(\bmod p_{i}\right)$ for all $i$. Note that the $\left(p_{i}\right)$ are pairwise coprime, but a priori we cannot assert that $p_{i}$ is coprime with $\prod_{i=1}^{k}\left(p_{i}-1\right)$ for all $i$.

If for all $(i, j)$ between 1 and $k, p_{i}$ does not divide $p_{j}-1$, in this case $p_{i}$ is coprime with $\prod_{i=1}^{k}\left(p_{i}-1\right)$ for all $i$, so by the Chinese remainder theorem we can find $x$ such that $x \equiv 1\left(\bmod \prod_{i=1}^{k}\left(p_{i}-1\right)\right)$ and $x \equiv y$ $\left(\bmod p_{i}\right)$ for all $i$, thus $x^{x} \equiv y(\bmod n)$.

Suppose there exists $(i, j)$ such that $p_{i}$ divides $p_{j}-1$. Since $i \neq j$, it suffices in this case to verify that $f$ is not surjective modulo $m$ with $m=p_{i} p_{j}$, suppose that $f$ is surjective modulo $m$. Let $a \in \mathbb{N}, y$ such that $y \equiv 0\left(\bmod p_{i}\right)$ and $y \equiv a\left(\bmod p_{j}\right)$ by the Chinese remainder theorem. Suppose there exists $x$ such that $x^{x} \equiv y\left(\bmod p_{i} p_{j}\right)$. In this case $x^{x} \equiv 0\left(\bmod p_{i}\right)$ so $p_{i}$ divides $x$, let then $x=k p_{i}$. In this case, $x^{x} \equiv\left(x^{k}\right)^{\mathfrak{p}_{i}} \equiv a\left(\bmod p_{j}\right)$. We obtain, by raising to the power $\frac{p_{j}-1}{p_{i}}, a^{\frac{p_{j}-1}{p_{i}}}=\left(x^{k}\right)^{p_{j}-1}=1$ $\left(\bmod p_{j}\right)$. In particular, if $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p_{j}$, since $a$ has order exactly $p_{j}-1$, we obtain a contradiction, the function $\mathrm{f}$ is not surjective.

Thus the function is surjective if and only if $n=p_{1} \ldots p_{k}$ with the $\left(p_{i}\right)$ primes and pairwise distinct and for all $(i, j)$ between 1 and $k, p_{i}$ does not divide $p_{j}-1$.

Graders' Comments

The submissions received on this problem were of very high quality. The problem was relatively difficult, but many made good progress. Some submissions tried to use the Chinese remainder theorem, which could be useful, but could cause many errors: notably, it is not because the function is surjective modulo $p$ for all prime numbers $p$ that it is surjective for all "squarefree" numbers, that is, without any prime factor with multiplicity greater than or equal to 2. Also be careful with the use of Euler's theorem $\left(\mathrm{a}^{\Phi(\mathrm{n})}=1(\bmod \mathrm{n})\right)$: to be able to use it, the number must be coprime with $\mathrm{n}$.

problem: 6.4. At a round table, 120 people are sitting - knights, who always tell the truth, and liars, who always lie. Each of them made exactly one of the following two statements: 1) "My right neighbor is a knight"; 2) "The person who is one to the right of my right neighbor is a knight." How many liars could there be at the table? (Don't forget to explain your answer.)
solution:
Answer: $0,60,120$. Solution. The cases where all sitting at the table are liars, or all sitting at the table are knights, are obviously valid. Suppose there are both knights and liars sitting at the table. Then there is a liar (L) whose right neighbor is a knight (R). L could not have made statement 1). Therefore, he made statement 2), and to the right of R sits a liar (L2). This means R also could not have made statement 1, i.e., he made statement 2), so to the right of L2 is again a knight. Continuing this reasoning, we see that knights and liars alternate around the table.

Comment. Any answer without justification is 0 points. One answer with justification is 0 or 1 point for the answer $120-1$, both of these answers - 2 points. The answer 60 with justification - 5 points.

problem: 8.3. Workers were laying a floor of size $n \times n$ using two types of tiles: $2 \times 2$ and $3 \times 1$. It turned out that they managed to completely cover the floor such that the same number of tiles of each type was used. For which $n$ could this have been possible? (Cutting tiles or overlapping them is not allowed.)
solution:
Answer. For $n$ divisible by 7.

Solution. Let the workers use $x$ tiles of each type. Then the area covered by the tiles is $4x + 3x = 7x = n^2$. Therefore, $n$ must be divisible by 7.

If $n$ is divisible by 7, then the floor can be laid. It is sufficient to note that a $7 \times 7$ square can be laid using 7 tiles of each type (see Fig. 5). And a $7k \times 7k$ square can be divided into $7 \times 7$ squares.

problem: Ivan, Petr, and Sidor were eating candies. Their last names are Ivanov, Petrov, and Sidorov. Ivanov ate 2 candies less than Ivan, Petrov ate 2 candies less than Petr, and Petr ate the most. What is the last name of each of them?
solution:
Ivanov ate less than Ivan, and Peter ate more than everyone, so Peter is not Ivanov. For the same reason, Peter is not Petrov, which means Peter's last name is Sidorov. Ivanov is not Ivan, so Ivanov's first name is Sidor. Therefore, Petrov's first name is Ivan.

Exercise 1. Calculate

$$
\frac{1 \times 2 \times 4 + 2 \times 4 \times 8 + 3 \times 6 \times 12 + 4 \times 8 \times 16}{1 \times 3 \times 9 + 2 \times 6 \times 18 + 3 \times 9 \times 27 + 4 \times 12 \times 36}
$$

Only a numerical answer is expected here. The answer should be given as an irreducible fraction (i.e., in the form $\frac{a}{b}$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers with no common divisors).
solution:
Solution to Exercise 1 Instead of calculating the numerator and the denominator, we can notice that the terms of the sum in the numerator are the numbers $i \times(2 i) \times(4 i)=8 i^{3}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 4$ and that the terms of the sum in the denominator are the numbers $i \times(3 i) \times(9 i)=27 i^{3}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 4$. By simplifying the numerator and the denominator by the number $\left(1^{3}+2^{3}+3^{3}+4^{3}\right)$, we obtain the irreducible fraction $\frac{8}{27}$.

The expected answer is therefore $\frac{8}{27}$.

Alternative Solution $n^{\circ} 1$ We can directly simplify the fraction by doing all the calculations by hand:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1 \times 2 \times 4+2 \times 4 \times 8+3 \times 6 \times 12+4 \times 8 \times 16}{1 \times 3 \times 9+2 \times 6 \times 18+3 \times 9 \times 27+4 \times 12 \times 36} & =\frac{8+64+216+512}{27+216+729+1728} \\
& =\frac{800}{2700}=\frac{8}{27}
\end{aligned}
$$

The expected answer is therefore $\frac{8}{27}$.

problem:
Konyagin S.V.

For which $n$ does there exist a closed non-self-intersecting broken line with $n$ segments such that every line containing one of the segments of this broken line contains at least one more of its segments?
solution:
It is easy to see that $n>8$.

We will prove that any non-self-intersecting closed broken line with an odd number of segments not exceeding 13 has the property that there always exists a straight line containing exactly one segment of this broken line.

Suppose that for such a broken line, there is no straight line containing exactly one segment. Then, on one of the straight lines, there must be at least three segments of our broken line. These three segments have six ends, and from each end, another segment of the broken line extends, meaning there are six new segments, and no two of these segments lie on the same straight line. Therefore, each straight line containing one of these six segments of the broken line must, by our assumption, contain at least one more segment, different from the already considered nine segments. Thus, the broken line in question must have at least six more segments, meaning it must have at least 15 segments. This is a contradiction.

We will show that for any even $n \geq 10$ and odd $n \geq 15$, the broken line described in the problem exists. For even $n \geq 10$, these are the well-known $n / 2$-pointed stars (for $n=10$ and $n=12$).

problem: 4. There is a pile of 2016 stones. Two players are playing a game. The first player can take either 1, 3, or 4 stones on each of their turns. The second player can take either 1, 2, or 3 stones on each of their turns. The player who cannot make a move loses. Who can win, no matter how the opponent plays?
solution:
Answer: The second.

## Solution:

The second player's strategy: each time leave a number of stones in the pile that gives a remainder of 2 when divided by 3. Note that he can do this after any move by the opponent, as his set of moves allows him to change the remainder of the remaining stones to any value. The first player cannot end the game with such a number of remaining stones, so the last move will remain with the second player.

The problem allows for a solution that does not require the second player to follow the non-obvious strategy of "making the remainder from division by 3 equal to 2" from the beginning of the game:

Consider the following strategy (for the second player).

The main idea of the solution: it is easy to see that if exactly 2 stones are left for the first player, then he (the first player) will lose, and the second player will win. Indeed, from a pile of 2 stones, the first can only take one, but then the remaining stone is taken by the opponent (the second), and he wins.

Let's analyze the actions of the second player depending on the number of stones in the pile before his move.

- If there are 1, 2, or 3 stones in the pile, the second player wins (he simply takes all the stones on his turn).
- If there are 4 or 5 stones in the pile, the second player takes 2 or 3 stones respectively, leaving the first player with a pile of 2 stones (in which case the first player loses).
- If there are 6, 7, or 8 stones in the pile, the second player takes 1, 2, or 3 stones respectively, leaving the first player with a pile of 5 stones. After this, no matter how many stones the first player takes, there will be stones left (it will be the second player's turn), and there will be fewer than five stones. But if the second player is left with fewer than 5 stones, the second player wins (the strategy has been considered above).
- If there are more than 8 stones in the pile, the second player simply takes any number of stones.

In other words, the second player makes moves as he pleases at the beginning of the game—until the number of stones (before his turn) is 8 or fewer. This moment will come, as after a couple of moves (by the first and second players), the number of stones decreases by at least 2 and at most 7 (that is, the second player will not miss the moment when he will play according to a meaningful strategy).

Instructions for checking:

Carefully follow the justification of the winning strategy for the second player and the justification of the possibility for the second player to make the next move.

problem: 6. Pete came up with all the numbers that can be formed using the digits 2, 0, 1, 8 (each digit can be used no more than once). Find their sum.
solution:
Answer: 78331

Solution: First, consider the units place. Each of the digits 1, 2, 8 appears once in this place for single-digit numbers, twice for two-digit numbers, four times for three-digit numbers, and four times for four-digit numbers - a total of 11 times.

In the tens place, each of them appears 3 times for two-digit numbers, 4 times for three-digit numbers, and 4 times for four-digit numbers - also 11 times.

In the hundreds place, each appears 6 times in three-digit numbers and 4 times in single-digit numbers.

In the thousands place, each appears 6 times.

## Problem Statement

Based on the definition of the derivative, find $f^{\prime}(0)$:

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{c}
\operatorname{arctg}\left(x \cos \left(\frac{1}{5 x}\right)\right), x \neq 0 \\
0, x=0
\end{array}\right.
$$
solution:
## Solution

By definition, the derivative at the point $x=0$:

$f^{\prime}(0)=\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0+\Delta x)-f(0)}{\Delta x}$

Based on the definition, we find:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f^{\prime}(0)=\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0+\Delta x)-f(0)}{\Delta x}=\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\operatorname{arctg}\left(\Delta x \cdot \cos \left(\frac{1}{5 \Delta x}\right)\right)-0}{\Delta x}= \\
& =\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\operatorname{arctg}\left(\Delta x \cdot \cos \left(\frac{1}{5 \Delta x}\right)\right)}{\Delta x}=
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the substitution of equivalent infinitesimals:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{arctg}\left(\Delta x \cdot \cos \left(\frac{1}{5 \Delta x}\right)\right) \sim \Delta x \cdot \cos \left(\frac{1}{5 \Delta x}\right), \text { as } \\
& \Delta x \rightarrow 0\left(\Delta x \cdot \cos \left(\frac{1}{5 \Delta x}\right) \rightarrow 0\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

We get:

$$
=\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Delta x \cdot \cos \left(\frac{1}{5 \Delta x}\right)}{\Delta x}=\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \cos \left(\frac{1}{5 \Delta x}\right)_{- \text { the limit does not exist. }}
$$

Thus, $f^{\prime}(0)$ - does not exist.

problem:
6. All natural numbers, the sum of the digits of each of which is equal to 5, were arranged in ascending order. What number is in the 125th place

#
solution:
# Answer: 41000.

Solution. Let's calculate the number of $n$-digit numbers, the sum of the digits of each of which is equal to 5, for each natural $n$. Subtract 1 from the leading digit, we get a number (which can now start with zero), the sum of the digits of which is equal to 4. Represent the digits of this number as cells, in each of which there is a number of balls equal to the digit in the corresponding place. Distributing 4 balls into $n$ cells is the same as placing $n-1$ partitions between 4 balls (there may be no balls between some partitions). This can be done in $C_{n+3}^{4}=\frac{(n+3)(n+2)(n+1) n}{24}$ ways, which is also the number of the desired $n$-digit numbers.

For $n=1,2,3,4,5$, we get $C_{4}^{4}=1, C_{5}^{4}=5, C_{6}^{4}=15, C_{7}^{4}=35, C_{8}^{4}=70$, totaling 126 numbers. The 126th place is occupied by the largest such five-digit number, i.e., 50000. Therefore, the 125th place is occupied by the previous one - 41000.

The centers of the three large spheres all lie in a plane parallel to the tabletop at a distance of \(r\). They form an equilateral triangle \(\triangle M_{1} M_{2} M_{3}\) with side length \(2 r\), and let \(S\) be the centroid of this triangle.

Then \(\left|M_{1} S\right|=\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3} r\), since the centroid divides the medians in the ratio \(2: 1\) and each median in an equilateral triangle is also an altitude, whose length can be determined by applying the Pythagorean theorem as \(\sqrt{(2 r)^{2}-r^{2}}\).

Let \(M\) be the center of the fourth sphere. Since it touches the three large spheres, \(M\) must, due to symmetry, lie on the perpendicular from \(S\) to the tabletop. This forms a right triangle \(\triangle M_{1} S M\) with a right angle at \(S\).

If \(R\) is the desired radius of the fourth sphere, then on the one hand \(|S M|=r-R\), since the fourth sphere also touches the tabletop from above and the radii of all spheres perpendicular to the tabletop, including that of the fourth sphere, lie on the line \(M S\). On the other hand, the fourth and the first sphere also touch each other, so their centers \(M_{1}\) and \(M\) have the distance \(r+R\).

Substituting this into the equation given by the Pythagorean theorem for the right triangle \(\triangle M_{1} S M\), we get

\[
(r+R)^{2}=\left|M_{1} M\right|^{2}=\left|M_{1} S\right|^{2}+|S M|^{2}=\frac{4}{3} r^{2}+(r-R)^{2}
\]

or \(4 r R=(r+R)^{2}-(r-R)^{2}=\frac{4}{3} r^{2}\), and thus, due to \(r>0\), finally \(R=\frac{1}{3} r\).

problem:
[ Weighing ]

There are balance scales without weights and 3 identical-looking coins. One of the coins is counterfeit, and it is unknown whether it is lighter or heavier than the genuine coins (genuine coins weigh the same). How many weighings are needed to determine the counterfeit coin? Solve the same problem in the cases where there are 4 coins and 9 coins.

#
solution:
Note: It is required to identify the counterfeit coin, without specifying whether it is lighter or heavier than the genuine ones.

## Solution

| If we have 3 coins, two weighings are sufficient. Place one coin on each pan of the balance. If the balance is not in equilibrium, the coin that remains is genuine. Place it on the balance with any of the others, and immediately determine which one is counterfeit. If the balance is in equilibrium, the counterfeit coin is the one that remains, and the second weighing can even determine whether it is lighter or heavier than the genuine ones. If we have 4 coins, two weighings are sufficient again. Divide the coins into two piles of 2 coins each and place one of the piles on the balance - one coin on each pan. If the balance is in equilibrium, both coins on it are genuine. If the balance is not in equilibrium, both coins on the table are genuine. Thus, we now know which pile contains the counterfeit coin. Place one coin from the pile where both are genuine on one pan of the balance, and one coin from the pile where the counterfeit is on the other pan. If the balance is in equilibrium, the counterfeit coin is the one that remains on the table; if not in equilibrium, we have placed it on the balance (in this case, we will even know whether it is lighter or heavier). If we have 9 coins, three weighings are required. Divide the coins into three piles of 3 coins each and place two of these piles on the two pans of the balance. If the balance is in equilibrium, the counterfeit coin is in the remaining pile, and in two weighings (as shown in the first part of the problem), we can determine the counterfeit coin. Thus, we need a total of three weighings. Now, let the balance not be in equilibrium, meaning one of the piles on the balance contains the counterfeit coin, while the pile that remained contains only genuine ones. Place this pile on the balance and any of the first two. This way, we will not only find the pile with the counterfeit coin but also immediately determine whether it is lighter or heavier than the genuine ones. We have performed two weighings, but now we can determine the counterfeit coin with just one more weighing (as shown in the first part of the problem 49). Thus, we need a total of three weighings.

## Answer

$2 ; 2 ; 3 ; 4$.

In the region $A(x>a, y>2 a)$, the system will take the form: $\left\{\begin{array}{l}x+y=5 a \\ x+2 y=2\end{array} \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}x_{1}=10 a-2 \\ y_{1}=2-5 a\end{array}\right.\right.$. ## Taylor and Laurent Series

A function $f(z)$, which is single-valued and analytic at the point $z=z_{0}$, can be expanded in a power series of Taylor in the neighborhood of this point:

$$
f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_{n}^{\prime}\left(z-z_{0}\right)^{n}
$$

the coefficients of which $c_{n}$ are calculated by the formulas

$$
c_{n}=\frac{1}{2 \pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(z) d z}{\left(z-z_{0}\right)^{n+1}}=\frac{f^{(n)}\left(z_{0}\right)}{n!} \quad(n=0,1,2, \ldots)
$$

where $\Gamma$ is a circle centered at the point $z=z_{0}$, entirely lying in the neighborhood of the point $z_{0}$, where the function $f(z)$ is analytic. The center of the circle of convergence is at the point $z_{0}$; this circle passes through the singular point $\zeta$ of the function $f(z)$, closest to the point $z_{0}$, i.e., the radius of convergence of the series (8) will be equal to the distance from the point $z_{0}$ to the nearest singular point of the function $f(z)$.

For the functions

$$
\ln (1+z), \quad(1+z)^{\alpha}
$$

the following Taylor series expansions in the neighborhood of the point $z_{0 .}=0$ are valid:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln (1+z) & =z-\frac{z^{2}}{2}+\frac{z^{3}}{3}-\ldots+(-1)^{n-1} \frac{z^{n}}{n}+\ldots \quad(R=1) \\
(1+z)^{\alpha} & =1+\alpha z+\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}{2!} z^{2}+\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)}{3!} z^{3}+\ldots \\
& \cdots+\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1) \ldots(\alpha+n-1)}{n!} z^{n}+\ldots \quad(R=1)
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, for $\alpha=-1$ we get

$$
\frac{1}{1+z}=1-z+z^{2}-\ldots+(-1)^{n} z^{n}+\ldots \quad(R=1)
$$

Formula (10) gives the Taylor series expansion in the neighborhood of the point $z=0$ of the principal value of the logarithm; to obtain the Taylor series for other values of the multivalued function $\operatorname{Ln}(1+z)$, one should add the numbers $2 n \pi i, n= \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots$ to the series (10):

$$
\ln (1+z)=z-\frac{z^{2}}{2}+\frac{z^{3}}{3}-\ldots+2 n \pi i
$$

where $n_{5}$ denotes the nearest multiple of five to the number $n$, for example, $(-3)_{5}=-5$.
solution:
1. Based on the remainder when the number $x$ is divided by 5, we can distinguish five cases: (i) $x=5k$, (ii) $x=5k+1$, (iii) $x=5k+2$, (iv) $x=5k+3$ and (v) $x=5k+4$ ($k$ denotes any integer). Since the left side of the equation is clearly a multiple of five for every integer $x$, at least one of the factors $3x-2, x+2$ on the right side must be a multiple of five. The number $3x-2$ is divisible by five only for $x=5k+4$, and the number $x+2$ only for $x=5k+3$. Therefore, it suffices to analyze cases (iv) and (v) ($L$ denotes the left and $P$ the right side of the given equation):

(iv) For $x=5k+3$, we have $x^2=25k^2+30k+9$, $(x^2)_5=25k^2+30k+10$, $3x=15k+9$, $(3x)_5=15k+10$, $L=75k^2+105k+40$ and $P=75k^2+110k+35$, so from $L=P$ we get $k=1$, which corresponds to $x=5+3=8$.

(v) For $x=5k+4$, we have $x^2=25k^2+40k+16$, $(x^2)_5=25k^2+40k+15$, $3x=15k+12$, $(3x)_5=15k+10$, $L=75k^2+135k+55$ and $P=75k^2+140k+60$, so from $L=P$ we get $k=-1$, which corresponds to $x=-5+4=-1$.

Answer: The given equation has exactly two integer solutions, namely $x=-1$ and $x=8$.

For a complete solution, award 6 points (even if the student correctly analyzes all possibilities (i)-(v)), in other cases award 1 point for each correct solution, 2 points for justifying that $x$ is of the form $5k+3$ or $5k+4$.

problem: 454. Several identical boxes together weigh 10 tons, with each of them weighing no more than 1 ton. What is the minimum number of three-ton trucks needed to haul away all this cargo in one trip?
solution:
$\triangle$ Four trucks may not be enough. For example, if there are 13 identical boxes weighing $\frac{10}{13}$ tons each, then in one of the trucks, you cannot place more than three boxes, because with four boxes, the weight is $4 \cdot \frac{10}{13}$ tons, which is more than 3 tons. In this case, with four trucks, you can transport no more than 12 boxes out of 13.

Five trucks are sufficient in all cases. Indeed, we can load at least 2 tons of cargo into each truck: if less than 2 tons are loaded, then you can add another box (or boxes) since each box weighs no more than one ton by the condition. Therefore, with five trucks, you can load at least 10 tons of cargo.

Answer: 5.

problem: Given the square $A B C D$. What is the set of points $M$ in the plane of the square for which the sum of the areas of triangles $M A C$ and $M B D$ is equal to the area of the square?
solution:
I. solution. Let the side of the square be $a$. Let $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from a point $M$ in the plane to the lines $AC$ and $BD$, respectively, and let $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ be the distances $MM_{1}$ and $MM_{2}$, respectively!

# 1986-05-211-1.eps 

Figure 1

Then, according to the conditions, the point $M$ belongs to the desired set if and only if

$$
\frac{a \cdot \sqrt{2} \cdot m_{1}}{2}+\frac{a \cdot \sqrt{2} \cdot m_{2}}{2}=a^{2}
$$

or equivalently,

$$
m_{1}+m_{2}=a \cdot \sqrt{2}
$$

Thus, we are looking for the points in the plane whose distances from the lines $AC$ and $BD$ sum up to $a \cdot \sqrt{2}$.

The lines $AC$ and $BD$ divide the plane into four regions; these regions are mapped onto each other by $90^{\circ}$ rotations around the intersection point $O$ of the two lines. Therefore, it suffices to determine the points of the desired set in the quadrant bounded by the rays $OB$ and $OC$.

Let $M$ be an arbitrary point in this quadrant. Let the line through $M$ parallel to $BC$ intersect the rays $OB$ and $OC$ at points $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$, respectively! Then $M M_{1}=M_{1} C_{1}$ and $M M_{2}=M_{1} O$, so $m_{1}+m_{2}=O C_{1}$. Therefore, the point $M$ belongs to the desired set if and only if $O C_{1}=a \cdot \sqrt{2}$. Since $O C=\frac{a \cdot \sqrt{2}}{2}$, this is true if and only if $M$ lies on the image of the segment $BC$ under a dilation centered at $O$ with a ratio of $2:1$. Thus, taking into account the $90^{\circ}$ rotations around $O$, the desired set is the perimeter of the square obtained by dilating the square $ABCD$ from the center $O$ with a ratio of $2:1$.

Remark. If the point $M$ is one of the vertices of the dilated square, then one of the triangles $MAC$ and $MBD$ degenerates, having an area of 0. If we do not consider this a triangle, then the vertices of the dilated square must be excluded from the desired set.

II. solution. Let $M$ be an arbitrary point in the plane, and reflect $M$ over the center $O$ of the square (we can assume $M \neq O$). If $M^{\prime}$ denotes the reflection, then the line $M M^{\prime}$ must intersect two opposite sides of the square. Let these sides be $AB$ and $CD$. This means that $M$ is in one of the right-angle sectors $COD$ (including the boundary lines).

Due to the reflection,

$$
M A C=M M^{\prime} C \quad \text { and } \quad M B D=M M^{\prime} D
$$

Thus, the points $M$ in the sector $COD$ belong to the desired set if and only if the area of the quadrilateral $M D M^{\prime} C$ is equal to the area of the square.

The desired set can only have points outside the square, since for interior or boundary points, the quadrilateral $M D M^{\prime} C$ is a proper subset of the square (Figure 2a).

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text { 1986-05-212-1.eps } \\
2a \text { figure }
\end{gathered}
$$

$1986-05-212-2$. eps

$2b$ figure

If $M$ and thus $M^{\prime}$ are external points, then the area of the quadrilateral will be equal to the area of the square if and only if the sum of the distances from $M$ and $M^{\prime}$ to the common side $DC$ of the square - as the sum of the heights of the triangles $MDC$ and $M^{\prime}DC$ - is exactly twice the side length of the square (Figure 2b).

Due to symmetry, this sum of the two heights is exactly twice the distance from $M$ to $DC$ (or $AB$) minus the side length of the square. Thus, $M$ belongs to the part of the desired set in the sector $COD$ if and only if the distance from $M$ to $DC$ (or $AB$) is equal to half the side length of the square and $M$ is outside the square. This way, we obtain exactly the set found in the first solution, specifically the part of that set in the sectors $COD$ (Figure 3). The desired set is obtained by repeating the above reasoning for the sector $COB$.

problem: Task B-4.3. Determine the complex number $z^{3}$, if the imaginary part of the number $z$ is equal to $-\frac{1}{3}$ and if the argument of the number $z$ is equal to $\frac{7 \pi}{6}$.
solution:
Solution. Let $z=a+bi$, argument $z=\varphi$, then $b=-\frac{1}{3}$ and $\varphi=\frac{7 \pi}{6}$.

From $\operatorname{tg} \varphi=\frac{b}{a}$ we get $a=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$.

(1 point)

Since $|z|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}=\frac{2}{3}$, we have

$$
z^{3}=|z|^{3}(\cos 3 \varphi+i \sin 3 \varphi)
$$

or

$$
z^{3}=\frac{8}{27}\left(\cos \frac{7 \pi}{2}+i \sin \frac{7 \pi}{2}\right)=-\frac{8}{27} i
$$

problem: For each real number $m$, the function $f(x)=x^{2}-2 m x+8 m+4$ has a minimum value. What is the maximum of these minimum values?
solution:
A quadratic function of the form $f(x)=a x^{2}+b x+c$ with $a>0$ attains its minimum when $x=-\frac{b}{2 a}$.

One way to see this is to complete the square to get

$$
f(x)=a\left(x+\frac{b}{2 a}\right)^{2}+\frac{4 a c-b^{2}}{4 a}
$$

and note that since $a\left(x+\frac{b}{2 a}\right)^{2}$ is nonnegative, the minimum will occur when this quantity equals 0 .

In a similar way, if $a<0$, the function attains its maximum when $x=-\frac{b}{2 a}$.

For $f(x)=x^{2}-2 m x+8 m+4$, the minimum occurs when $x=-\frac{-2 m}{2}=m$. The minimum value of $f(x)$ is therefore

$$
f(m)=m^{2}-2 m(m)+8 m+4=-m^{2}+8 m+4
$$

This is a quadratic function in the variable $m$ with a negative leading coefficient.

Therefore, the maximum occurs when $m=-\frac{8}{2(-1)}=4$.

The maximum of these minimum values is $-4^{2}+8(4)+4=20$.

ANSWER: 20

problem:
3. $n$ is a positive integer, $A$ is a set of subsets of the set $\{1,2, \cdots, n\}$, such that no element of $A$ contains another element of $A$. Find the maximum number of elements in $A$.
(1994 Bulgarian Olympiad Problem)
solution:
3. Consider the permutations of $n$ elements $1,2, \cdots, n$. Clearly, the number of such permutations is $n!$. Let $A$ contain $f_{k}$ $k$-element subsets as elements, where $f_{k}(k=1,2, \cdots, n)$ are non-negative integers, then $|A|=\sum_{k=1}^{n} f_{k}$.

When $f_{k}>0$, for any $k$-element subset $\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{k}\right\}$ among the $f_{k}$ $k$-element subsets, in the permutations of $1,2, \cdots, n$, the permutations that exactly form the subset $\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{k}\right\}$ are $k!(n-k)!$ in number. Since any two elements in $A$ are distinct, the permutations obtained by the above method for all elements in $A$ are necessarily distinct. Therefore, we have $\sum_{k=1}^{n} f_{k} \cdot k!(n- \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{f_{k}}{C_{n}^{k}}=C_{n}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor} \cdot \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{k=1}^{n} f_{k} \cdot k!(n-k)!\leqslant C_{n}^{\left\{\frac{n}{2}\right]}$. When $A$ is the set of all $\left[\frac{n}{2}\right]$-element subsets of $\{1,2, \cdots, n\}$, it exactly reaches $|A|=C_{n}^{\left\{\frac{n}{2}\right]}$. In summary, the maximum number of elements in $A$ is $C_{n}^{\left[\frac{n}{2}\right)}$ (where $\left[\frac{n}{2}\right]$ denotes the greatest integer not exceeding $\frac{n}{2}$).

problem: From point $M$, an ant crawls along a plane at a constant speed. Its path is a spiral that winds around point $O$ and is homothetic to some part of itself relative to this point. Will the ant be able to complete its entire path in a finite time?
solution: An ant travels the entire path along a spiral from $M$ to $O$ in a finite time. Indeed, if the homothety coefficient $k<1$, and the ant spends time $t$ on the first turn, then on the remaining turns it will spend time $k t, k^{2} t$, $k^{3} t, \ldots$; therefore, the time for the entire path is $t\left(1+k+k^{2}+\ldots\right)=\frac{t}{1-k}$.

problem: Task 1. Given is a square board. Parallel to the sides and lines (7 lines in each direction) are drawn, which divide the board into 64 rectangular fields. These fields are colored in a checkerboard pattern. Their sizes can be different, but it is known that the ratio of the area of each white field to the area of each black field does not exceed 2. Find the maximum possible value of the ratio of the total area of the white fields to the total area of the black fields.
solution:
Solution: Let's consider the rectangles into which the board is divided by the second, fourth, and sixth vertical and horizontal lines. Each of these 16 rectangles contains four chess-colored rectangles. For each of the 16 rectangles, we will prove that the ratio of the total area of the white fields to the total area of the black fields does not exceed $\frac{5}{4}$.

Let a rectangle $a \times b$ be divided into four chess-colored rectangles, and let one of the white rectangles have dimensions $x \times y$. Then the other white rectangle has dimensions $(a-x) \times (b-y)$, and the dimensions of the black rectangles are $(a-x) \times y$ and $x \times (b-y)$. From the condition that the area of each white field does not exceed twice the area of each black field, we get

$$
\frac{a}{3} \leq x \leq \frac{2a}{3}, \quad \frac{b}{3} \leq y \leq \frac{2b}{3}
$$

Then the inequality

$$
(3x - 2a)(3y - b) + (3y - 2b)(3x - a) \leq 0
$$

holds, which is equivalent to

$$
xy + (a-x)(b-y) \leq \frac{5}{4}((a-x)y + x(b-y))
$$

i.e., the total area of the white fields does not exceed $\frac{5}{4}$ of the total area of the black fields.

Since for each of the 16 rectangles the ratio of the total area of the white fields to the total area of the black fields does not exceed $\frac{5}{4}$, this property holds for the entire board.

The value $\frac{5}{4}$ is achieved by dividing the board into 16 equal squares and for each of them choosing $x = \frac{a}{3}$ and $y = \frac{b}{3}$.

problem: 6. Let $S$ be the set of points inside and on the boundary of a regular hexagon with side length 1. Find the smallest $r$ such that there exists a way to three-color the points in $S$ so that the distance between any two points of the same color is less than $r$.
solution:
6. $r_{\min }=\frac{3}{2}$.

On one hand, construct the following coloring: let the regular hexagon $A B C D E F$, with center $O$. Draw perpendiculars from $O$ to $A F$, $B C$, and $D E$, with feet at $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ respectively. Color the three regions marked in the diagram with colors I, II, and III respectively. Specifically, points $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are colored with colors I, II, and III respectively (the points at the intersections of the regions can be colored with the color of either adjacent region).

In this way, the maximum distance between any two points in the same region is $X Y=Y Z=Z X=\frac{3}{2}$, and this maximum value is not achieved by two points in the same region.
Therefore, the distance between any two points of the same color is less than $\frac{3}{2}$, meaning $r=\frac{3}{2}$ is feasible.
Next, we prove that when $r<\frac{3}{2}$, a contradiction arises. Consider a circle of radius $r$ centered at a point $A$. For any point $B$ on the circle, there exists a positive $\varepsilon$ such that if $A^{\prime}$ is another point on the circle satisfying $A A^{\prime}<\varepsilon$, then $A B>r$, $A^{\prime} B>r$, and $A A^{\prime}<\varepsilon$. Since $A$ and $B$ are colored differently, and $A^{\prime}$ and $B$ are also colored differently, $A^{\prime}$ must be colored the same as $A$. Therefore, any two points within a distance of $\varepsilon$ must be colored the same, leading to the entire circle being colored the same, which is a contradiction! Thus, $r$ must not be less than $\frac{3}{2}$.
In conclusion, $r_{\min }=\frac{3}{2}$.

problem: 6. In her fourth year at Hogwarts, Hermione was outraged by the infringement of house-elf rights and founded the Association for the Restoration of Elven Independence. Of course, even the brightest and noblest idea requires funding for promotion, so Hermione decided to finance her campaign by producing merchandise, starting with the production of badges. Everyone at Hogwarts liked this idea, and Hermione secured the right to produce such badges by obtaining the relevant patent. Ron, who has known the nuances of magical technologies since childhood, convinced Hermione that the cost of producing badges would be $T C(Q)=5 Q^{2}$, where $Q$ is the number of badges produced. Harry, with the help of his friends and the time-turner potion, found out that the demand for badges from students of all houses except Slytherin can be represented by the demand function $q_{w s}=26-2 P$, and from Slytherin by the demand function $q_{s}=10-P$ (Slytherin students are prejudiced against ideas from Gryffindors, especially those of Muggle descent, but would not refuse to support the Association). What is the maximum amount Hermione can earn for her company by selling badges if the prices for the same product for different Hogwarts houses must be the same?
solution:
# Solution:

Since the prices must be the same for the faculties, Hermione Monopolist must take into account the aggregate demand for badges, which is given by:

$$
Q(P)=q_{w s}+q_{s}=\left\{\begin{array}{l}
26-2 P, P \geq 13 \\
36-3 P, P<13
\end{array}\right.
$$

Then the marginal revenue of Hermione's monopoly is given by:

$$
M R(Q)=(P(Q) Q)^{\prime}=\left\{\begin{array}{c}
13-Q, Q \leq 6 \\
12-2 Q / 3, Q>6
\end{array}\right.
$$

Since the marginal revenue of Hermione's monopoly is decreasing, and the marginal costs are increasing, the maximum profit of Hermione's enterprise will be achieved when $M R\left(Q^{*}\right)=M C\left(Q^{*}\right)$. Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M R\left(Q^{*}\right)=M C\left(Q^{*}\right) \\
& \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
13-Q=10 Q, \quad Q=13 / 11 \leq 6 \\
12-\frac{2 Q}{3}=10 Q, \quad Q=\frac{9}{8}, \text { which does not satisfy the condition } Q>6
\end{array}\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, only students from all faculties except Slytherin will buy the product.

In this case, $\frac{13}{11}$ units of the product will be sold at a price of $P=13-\frac{13}{22}=\frac{273}{22}$

It should be noted that the problem does not specify the units in which the quantity of badges is measured (for example, it could be pairs, tens, dozens, etc.).

Then the Association will earn $\frac{13}{11} * \frac{273}{22}-5 *\left(\frac{13}{11}\right)^{2} \approx 7.682$

## Criteria:

15 points for a fully justified solution.

10 points for a solution with incomplete justification. (The most common deficiency: the participant did not explain on which segment of the piecewise-defined demand to look for the solution to the optimization problem.)

5 points for an incomplete solution. (The most common deficiencies: the participant solved the problem by trying integer values of quantity, the participant did not take into account that the aggregate demand for badges is a piecewise-defined function.) 0 points for an incorrect solution.

The lack of justification for the sufficiency of the conditions for obtaining the maximum of the function was penalized by 1 point.

Rounding the final answer to an integer value is penalized by 1 point.

problem: Problem 3. There were several whole cheese heads on the warehouse. At night, rats came and ate 10 heads, and everyone ate equally. Several rats got stomachaches from overeating. The remaining 7 rats the next night finished off the remaining cheese, but each rat could eat only half as much cheese as the night before. How much cheese was originally on the warehouse? [5 points] (A.D. Blyunkov, I. V. Raskina)
solution:
Answer: 11 cheese heads

Solution: Let the total number of rats be $k$ ( $k>7$ ), then each rat ate $10 / k$ cheese heads on the first night. On the second night, each rat ate half as much, that is, $5 / k$ cheese heads. Thus, the 7 rats ate a total of $35 / k$ cheese heads. This is an integer. The only divisor of the number 35 that exceeds $7$ is the number 35 itself. Therefore, $35 / k=1$, and the total number of cheese heads on the warehouse before the rat invasion was $10+1=11$ cheese heads.

problem: Let $(x, y, z, t) \in\left(\mathbb{N}^{*}\right)^{4}$ be a quadruplet satisfying $x+y=z+t$ and $2 x y=z t$, and such that $x \geqslant y$. Find the largest value of $m$ such that $m \leqslant x / y$ for sure.
solution:
The first equation squared minus four times the second gives

$$
\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^{2}-6\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)+1=\left(\frac{z-t}{y}\right)^{2}
$$

The left-hand side is a quadratic in $x / y$, which is positive given the right-hand side. Note that $x / y > 1$ according to the problem statement. The function $g: m \mapsto m^{2}-6 m+1$ is negative for $1 \leqslant m \leqslant r_{1}$ and positive for $m \geqslant r_{1}$, where $r_{1}=3+2 \sqrt{2}$ is the larger root of the quadratic. Therefore, $x / y \geqslant 3+2 \sqrt{2}$. It remains to show that there exist solutions such that $\frac{z-t}{y}$ is arbitrarily small, which will imply that $x / y$ is arbitrarily close to $r_{1}$. Note that this is not due to the continuity of $g$, but to the fact that for any $\delta>0$, there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that if $w>r_{1}+\delta, g(w)>\varepsilon$ (exercise: prove this) and we will have shown that $m=3+2 \sqrt{2}$.

We revisit the statement: the first equation squared minus two times the second gives

$$
(x-y)^{2}=z^{2}+t^{2}
$$

Without loss of generality, we can assume $\operatorname{gcd}(x-y, z, t)=1$, and that $t$ is even. A useful theorem on Pythagorean triples (proof left to the reader) states that there exist $a>b$ coprime such that

$$
x-y=a^{2}-b^{2}, t=2 a b, z=a^{2}-b^{2}
$$

up to swapping $z$ and $t$. With $x+y=z+t$, we get $y=b(a-b)$. Can we have $z-t=1$? This amounts to solving $a^{2}-b^{2}-2 a b=1$, or $(a-b)^{2}-2 b^{2}=1$. The Pell equation $M^{2}-2 N^{2}=1$ has infinitely many solutions, so for $b=N$ and $a=N+M, z-t=1$. Moreover, $y=M N$ can be arbitrarily large, in which case $\frac{z-t}{y}=\frac{1}{M N}$ is arbitrarily small, which concludes the proof.

problem:
## Task B-1.1.

Solve the inequality in the set of real numbers

$$
\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{x-1}}} \leqslant 2019
$$
solution:
## Solution.

The condition for the solution of the given inequality is $x-1 \neq 0$ and $1+\frac{1}{x-1} \neq 0,1$, that is, $x \neq 0$ and $x \neq 1$.

By simplifying the left side of the inequality, we sequentially obtain

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{\frac{x}{x-1}}} \leqslant 2019 . & 1 \text{ point} \\
\frac{1}{1-\frac{x-1}{x}} \leqslant 2019 . & \\
\frac{1}{\frac{x-x+1}{x}} \leqslant 2019 . & 1 \text{ point } \\
&
\end{array}
$$

Thus, $x \leqslant 2019$.

Finally, the solution to the given inequality is $x \in (-\infty, 2019] \setminus \{0,1\}$.

problem: 10. (5 points) Arrange 6 balls in a row, where balls 1, 2, and 3 are black, and balls 4, 5, and 6 are white, as shown in Figure 1. If balls 2 and 5 are swapped, the 6 balls will be arranged in an alternating black and white pattern, as shown in Figure 2. Now, there are 20 balls arranged in a row in sequence, with balls 1 to 10 being black and balls 11 to 20 being white. If we want to arrange these 20 balls in an alternating black and white pattern, what is the minimum number of swaps required? $\qquad$
solution:
【Analysis】From the problem, we know that 6 balls (3 black, 3 white) only need to swap the middle two balls once to form a black and white alternating arrangement, i.e., the middle 2 balls remain unchanged, and the remaining 4 balls need to be swapped once. Therefore, these 4 balls can be considered as one cycle. 
If we want to arrange 20 balls (10 black, 10 white) in a black and white alternating pattern, apart from the middle 2 balls, there are \(20-2=18\) balls left. \(18 \div 4=4\) (times) \(\cdots 2\) (balls), so we know that the minimum number of swaps required is \(4+1=5\) times; according to this, we can solve the problem.
【Solution】Solution: 6 balls (3 black, 3 white), the middle 2 balls remain unchanged, and the remaining 4 balls need to be swapped once,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
20-2=18 \text { (balls) } \\
18 \div 4=4 \text { (times) } \cdots 2 \text { (balls) } \\
4+1=5 \text { (times) }
\end{array}
$$

Answer: The minimum number of swaps required to arrange 20 balls in a black and white alternating pattern is 5 times.
The answer is: 5.
【Comment】The key to solving this problem is to understand that for every 6 balls (3 black, 3 white), only the middle two balls need to be swapped once to form a black and white alternating arrangement, i.e., to consider these 4 balls as one cycle, and solve it as a periodic problem.

problem: 7. Find $(x+1)\left(x^{2}+1\right)\left(x^{4}+1\right)\left(x^{8}+1\right) \cdots$, where $|x|<1$.

problem:
For what values of $t$ is the two-variable operation $x * y=x+y+t \sqrt{x y}$, defined on positive numbers, associative?

---

The translation maintains the original text's format and line breaks as requested.
solution:
We can only speak of an operation if for all $x, y > 0$, $x * y > 0$ is satisfied, that is,

$$
x + y + t \sqrt{x y} > 0, \quad t > -\left(\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}} + \sqrt{\frac{y}{x}}\right)
$$

This is precisely satisfied for all positive pairs $(x, y)$ if $t > -2$.

The desired identity $(x * y) * z = x * (y * z)$ clearly holds if $t = 0$. If $t \neq 0$, then it is equivalent to the identity

$$
\sqrt{x y} + \sqrt{x z + y z + t \sqrt{x y} z} = \sqrt{y z} + \sqrt{x y + x z + t \sqrt{y z} x}
$$

Testing with the values $x = 4, y = z = 1$:

$2 + \sqrt{5 + 2 t} = 1 + \sqrt{8 + 4 t}, \quad 1 + \sqrt{5 + 2 t} = \sqrt{8 + 4 t} .6 + 2 t + 2 \sqrt{5 + 2 t} = 8 + 4 t, \quad \sqrt{5 + 2 t} = 1 + t, \quad 5 + 2 t = 1 + 2 t + t^{2}, \quad 4 = t^{2}$.

Thus, apart from $t = 0$, only $t = 2$ is possible. In the latter case, $x * y = x + y + 2 \sqrt{x y} = (\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y})^{2}$, so indeed $(x * y) * z = (\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} + \sqrt{z})^{2} = x * (y * z)$. The requirements of the problem are only satisfied by the values $t = 0$ and 2.

David Papp (Budapest, Szent István Gymnasium, 11th grade)
