problem: 197. The device consists of $n$ elements. The probability of failure of any element during the experiment is $p$. Find the mathematical expectation of the number of such experiments, in each of which exactly $m$ elements will fail, if a total of $\boldsymbol{N}$ experiments are conducted. It is assumed that the experiments are independent of each other.
solution:
Solution. Let $X$ be the number of trials in which exactly $m$ elements will fail. Since the trials are independent and the probability of the event of interest (exactly $\boldsymbol{m}$ elements will fail in one trial) is the same in these trials, the formula

$$
M(X)=N P
$$

can be applied, where $N$ is the total number of trials; $P$ is the probability that exactly $m$ elements will fail in one trial.

We will find the probability $P$ using the Bernoulli formula:

$$
P=C_{n}^{m} p^{m} q^{n-m}
$$

Substituting (**) into (*), we obtain the desired expected value:

$$
M(X)=N C_{n}^{m} p^{m} q^{n-m}
$$

In how many ways can the network of the solid examined in Exercise 1120[² be constructed so that the total length of the edges to be joined is seven times the length of the original cube edge? We do not consider two networks different if they only differ in the pairwise exchange of letters.[^0]


[^0]:    ${ }^{2}$ K. M. L. $36(1968) 64$. o.
solution:
The solid in question was formed from a cube defined by the base $A B C D$ and the side edges $A E, B F, C G, D H$, by cutting out the triangular pyramids $A D G H$ and $B C E F$ (Figure 1).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_4356800a3f5f4dca0700g-1.jpg?height=526&width=542&top_left_y=274&top_left_x=778)

Figure 1

We observed that the total length of the edges to be glued in the net is shortest - exactly 7 cube edges, if only the original cube edges are left as glueable, in other words, if the edges resulting from the 4 face diagonals and 2 space diagonals of the cube are formed by folding the paper in the net.

Accordingly, the combined set of the $A B E, B E C, E C F$, and $C F G$ triangular faces remains connected, and the same applies to the combined set of the mirror images of these faces with respect to the center $O$ of the cube (the common midpoint of the diagonals $C E, A G$, and the edges). Let's call these combined sets of faces complexes. When these complexes are unfolded, their boundary lines form a centrally symmetric hexagon with a side length of one cube edge, $A B C G F E=\mathrm{I}$, and $C D A E H G=\mathrm{II}$, which are congruent to each other. The first three angles (in the order of the vertices) are $90^{\circ}, 135^{\circ}, 135^{\circ}$. Thus, we only need to examine how the two complexes and the $A B C D=I I I, E F G H=I V$ square faces can be connected to form a net, or in other words, how the 3 cube edges (out of the 10 remaining on the solid) that are formed by folding the paper can be chosen.

We note that the line passing through $O$ and parallel to $A E$ is a rotational symmetry axis of the solid, a $180^{\circ}$ rotation about this axis maps the solid onto itself, swapping the vertex pairs $(A, C),(B, D),(E, G),(F, H)$, and also swapping I with II. Similarly, the line passing through the midpoints of the edges $A E$ and $C G$ is also a symmetry axis, a $180^{\circ}$ rotation about this line swaps the two complexes and also the two square faces.

First, we consider nets where I and II are adjacent. Their common edges, $A E$ and $C G$, can be mapped onto each other by the first symmetry, so it is sufficient to examine the case where the connecting edge is $A E$ (Figure 2).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_4356800a3f5f4dca0700g-1.jpg?height=441&width=640&top_left_y=1601&top_left_x=710)

Figure 2

Their combined set is centrally symmetric about the midpoint $K$ of the segment $A E$. The III square face connects along one of the edges $3_{1}, 3_{2}, 3_{3}, 3_{4}$, and the IV square face similarly along one of the edges $4_{1}, 4_{2}, 4_{3}, 4_{4}$. Choosing the connecting edges independently, $4 \cdot 4=16$ pairings can be thought of.

However, among these, the pairings $3_{i}, 4_{j}$ and $3_{j}, 4_{i}$ (where $i$ and $j$ are different indices from 1, 2, 3, 4) are not distinct, as they can be rotated into each other about $K$. The choice $3_{i} 4_{i}$, on the other hand, gives a different net for each value of $i$. The number of such pairings is 4, and of the remaining 12 pairings, only half, 6, are distinct.

Moving on, if I and II are not adjacent, then one of the square faces connects to both, and by the second symmetry, it is sufficient to choose III. I and II connect to III either along two opposite sides or along two adjacent sides. There are two distinct possibilities for the former, for example, the edge $A B$ is not equivalent to the edge $B C$, as different shaped faces connect to them on the solid (Figures 3 and 4).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_4356800a3f5f4dca0700g-2.jpg?height=608&width=418&top_left_y=127&top_left_x=840)

Figure 3

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_4356800a3f5f4dca0700g-2.jpg?height=455&width=621&top_left_y=865&top_left_x=730)

Figure 4

The combined set of the I and III faces is centrally symmetric about the center of the III face in both cases, and the 4 edges (drawn thickly) suitable for connecting the IV face are pairwise images of each other. Thus, the connecting edge can be chosen in 2 ways on both figures.

If I and II connect to III along adjacent sides, the common vertex of these two sides can only be $A$ and $C$ - for example, the edges $B A$ and $B C$ both connect I to III. By the first symmetry, it is sufficient to take $A$ as the common vertex (Figure 5).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_4356800a3f5f4dca0700g-2.jpg?height=369&width=525&top_left_y=1713&top_left_x=781)

Figure 5

The combined set of the first three faces is thus not symmetric, and connecting the IV face along any of the possible edges results in a different net.

According to all this, the number of essentially different nets is $(4+6)+2+2+4=18$. We list the 3 cube edges formed by folding in these nets:

On a tower of height $b$, we see a rod of length $a$. At what distance from the tower do we see this rod at the largest angle?
solution:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_8b9c89007d32d76ebd68g-1.jpg?height=504&width=498&top_left_y=122&top_left_x=800)

I. Solution. From the diagram, it is clear that

$$
\operatorname{tg} \delta=\operatorname{tg}(\varphi-\psi)=\frac{\operatorname{tg} \varphi-\operatorname{tg} \psi}{1+\operatorname{tg} \varphi \cdot \operatorname{tg} \psi}=\frac{\frac{x}{b}-\frac{x}{a+b}}{1+\frac{x^{2}}{b(a+b)}}=\frac{a x}{b(a+b)+x^{3}}=m
$$

Rearranging,

$$
m x^{2}-a x+b(a+b) m=0
$$

Thus,

$$
x=\frac{a \pm \sqrt{a^{2}-4 b(a+b) m^{2}}}{2 m}
$$

Since \( x \) represents a distance, it must be that

$$
a^{2} \geqq 4 b(a+b) m^{2}
$$

Therefore,

$$
m_{\max }=\frac{a}{2 \sqrt{b(a+b)}}
$$

Since \( m = \operatorname{tg} \delta \), the maximum value of \( m \) also corresponds to the maximum value of \( \delta \). Thus,

$$
x=\frac{a}{\frac{a}{\sqrt{b(a+b)}}}=\sqrt{b(a+b)}
$$

So \( x \) is the geometric mean of the actual height of the tower and the height increased by the rod.

(István Pivnyik, Nyíregyháza.)

II. Solution. Let \( D \) be the desired point. The angle \( \angle BDA \) is thus a peripheral angle of the circle centered at \( O \) passing through points \( A \), \( B \), and \( D \). This angle is larger when the radius of the circumcircle of triangle \( ABD \) is smaller, given a fixed length of the chord \( AB \).

The circle with the smallest radius passing through points \( A \) and \( B \) and having a common point with the line \( CD \) is the one that is tangent to \( CD \). The angle \( \delta \) is maximized in this circle. The radius of this circle is \( BO = OD = LC = b + \frac{a}{2} \). Therefore, the desired distance is

$$
CD = LO = \sqrt{\overline{BO}^{2} - \overline{BL}^{2}} = \sqrt{b^2 + ab} = \sqrt{b(a+b)}
$$

The point \( O \) is constructed by raising a perpendicular from the midpoint \( L \) of the line \( AB \) and intersecting it with a circle of radius \( b + \frac{a}{2} \) centered at \( B \).

(Imre Bartók, Budapest.)

Example 12. Map the upper half-plane $\operatorname{Im} z>0$ onto the unit disk $|w|<1$ so that the point $z=i$ (where $\operatorname{Im} z>0$) is mapped to the center $\boldsymbol{w}=0$ of the disk.
solution:
Solution. Since the point $z_{0}$ is mapped by the sought fractional-linear function $w=w(z)$ to the center of the circle, i.e., $w\left(z_{0}\right)=0$, then the conjugate point $\bar{z}_{0}$ must be mapped to the point $w:=\infty$ (by the property of symmetry). Next, we use formula (8) and obtain

$$
w=K \frac{z-z_{0}}{z-\bar{z}_{0}}
$$

where $K$ is a constant multiplier. For any $K$, this function maps the upper half-plane to some circle centered at the point $w=0$. We choose $K$ so that the circle is the unit circle. For this, it is sufficient to require that the point $z=0$ (a boundary point of the region $\operatorname{Im} z>0$) is mapped to a point on the unit circle $|w|=1$. Then

$$
1=|w|=|K| \cdot\left|\frac{z_{0}}{\bar{z}_{0}}\right|, \quad \text { from which } \quad|K|=1, \quad \text { so that } \quad K=e^{i \alpha},
$$

where $\alpha$ is any real number. Thus,

$$
w=e^{i \alpha} \frac{z-z_{0}}{z-\bar{z}_{0}}
$$

Remark. Let's find the derivative $\boldsymbol{w}^{\prime}$ at the point $z_{0}=a+i b(b>0)$.

$$
w^{\prime}\left(z_{0}\right)=-\frac{i e^{i \alpha}}{2 b}, \quad \text { or } \quad w^{\prime}\left(z_{0}\right)=\frac{1}{2 b} e^{i \alpha} \cdot e^{-i \pi / 2}=\frac{1}{=} \frac{e^{i(\alpha-\pi / 2)}}{2 b}
$$

Thus, arg $\boldsymbol{w}_{?}^{\prime}\left(z_{0}\right)=\alpha-\frac{\pi}{2}$, so by the geometric meaning of the derivative, the angle of rotation of curves at the point $z_{0}$ is $\alpha-\frac{\pi}{2}$.

By the Riemann mapping theorem, there exists a unique mapping $w=w(z)$ of the half-plane $\operatorname{Im} z>0$ onto the circle $|w|<1$ which has the form (9).

problem:
$4 \cdot 126$ Solve the system of equations
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x+y+z=a \\
x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=b^{2} \\
x y=z^{2}
\end{array}\right.
$$

where $a, b$ are known numbers. Also, indicate the conditions that $a, b$ must satisfy for $x, y, z$ to be distinct positive numbers.
solution:
[Solution] From (1) $)^{2}-$ (2) we get $x y+y z+z x=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right)$, i.e., $\approx a=\frac{1}{2}\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right)$.
Therefore, the solution is
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x=\frac{1}{4 a}\left(a^{2}+b^{2} \pm \sqrt{10 a^{2} b^{2}-3 a^{4}-3 b^{4}}\right), \\
y=\frac{1}{4 a}\left(a^{2}+b^{2} \mp \sqrt{10 a^{2} b^{2}-3 a^{4}-3 b^{4}}\right), \\
z=\frac{1}{2 a}\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right) .
\end{array}\right.
$$

When and only when $|b|<a<\sqrt{3}|b|$, $x$, $y$, and $z$ are distinct positive numbers.

problem: 2. It is known that $\frac{\cos 3 x}{(2 \cos 2 x-1) \cos 2 y}=\frac{1}{6}+\sin ^{2}(x+2 y)$ and $\frac{\sin 3 x}{(2 \cos 2 x+1) \sin 2 y}=\frac{5}{6}+\cos ^{2}(x+2 y)$. Find all possible values of the expression $\cos (x+6 y)$, given that there are at least two. Answer: -1 or $-\frac{2}{3}$.
solution:
Solution. Note that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \cos 3 x=\cos (2 x+x)=\cos 2 x \cos x-\sin 2 x \sin x=\cos 2 x \cos x-2 \sin ^{2} x \cos x= \\
& \quad=\cos 2 x \cos x-(1-\cos 2 x) \cos x=(2 \cos 2 x-1) \cos x \\
& \sin 3 x=\sin (2 x+x)=\sin 2 x \cos x+\sin x \cos 2 x= \\
& \quad=2 \sin x \cos ^{2} x+\sin x \cos 2 x=\sin x(1+\cos 2 x)+\sin x \cos 2 x=(2 \cos 2 x+1) \sin x
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking this into account, the given equalities take the form

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\cos x}{\cos 2 y}=\frac{1}{6}+\sin ^{2}(x+2 y) \\
\frac{\sin x}{\sin 2 y}=\frac{5}{6}+\cos ^{2}(x+2 y)
\end{array}\right.
$$

(it is also necessary to take into account that $\cos 2 x \neq \pm \frac{1}{2}$). Adding the equations (??) we get $\frac{\cos x}{\cos 2 y}+$ $\frac{\sin x}{\sin 2 y}=2$, from which $\cos 2 y \neq 0, \sin 2 y \neq 0$ and $\cos x \sin 2 y+\sin x \cos 2 y=2 \sin 2 y \cos 2 y$. The last equality is equivalent to the following:

$$
\sin (x+2 y)=\sin 4 y \Leftrightarrow\left[\begin{array} { l } 
{ x + 2 y = 4 y + 2 \pi k } \\
{ x + 2 y = \pi - 4 y + 2 \pi k , k \in \mathbb { Z } }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left[\begin{array}{l}
x=2 y+2 \pi k \\
x=\pi-6 y+2 \pi k, k \in \mathbb{Z}
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Let's consider these two possibilities separately.

If $x=2 y+2 \pi k, k \in \mathbb{Z}$, then the system (??) takes the form $\left\{\begin{array}{l}1=\frac{1}{6}+\sin ^{2} 4 y, \\ 1=\frac{5}{6}+\cos ^{2} 4 y ;\end{array} \quad\right.$ from which $\sin ^{2} 4 y=\frac{5}{6}$, $\cos ^{2} 4 y=\frac{1}{6}$. It is easy to see that this system has solutions. In this case, $\cos (x+6 y)=\cos 8 y=$ $2 \cos ^{2} 4 y-1=2 \cdot \frac{1}{6}-1=-\frac{2}{3}$.

If $x=\pi-6 y+2 \pi k, k \in \mathbb{Z}$, then (??) takes the form

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ - \frac { \operatorname { c o s } 6 y } { \operatorname { c o s } 2 y } = \frac { 1 } { 6 } + \operatorname { s i n } ^ { 2 } 4 y , } \\
{ \frac { \operatorname { s i n } 6 y } { \operatorname { s i n } 2 y } = \frac { 5 } { 6 } + \operatorname { c o s } ^ { 2 } 4 y }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
3-4 \cos ^{2} 2 y=\frac{1}{6}+\sin ^{2} 4 y \\
3-4 \sin ^{2} 2 y=\frac{5}{6}+\cos ^{2} 4 y
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Each of the equations in the last system reduces to the equation $\cos ^{2} 4 y-2 \cos 4 y-\frac{1}{6}=0$, which has solutions, since $\cos 4 y=1-\sqrt{\frac{7}{6}}$. Therefore, this case is also possible, and we get that $\cos (x+6 y)=\cos (\pi+2 \pi k)=-1$.

Thus, $\cos (x+6 y)$ can be equal to $-\frac{2}{3}$ or -1.

Note that in both cases all the restrictions that appeared in connection with the domain of definition $\left(\cos 2 x \neq \pm \frac{1}{2}\right.$, $\cos 2 y \neq 0, \sin 2 y \neq 0$) are satisfied.

Remark. Since the problem states that the expression $\cos (x+6 y)$ has at least two different values, checking the possibility of the cases is not mandatory.

problem: 2. In an infinite arithmetic progression with a positive difference, the numbers 25, 41, 65 are included (not necessarily consecutively). Is the number 2017 a member of this sequence? Justify your answer.
solution:
2. Since $25, 41, 65$ are terms of an arithmetic progression, then $25=a_{1}+k d ; 41=a_{1}+n d ; 65=a_{1}+m d$, where $k, n, m$ are natural numbers. From these three equations, it follows that $16=(n-k) d, 24=(m-n) d$. From these two equations, we get:

$8=(m-2 n+k) d$. Since $2017=1+2016$, and $2016=252 \cdot 8=3 \cdot 8+249 \cdot 8=24+$ $+249 \cdot 8=24+249(m-2 n+k) d$, then $2017=1+24+249(m-2 n+k) d=25+$ $+249(m-2 n+k) d=a_{1}+k d+249(m-2 n+k) d=a_{1}+(249 m-498 n+250 k) d$ or $2017=a_{1}+l d$, where $l-$ is a positive natural number. Therefore, 2017 is a term of this sequence.

Answer: Yes, it is.

problem: 57. Decompose the number 0 into the product of two factors in all possible ways (in the sense of 10-arithmetic).
solution:
## 57. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
0=0 \cdot 0 & =0 \cdot 1=0 \cdot 2=0 \cdot 3=0 \cdot 4=0 \cdot 5=0 \cdot 6=0 \cdot 7 \approx \\
& =0 \cdot 8=0 \cdot 9=2 \cdot 5=4 \cdot 5=6 \cdot 5=8 \cdot 5 .
\end{aligned}
$$

The product of the number 0 with any number, as in ordinary arithmetic, is always zero. However, unlike in ordinary arithmetic, the product can be zero even when neither of the factors is zero. The numbers \(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 5\), which can yield zero when multiplied by a number not equal to zero, are called divisors of zero.

problem: 8. Let the positive integer $n$ satisfy $n \leq 2016$, and $\left\{\frac{n}{2}\right\}+\left\{\frac{n}{4}\right\}+\left\{\frac{n}{6}\right\}+\left\{\frac{n}{12}\right\}=3$. The number of such $n$ is $\qquad$. Here $\{x\}=x-[x]$, where $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer not exceeding $x$.
solution:
Answer: 168.
Solution: For any integer $n$, we have
$$
\left\{\frac{n}{2}\right\}+\left\{\frac{n}{4}\right\}+\left\{\frac{n}{6}\right\}+\left\{\frac{n}{12}\right\} \leq \frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{4}+\frac{5}{6}+\frac{11}{12}=3,
$$

The equality holds if and only if $n \equiv-1(\bmod 12)$. Combining with $1 \leq n \leq 2016$, we know that all the positive integers satisfying the condition are $n=12 k-1(k=1,2, \cdots, 168)$, totaling 168.

problem: 10.191. The center of the circle inscribed in a right trapezoid is at distances of 3 and 9 cm from the ends of its lateral side. Find the sides of the trapezoid.
solution:
Solution.

Given $O C=3$ cm, $O D=9$ cm (see Fig. 10.1). Let $N, P, M, E$ be the points of tangency of the circle with the sides of the trapezoid $B C, C D, A D$, $A B$ respectively. By the property of tangents:

1) $O N \perp B C, O P \perp C D, O M \perp A D$.
2) $\angle N C O=\angle P C O, \angle M D O=\angle P D O$.

Then $\angle O C D+\angle O D C=\frac{1}{2}(\angle B C D+\angle A D C)=90^{\circ} \Rightarrow \triangle C O D-$ is a right triangle, from which $C D=\sqrt{3^{2}+9^{2}}=3 \sqrt{10}$ cm. Let $r$ be the radius of the inscribed circle. $S_{\triangle C O D}=\frac{1}{2} C D \cdot O K=\frac{1}{2} O C \cdot O D$ or $3 \cdot \sqrt{10} \cdot r=3 \cdot 9$, $r=\frac{9}{\sqrt{10}}=\frac{9 \sqrt{10}}{10} \cdot$ From $\triangle C P O:$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& C P=\sqrt{O C^{2}-O P^{2}}=\sqrt{3^{2}-\frac{9^{2}}{10}}=3 \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{10}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}=\frac{3 \sqrt{10}}{10} \\
& P D=C D-C P=3 \sqrt{10}-\frac{3 \sqrt{10}}{10}=3 \sqrt{10}\left(1-\frac{1}{10}\right)=\frac{27 \sqrt{10}}{10}
\end{aligned}
$$

By the property of the tangent, $M D=P D, N C=C P$. Clearly, $B N O E$ is a square, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
& B E=B N=r=\frac{9 \sqrt{10}}{10} \cdot A B=2 r=\frac{9 \sqrt{10}}{5} \mathrm{~cm} \\
& B C=B N+C N=\frac{9 \sqrt{10}}{10}+\frac{3 \sqrt{10}}{10}=\frac{6 \sqrt{10}}{5} \mathrm{~cm} \\
& A D=A N+N D=\frac{9 \sqrt{10}}{10}+\frac{27 \sqrt{10}}{10}=\frac{18 \sqrt{10}}{5} \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: $\frac{9 \sqrt{10}}{5}, \frac{6 \sqrt{10}}{5}, 3 \sqrt{10}, \frac{18 \sqrt{10}}{5} \mathrm{~cm}$.
